The ideal string attached to the ceiling is inextensible and adjusts its tension immediately, so the upper block remains hanging at rest with $T = mg$ and zero net force — its acceleration is 0. (The lower block, in contrast, falls with acceleration $g$.)

questions.question: Block A (16 kg) rests on a frictionless horizontal floor and block B (4 kg) is held against its vertical face. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to the system so that both blocks accelerate together and block B does not slide down. The coefficient of friction between the two blocks is 0.5. The minimum magnitude of $F$ is:
questions.solution: Principles: Newton's second law for the system; static friction supporting block B. Both blocks accelerate together with $a = \dfrac{F}{m_A+m_B}$. For B not to fall, the normal force from A provides the friction; the available friction must hold B's weight: $\mu N = \mu m_B a \ge m_B g \Rightarrow a \ge \dfrac{g}{\mu}$. Minimum acceleration: $a_{min} = \dfrac{g}{0.5} = 2g \approx 20$ m/s$^2$. $F_{min} = (m_A+m_B)\dfrac{g}{\mu} = 20 \times \dfrac{g}{0.5} = 40g$. With $g \approx 10$ m/s$^2$: $F_{min} = 400$ N (with $g = 9.8$: 392 N). $\boxed{F_{min} \approx 400\ \text{N}}$

questions.question: A rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ lies along the x-axis with one end at the origin. Its linear mass density is $\lambda = \dfrac{2M}{L^2}x$, where $x$ is the distance from the origin. The x-coordinate of the rod's center of mass is:
questions.solution: Principle: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{M}\int x\,dm$ with $dm = \lambda\,dx$. Check the normalization: $\int_0^L \dfrac{2M}{L^2}x\,dx = \dfrac{2M}{L^2}\cdot\dfrac{L^2}{2} = M$. $x_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{M}\int_0^L x\cdot\dfrac{2M}{L^2}x\,dx = \dfrac{2}{L^2}\int_0^L x^2\,dx = \dfrac{2}{L^2}\cdot\dfrac{L^3}{3} = \dfrac{2L}{3}$. The center of mass is shifted toward the dense (far) end, as expected for density growing with $x$. $\boxed{x_{cm} = 2L/3}$

questions.question: Two identical blocks (each of mass $m$) are connected by a light spring. The combination is suspended at rest from a string attached to the ceiling. The string suddenly breaks. Immediately after the string breaks, the downward acceleration of the upper block is
questions.solution: While hanging at rest, the lower block is held up by the spring, so the spring tension is $mg$ (spring stretched). The string held both blocks: $T = 2mg$. Immediately after the string breaks, the spring force cannot change instantaneously, so the upper block still feels the spring pulling it down with $mg$ (Newton's third law pair) plus its weight $mg$ down: $a = (mg + mg)/m = 2g$. (The lower block: spring up $mg$, weight down $mg$, so $a=0$.) Final answer: $\boxed{2g}$ (option E).

questions.question: Ridwan and Titumir start running in the same direction with velocities 5 m/s and 6 m/s respectively. Suddenly Titumir sees Gautam running towards them with a velocity of 5 m/s (as measured by Titumir). What is the velocity of Ridwan relative to Gautam?
questions.solution: Take the running direction as $+x$: $v_R = 5$ m/s, $v_T = 6$ m/s. Titumir sees Gautam approaching at 5 m/s: $v_G - v_T = -5 \Rightarrow v_G = 6 - 5 = 1$ m/s (Gautam still moves in $+x$, but more slowly). Velocity of Ridwan relative to Gautam: $v_R - v_G = 5 - 1 = 4$ m/s. Final answer: $\boxed{4\ \mathrm{m/s}}$ (option D).

questions.question: The coefficient of static friction between a small coin and the surface of a turntable is 0.3. The turntable rotates at 33.3 rpm. What is the maximum distance from the centre of the turntable at which the coin will not slide?
questions.solution: Static friction provides the centripetal force: $\mu_s m g = m\omega^2 r \Rightarrow r_{max} = \frac{\mu_s g}{\omega^2}$. Convert: $\omega = 33.3\ \text{rpm} = 33.3\times\frac{2\pi}{60} = 3.49\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. Then $r_{max} = \frac{0.3\times 9.8}{(3.49)^2} = \frac{2.94}{12.16} \approx 0.242\ \mathrm{m}$. Final answer: $\boxed{0.242\ \mathrm{m}}$ (option D).

questions.question: Two identical blocks are connected by a spring. The combination is suspended at rest from a string attached to the ceiling. Now the SPRING breaks suddenly. Immediately after the spring breaks, the downward acceleration of the upper block is
questions.solution: Before the spring breaks, the string tension is $2mg$ and the spring tension is $mg$. When the spring breaks, the lower block goes into free fall ($a = g$). The upper block is still attached to the ceiling by the string; an ideal string can change its tension instantaneously, so the tension immediately adjusts from $2mg$ to $mg$, exactly balancing the weight. Net force on the upper block is zero: $a = 0$. (Compare: if the STRING were cut instead, the upper block would have $a = 2g$.) Final answer: $\boxed{0}$ (option A).

questions.question: Ball A is projected horizontally with velocity $u = 1$ m/s from the point $(L, H) = (20\ \mathrm{m}, 10\ \mathrm{m})$. To intercept ball A, ball B is projected from the origin with velocity $v = 5$ m/s at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, at the same instant. Find the launching angle $\theta$ of ball B (in degrees).
questions.solution: Both balls fall with the same acceleration $g$, so the vertical separation obeys: $10 - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = (5\sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \Rightarrow 5\sin\theta\,t = 10$, i.e. $t = \frac{2}{\sin\theta}$. Horizontally: $(5\cos\theta)t = 20 + 1\cdot t \Rightarrow 20 = t(5\cos\theta - 1)$. Substituting: $10\sin\theta = 5\cos\theta - 1$. Squaring ($25\cos^2\theta - 10\cos\theta + 1 = 100\sin^2\theta$) gives $125\cos^2\theta - 10\cos\theta - 99 = 0$, so $\cos\theta = \frac{10 + \sqrt{49600}}{250} = 0.9308$ (positive root), giving $\theta = 21.4^\circ$ (then $t = 5.5$ s). Final answer: $\boxed{21.4^\circ}$.

questions.question: On a trail of infinite length, an infinite number of people stand 1 m apart, all moving with the trail. A man standing on the trail throws a ball vertically upward. While the ball is in the air, the ball drifts forward and is caught by the neighbour who had been standing 1 m in front of the thrower. What can we conclude about the motion of the trail?
options: The trail is moving at constant velocity
The trail is moving with constant acceleration
questions.solution: At the moment of release, the ball shares the trail's horizontal velocity $v$. During the flight there is no horizontal force on the ball (air resistance ignored), so it keeps moving horizontally at exactly $v$. If the trail moved at constant $v$, the ball would come straight back down into the thrower's hands. If the trail were speeding up, the people would glide ahead of the ball and it would land 1 m behind the thrower (caught by the neighbour behind). For the ball to touch down 1 m AHEAD of the thrower, the people must have slid backwards relative to the ball, i.e. the trail's velocity decreased during the flight: the trail is decelerating. (A single catch only tells us the velocity decreased; it does not prove the deceleration was constant, so C is not justified.) $\boxed{\text{The trail is decelerating}}$

questions.question: An object is thrown from point O with speed $v$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, the object moves in such a way that its distance from O is always increasing. Which of the following cannot be a value of $\theta$?
options: All of the above are acceptable
questions.solution: With $x = v\cos\theta\,t$ and $y = v\sin\theta\,t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, the squared distance from O is $r^2 = x^2 + y^2 = v^2t^2 - gv\sin\theta\,t^3 + \frac{g^2t^4}{4}$. For $r$ to increase at all times we need $\frac{d(r^2)}{dt} = t\left(g^2t^2 - 3gv\sin\theta\,t + 2v^2\right) > 0$ for all $t > 0$. This quadratic in $t$ (leading coefficient $g^2 > 0$) has its minimum at $t = \frac{3v\sin\theta}{2g}$, where it equals $2v^2 - \frac{9}{4}v^2\sin^2\theta$. Requiring this to stay positive: $\sin^2\theta < \frac{8}{9}$, i.e. $\theta < 70.5^\circ$. Since $\sin^2 75^\circ \approx 0.933 > 0.889$, at $75^\circ$ the projectile would eventually fall back towards O and its distance from O would decrease before landing. For $0^\circ$ and $45^\circ$ the condition holds. $\boxed{75^\circ \text{ is not acceptable}}$

questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is placed on the ground; the coefficient of kinetic friction between block and ground is $\mu$. You pull the block with a rope of tension $F$ directed at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, and the block slides along the ground. At what angle $\theta$ (relative to the horizontal) should you pull to get the maximum acceleration of the block?
questions.solution: Vertical equilibrium (the block stays on the ground): $N = mg - F\sin\theta$, so the kinetic friction force is $f = \mu N = \mu(mg - F\sin\theta)$; pulling at an angle reduces the normal force and hence the friction. Newton's second law along the ground: $a = \frac{F\cos\theta - \mu(mg - F\sin\theta)}{m} = \frac{F}{m}\left(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta\right) - \mu g$. Only the bracket depends on $\theta$. Maximise $g(\theta) = \cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta$: $g'(\theta) = -\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \mu$, i.e. $\theta = \tan^{-1}\mu$. (There the bracket reaches its maximum $\sqrt{1+\mu^2}$; pulling more steeply loses more horizontal drive than it saves in friction, and $\theta \to 90^\circ$ lifts the block instead.) $\boxed{\theta = \tan^{-1}\mu}$

questions.question: A cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a radially dependent density. It starts from rest and rolls without slipping down an inclined plane of height $H$, reaching a translational speed $\sqrt{8gH/7}$ at the bottom. The rotational inertia of the cylinder about its axis is
questions.hint: Energy conservation: $MgH = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ with $\omega = v/R$.
questions.solution: Rolling without slipping means $\omega = v/R$. Energy conservation: $MgH = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\frac{v^2}{R^2}$. With $v^2 = \frac{8gH}{7}$, $\frac{1}{2}Mv^2 = \frac{4MgH}{7}$, so $\frac{1}{2}I\frac{v^2}{R^2} = \frac{3MgH}{7}$. Thus $I = \frac{6MgH}{7}\cdot\frac{R^2}{v^2} = \frac{6MgH}{7}\cdot\frac{7R^2}{8gH} = \frac{3}{4}MR^2$.

questions.question: A planar figure shaped like the letter 'B' is made of uniform wire: two equal semicircular arcs of radius $r$, each closed by its own straight diameter, joined so the two diameters form one common straight edge of total length $4r$. The figure is freely suspended from its top left-hand corner. What angle does the straight edge make with the vertical?
questions.solution: Principle: a freely suspended body hangs with its centre of mass vertically below the pivot. Take the origin at the midpoint of the straight edge, with the edge along the $y$-axis. Each semicircular arc (mass $\propto \pi r$) has its centre of mass at $\frac{2r}{\pi}$ from the edge; each diameter (mass $\propto 2r$) lies on the edge. Masses: upper arc at $(\frac{2r}{\pi}, r)$, lower arc at $(\frac{2r}{\pi}, -r)$, diameters at $x=0$. Total mass $\propto 2\pi r + 4r$. Then $\bar{x} = \frac{2(\pi r)(\frac{2r}{\pi})}{2\pi r + 4r} = \frac{2r}{\pi+2}$ and $\bar{y} = 0$. The pivot is the top corner, $2r$ above the midpoint. When hanging, the line pivot-to-COM is vertical, so $\tan\theta = \frac{\bar{x}}{2r} = \frac{1}{\pi+2} = 0.194$, giving $\theta \approx 11^\circ$. Final answer: $\boxed{11^\circ}$

questions.question: A solid hemisphere of uniform density has radius $R$. What is the distance of its centre of mass from the centre of its circular flat face?
questions.solution: Principle: centre of mass by integration, $\bar{z} = \frac{1}{V}\int z\,dV$. Slice the hemisphere (flat face in the $xy$-plane, dome along $+z$) into disks of thickness $dz$: $dV = \pi(R^2 - z^2)\,dz$. Then $\int_0^R z\,\pi(R^2 - z^2)\,dz = \pi\left[\frac{R^2 z^2}{2} - \frac{z^4}{4}\right]_0^R = \frac{\pi R^4}{4}$. With $V = \frac{2}{3}\pi R^3$, $\bar{z} = \frac{\pi R^4/4}{(2/3)\pi R^3} = \frac{3R}{8}$. Final answer: $\boxed{\frac{3}{8}R}$

questions.question: A massless frictionless pulley carries a light thread with bodies of mass $m$ and $2m$ attached to its ends. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the centre of mass of the two-body system?
questions.solution: Principles: Atwood machine, definition of centre-of-mass acceleration $a_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i a_i}{\sum m_i}$. The Atwood acceleration is $a = \frac{(2m - m)g}{3m} = \frac{g}{3}$: the $2m$ mass accelerates downward at $g/3$ and the $m$ mass upward at $g/3$. Taking upward positive: $a_{cm} = \frac{m(g/3) + 2m(-g/3)}{3m} = \frac{-g/3}{3} = -\frac{g}{9}$. The centre of mass accelerates downward with magnitude $g/9$. Final answer: $\boxed{g/9}$

questions.question: A disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is initially rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ about its central axis. While rotating, it is placed on a horizontal surface whose coefficient of friction is $\mu = 0.5$. How long will it take for the disk to stop rotating?
questions.hint: Frictional stress is uniform but the lever arm grows with radius; integrate the torque over annuli of the disk.
questions.solution: An annulus of radius $r$ and width $dr$ has mass $dm = \frac{M}{\pi R^2}2\pi r\,dr$ and exerts frictional torque $d\tau = \mu\,dm\,g\,r = \frac{2\mu Mg}{R^2}r^2\,dr$. Integrating from $0$ to $R$ gives $\tau = \frac{2}{3}\mu MgR$. With $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$, the angular deceleration is $\alpha = \frac{\tau}{I} = \frac{4\mu g}{3R}$, so the stopping time is $t = \frac{\omega}{\alpha} = \frac{3\omega R}{4\mu g} = \frac{3\omega R}{4(0.5)g} = \frac{3\omega R}{2g}$. Hence option (B).

questions.question: A planar figure is formed from uniform wire consisting of two equal semicircular arcs, each with its own closing diameter, joined so as to form the letter 'B' (two semicircular arcs bulging to the right of a common vertical straight edge). The figure is freely suspended from its top left-hand corner. What angle does the straight edge of the figure make with the vertical?
questions.hint: When freely suspended, the centre of mass lies directly below the pivot; compare the horizontal offset of the centre of mass with its vertical drop from the pivot.
questions.solution: Let each semicircular arc have radius $r$ and the wire have linear density $\lambda$. Each unit (arc + its diameter) has $x$-centre of mass $\bar{x} = \frac{\lambda\pi r\cdot(2r/\pi) + \lambda(2r)\cdot 0}{\lambda(\pi r + 2r)} = \frac{2r}{\pi+2}$, and both units share this offset, so the figure's centre of mass is at $\left(\frac{2r}{\pi+2}, 2r\right)$ if the spine runs from $y=0$ to $y=4r$. The pivot is the top of the spine at $(0, 4r)$; when hung freely the pivot and centre of mass align vertically, so $\tan\theta = \frac{2r/(\pi+2)}{2r} = \frac{1}{\pi+2} \approx 0.194$, giving $\theta \approx 11^\circ$. Hence option (C).
questions.figureNote: Wire letter 'B': a vertical spine formed by two stacked diameter segments, each closed by a semicircular arc bulging right.

questions.question: A particle, initially at rest, starts to move in a circular path with angular acceleration $\alpha = \theta + e^{\theta} + \tan\theta$ (with $\theta$ in radians). What is the angular velocity of the particle when its angular displacement equals $\pi/6$?
questions.hint: Use $\omega\,d\omega = \alpha\,d\theta$ and integrate the given $\alpha(\theta)$ from $0$ to $\pi/6$.
questions.solution: Since $\alpha = \omega\frac{d\omega}{d\theta}$, we have $\omega\,d\omega = \alpha\,d\theta$, so $\omega^2 = 2\int_0^{\pi/6}(\theta + e^{\theta} + \tan\theta)\,d\theta$. Evaluating each piece: $\int_0^{\pi/6}\theta\,d\theta = \frac{(\pi/6)^2}{2} = 0.1371$; $\int_0^{\pi/6}e^{\theta}d\theta = e^{\pi/6} - 1 = 0.6881$; $\int_0^{\pi/6}\tan\theta\,d\theta = \ln\sec\theta\big|_0^{\pi/6} = \ln\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 0.1438$. Thus $\omega^2 = 2(0.9690) = 1.938$, giving $\omega \approx 1.39$ rad/s. Hence option (C).

questions.question: A sphere of mass density $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and radius $3\ \mathrm{m}$ contains another sphere of density $2000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and radius $1\ \mathrm{m}$ inside it, whose center is situated at $x = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ (the origin is at the center of the larger sphere). Find the location of the center of mass of the system.
questions.hint: Treat the body as a uniform sphere of density 1000 (whose moment about its own center vanishes) plus the excess density $2000-1000$ occupying the small sphere.
questions.solution: View the body as a uniform sphere of density $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ filling the whole radius-3 sphere (its center of mass is at the origin, so it contributes no moment) plus an excess density $\Delta\rho = 2000 - 1000 = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ occupying the small sphere at $x = 1.5$ m. Since mass is proportional to $\rho R^3$, $x_{cm} = \frac{\Delta\rho (1)^3 (1.5)}{1000(3)^3 + \Delta\rho(1)^3} = \frac{1000 \times 1.5}{1000(27+1)} = \frac{1.5}{28} = 0.054\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.question: A plane is flying horizontally with a speed of 30 m/s at an altitude of 125 m above sea level when it drops a flare. Neglecting air resistance and assuming that the plane does not change its course, speed, or altitude, how far from the plane is the flare when it hits the ground at sea level?
questions.hint: Compare the horizontal motion of the flare with that of the plane during the fall.
questions.solution: With no air resistance the flare keeps the plane's horizontal velocity of 30 m/s throughout the fall, so it remains exactly below the aircraft. The fall time is $t=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{2\times125/9.8}\approx5.05$ s, during which both plane and flare move $30\times5.05\approx151$ m horizontally. So when the flare hits the sea it lies directly beneath the plane, and the only separation is the vertical altitude of 125 m.

questions.question: A plane flies horizontally at $30\,\text{m/s}$ at an altitude of $125\,\text{m}$ above sea level and drops a flare. Neglecting air resistance and assuming the plane does not change course, speed, or altitude, how far from the plane is the flare when it hits the sea?
questions.solution: Key idea: with no air resistance the flare keeps the plane's horizontal velocity of $30\,\text{m/s}$. Time to fall: $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = \sqrt{2\times125/9.8} = 5.05\,\text{s}$, during which the flare travels $30 \times 5.05 = 151.5\,\text{m}$ horizontally. But the plane travels exactly the same horizontal distance in that time! The horizontal separation between plane and flare stays zero, so at splashdown the distance between them is purely the vertical drop: $125\,\text{m}$. (Option D, $150\,\text{m}$, is the trap: it is the flare's horizontal travel, not its distance from the plane.) Answer: (C).

questions.question: Six missiles are initially located at the six vertices of a regular hexagon of side $a$. Each missile moves at speed $v$ in the plane, its navigation system always aiming it at the current position of its counterclockwise neighbor. Find the time taken for the missiles to meet.
questions.solution: By symmetry the six missiles always form a regular hexagon that shrinks and rotates, each missile spiraling toward the center where they all collide. For a regular hexagon the circumradius equals the side $a$, and the triangle formed by the center and two adjacent vertices is equilateral, so the angle between a missile's velocity (aimed at its neighbor) and the line toward the center is $60^{\circ}$. The centerward (radial) speed component is $v\cos 60^{\circ} = v/2$. The initial distance from vertex to center is $a$, so the meeting time is $t = \frac{a}{v/2} = \frac{2a}{v}$. Answer: (B). (Anomaly: options C and D were OCR-garbled; reconstructed as $\sqrt{3}a/v$ and $a/\sqrt{3}v$.)

questions.question: A ball of mass $m$ hangs from a massless string of length 1 m attached to a 3 kg platform resting on a surface with friction coefficient 0.25. The ball is released from rest in a horizontal position, and simultaneously a variable force keeps the platform moving at constant velocity. What is $m$ if a force of $8\,\text{N}$ is required when the string makes a $40^{\circ}$ angle with the vertical? ($g = 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$)
questions.solution: Pendulum dynamics: released from horizontal, at angle $\theta$ from the vertical energy conservation gives $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgL\cos\theta$, and the radial force balance $T - mg\cos\theta = \frac{mv^2}{L}$ gives $T = 3mg\cos\theta$. At $\theta = 40^{\circ}$: $T = 3m(9.8)(0.766) = 22.52m$. To keep the platform at constant velocity, the applied force must overcome friction $\mu Mg$ plus the string's pull on the platform; with the string segment pulling the platform horizontally with the full tension (the geometry assumed by the official key, e.g., string leaving over the platform edge) and $N = Mg$: $F = T + \mu Mg = 22.52m + 0.25\times3\times9.8 = 22.52m + 7.35 = 8\,\text{N}$, so $m = \frac{0.65}{22.52} = 0.0289\,\text{kg} = 28.9\,\text{g}$. Answer: (D). (Anomaly: if the string were attached directly at $40^{\circ}$, only $T\sin40^{\circ}$ would act horizontally with $N = Mg + T\cos40^{\circ}$, giving $m \approx 34.6\,\text{g}$, which matches no option; the official result requires the full tension to act horizontally on the platform.)

questions.question: Two blocks $A$ and $B$, each of mass $M$, rest on a long inclined plane of angle $\theta$, with $A$ higher up than $B$ and separated from it by distance $s$ along the slope. The friction coefficients are $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ with $\tan\theta > \mu_B > \mu_A$. Both are released from rest at $t = 0$. After what time do the blocks collide? ($g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$)
questions.solution: Principles: Newton's second law on an incline with kinetic friction, then relative kinematics. Since $\tan\theta > \mu_B > \mu_A$, both blocks slide down. Their accelerations are $a_A = g(\sin\theta - \mu_A\cos\theta)$ and $a_B = g(\sin\theta - \mu_B\cos\theta)$. The upper block $A$ has the larger acceleration (smaller friction), so it closes the initial gap $s$. The relative acceleration is $a_{rel} = a_A - a_B = g(\mu_B - \mu_A)\cos\theta$. Starting from rest, the gap closes as $s = \frac{1}{2}a_{rel}t^2$, hence $\boxed{t = \sqrt{\frac{2s}{g(\mu_B-\mu_A)\cos\theta}}}$. Note the common $g\sin\theta$ term and the mass $M$ cancel; only the friction difference matters.

questions.question: A sphere of mass $m$ and radius $r$ hangs vertically from a massless rope of length $L$. A steady wind exerts a constant horizontal force $\pi r^2 p$ on the sphere, where $p$ is the wind's force per unit area. The sphere is released from rest with the rope vertical. Assuming no energy loss, what is the maximum height $H$ above its starting point that the sphere rises?
questions.solution: Principles: work-energy theorem with a constant horizontal force; pendulum geometry. The wind pushes the sphere with constant horizontal force $F = \pi r^2 p$ (force per unit area times projected area $\pi r^2$). Let the rope make angle $\theta$ with the vertical at the highest point of the swing; there the sphere is momentarily at rest, so the wind's work equals the gain in gravitational potential energy: $F \cdot L\sin\theta = mgL(1-\cos\theta)$. With $\sin\theta = 2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}$ and $1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}$, this reduces to $F\cos\frac{\theta}{2} = mg\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$, i.e. $\tan\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{F}{mg}$. The rise height is $H = L(1-\cos\theta) = 2L\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{2LF^2}{F^2 + m^2g^2}$. Substituting $F = \pi r^2 p$: $\boxed{H = \frac{2L(\pi r^2 p)^2}{m^2 g^2 + (\pi r^2 p)^2}}$

questions.question: For a vertical circle, particle 1 slides from rest down a smooth chord starting at the highest point $H$ (time $t_1$), particle 2 slides from rest down a smooth chord ending at the lowest point $L$ (time $t_2$), and particle 3 drops freely from $H$ to $L$ along the vertical diameter (time $t_3$). All surfaces are smooth. Which comparison is correct?
questions.solution: Principles: constant acceleration along a frictionless incline, $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$, with the incline angle set by the chord geometry. Let the circle have radius $R$, so the vertical diameter $HL = 2R$. A chord from the top $H$ making angle $\alpha$ with the vertical has length $\ell = 2R\cos\alpha$ and the acceleration along it is $a = g\cos\alpha$, giving $t_1 = \sqrt{2\ell/a} = \sqrt{4R/g}$, independent of $\alpha$. A chord ending at the lowest point $L$ makes angle $\beta$ with the vertical and has length $2R\cos\beta$ with acceleration $g\cos\beta$, so $t_2 = \sqrt{4R/g}$ as well. Free fall from $H$ to $L$ covers $2R$: $t_3 = \sqrt{2 \cdot 2R/g} = \sqrt{4R/g}$. Hence $\boxed{t_1 = t_2 = t_3 = 2\sqrt{R/g}}$, and the result is independent of the masses $m_1, m_2, m_3$.

questions.question: Two highways intersect at right angles. At a certain instant car A is on one highway, $d = 5$ km from the intersection, driving toward it at $v_A = 80$ km/h, while car B is at the intersection driving along the other highway at $v_B = 60$ km/h. Find the closest distance the two cars come to each other.
questions.solution: Principles: relative kinematics and minimising a distance. Take the intersection as origin, car A on the $x$-axis at $(d, 0)$ heading toward it, car B on the $y$-axis. After time $t$ (hours): A is at $(d - v_A t,\ 0)$, B at $(0,\ v_B t)$, so $S^2 = (d - v_A t)^2 + (v_B t)^2$. Minimising: $\frac{d(S^2)}{dt} = -2v_A(d - v_A t) + 2v_B^2 t = 0 \Rightarrow t^* = \frac{v_A d}{v_A^2 + v_B^2} = \frac{80 \times 5}{6400 + 3600} = 0.04$ h. At that moment A is $5 - 80(0.04) = 1.8$ km and B is $60(0.04) = 2.4$ km from the junction: $S = \sqrt{1.8^2 + 2.4^2} = \sqrt{9}$. $\boxed{S_{min} = 3\ \mathrm{km}}$ (generally $S_{min} = \frac{d v_B}{\sqrt{v_A^2+v_B^2}}$).

questions.question: 2022 point particles are equally spaced on a circle of radius 1 m. The particles are identical with mass 1 kg except two, which each have mass $10^{11}$ kg. The angle between the radii joining these two heavy particles to the centre is $90^\circ$. What is the distance (in m) of the centre of mass of the system from the centre of the circle?
questions.hint: The unit vectors of 2022 equally spaced particles on a circle sum to zero — use that to find the centre of mass of the light particles.
questions.solution: The position vectors of all 2022 equally spaced particles sum to zero, so the 2020 light (1 kg) particles have vector sum $-(\hat{x}+\hat{y})R$, i.e. their centre of mass sits at $(-1,-1)/2020$ m — negligible. The two heavy masses ($M = 10^{11}$ kg) at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ m have combined vector moment $M(1,1)$ m·kg, placing their centre of mass at $(0.5, 0.5)$ m. Overall: $\vec{r}_{CM} = \frac{(M-1)(1,1)}{2M+2020}$, so $d = \sqrt{2}(M-1)/(2M+2020) \approx \sqrt{2}\times0.5 \approx 0.707$ m $= 1/\sqrt{2}$ m.

questions.question: A thin rigid homogeneous rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ is attached to a horizontal rail by a small massless ring at its end, so that it can slide without friction. The ring accelerates at a constant rate $a$, and the rod makes a constant angle $\alpha$ to the vertical. Find $\alpha$, given that the situation takes place on the Earth's surface with gravitational acceleration $g$ (neglect air resistance).
questions.hint: In the ring's frame the rod experiences gravity and a horizontal pseudo force; it aligns with the resulting effective gravity.
questions.solution: In the accelerating frame of the ring, every element of the rod experiences the real weight $mg$ downward and a horizontal pseudo force $ma$ opposite the acceleration. The rod hangs along the direction of this effective gravity, which is tilted from the vertical by an angle $\alpha$ with $\tan\alpha = \frac{ma}{mg} = \frac{a}{g}$. Hence $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(a/g)$, option (D).

questions.question: A thin rigid homogeneous rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ is attached to a horizontal rail by a small massless ring at its end, so that it can slide without friction. As the ring accelerates at a constant rate $a$, the rod makes a constant angle $\alpha$ with the vertical. Find this angle $\alpha$, given that the whole situation takes place on the Earth's surface in the presence of gravitational acceleration $g$ (neglect air resistance).
questions.hint: In the ring's accelerating frame, balance the torques of the weight and the pseudo force about the ring end.
questions.solution: In the frame of the accelerating ring, the rod experiences a horizontal pseudo force $ma$ acting at its center of mass plus its weight $mg$. For the rod to keep a constant angle, the net torque about the ring end must vanish: $mg\frac{l}{2}\sin\alpha = ma\frac{l}{2}\cos\alpha$, which gives $\tan\alpha = \frac{a}{g}$, i.e. $\alpha = \tan^{-1}(a/g)$ — the rod trails behind the direction of acceleration.

questions.question: An inclined plane of angle of elevation $\alpha = 30^\circ$ is placed on a horizontal support of length $L = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$, and an object of mass $m = 4\ \mathrm{kg}$ is placed at the top of the inclined plane. The small mass can slide on the slope without friction. With the help of the horizontal plane, the inclined plane is made to accelerate in the vertical direction at $a = 6\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ ($a < g$, take $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). What is the force exerted by the object on the slope?
questions.hint: In the frame of the downward-accelerating incline the effective gravity is $g - a$; the normal force is $m(g-a)\cos\alpha$.
questions.solution: Work in the frame of the incline accelerating downward at $a = 6\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$: the effective gravity is $g_{eff} = g - a = 9.8 - 6 = 3.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. The slope is frictionless, so the only force it exerts on the object is the normal force $N = m g_{eff}\cos\alpha = 4 \times 3.8 \times \cos 30^\circ = 13.2$ N. By Newton's third law the object presses on the slope with the same force, $13.2$ N.

questions.question: The turns of a uniform spring of natural length $l = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ and force constant $k = 500\ \mathrm{N/m}$ almost touch each other; a light glue is applied evenly between every adjacent turn and breaks when the local tension exceeds $F_b = 100\ \mathrm{N}$. The spring lies on a frictionless horizontal floor and one end is pulled with a force gradually increased to $F = 200\ \mathrm{N}$. What does the length of the spring become? (Where the glue is intact the spring cannot stretch; where it has broken the turns separate under the wire's own stiffness.)
questions.solution: Principle: Newton's second law applied to segments of a massive accelerating spring. Total mass $M$, so $a = F/M$. For the segment from the pulled end to natural-coordinate $x$: $F - T(x) = (Mx/l)a$, giving the linear tension distribution $T(x) = F(1 - x/l) = 200(1 - x/l)\ \mathrm{N}$. Glue breaks where $T > F_b = 100\ \mathrm{N}$: $200(1-x/l) > 100 \Rightarrow x < l/2$. So the half nearest the pulled end is glue-free and stretches, while the far half (tension at or below $100\ \mathrm{N}$) stays at its natural length. Consistency check: at the junction $T(l/2) = 100\ \mathrm{N} = F_b$, exactly the breaking threshold. Extension of the glue-broken half: an element of natural length $dx$ has stiffness $kl/dx$, so its extension is $T(x)dx/(kl)$. Total: $\Delta l = \frac{1}{kl}\int_0^{l/2} 200(1 - x/l)\,dx = \frac{1}{500 \times 1}\left[200(x - x^2/2)\right]_0^{0.5} = \frac{75}{500} = 0.15\ \mathrm{m}$. Final length: $1.00 + 0.15 = 1.15\ \mathrm{m}$. Boxed answer: $1.15\ \mathrm{m}$ (option C).

questions.question: In a vast region of uniform horizontal electric field $E = 10^4\ \mathrm{N/C}$, a small metal ball of mass $m = 4\ \mathrm{g}$, charged positively with $q = 3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$, is projected vertically upward with speed $v_0 = 2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ (take $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). What is the magnitude of the ball's displacement from the launch point at the instant its speed again equals $v_0$?
questions.solution: Principle: two-dimensional motion with constant acceleration (constant electric force $qE$ horizontal, weight $mg$ vertical). Accelerations: $a_x = qE/m = (3\times10^{-6})(10^4)/0.004 = 7.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $a_y = -g$. Velocities: $v_x = 7.5t$, $v_y = 2 - 9.8t$. Speed equals $v_0$ again when $v_x^2 + v_y^2 = v_0^2$: $56.25t^2 + (2-9.8t)^2 = 4 \Rightarrow 152.29t^2 - 39.2t = 0 \Rightarrow t = 0.2574\ \mathrm{s}$ (the root $t=0$ is the launch). Displacements: $x = \frac{1}{2}(7.5)(0.2574)^2 = 0.2485\ \mathrm{m}$, $y = 2(0.2574) - 4.9(0.2574)^2 = 0.1901\ \mathrm{m}$. Magnitude: $\Delta r = \sqrt{0.2485^2 + 0.1901^2} = 0.313\ \mathrm{m}$. Cross-check (work-energy): kinetic energy is back to its initial value, so $qEx = mgy$, i.e. $y/x = qE/mg = 0.765$, matching $0.1901/0.2485$. (With $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ one gets $0.307\ \mathrm{m}$, within tolerance.) Boxed answer: $\approx 0.31\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.question: Same situation: in a uniform horizontal field $E = 10^4\ \mathrm{N/C}$, a ball with $m = 4\ \mathrm{g}$ and $q = 3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$ is projected vertically upward at $v_0 = 2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ ($g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). How much time elapses from the launch until the ball's speed again equals $v_0$?
questions.solution: Principle: constant-acceleration kinematics. $a_x = qE/m = 7.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $a_y = -g$. Condition $v_x^2 + v_y^2 = v_0^2$: $(7.5t)^2 + (2 - 9.8t)^2 = 4$. Expanding: $56.25t^2 + 4 - 39.2t + 96.04t^2 = 4 \Rightarrow t(152.29t - 39.2) = 0$. Non-zero root: $t = 39.2/152.29 = 0.2574\ \mathrm{s} \approx 0.26\ \mathrm{s}$. (With $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$: $t = 0.256\ \mathrm{s}$, essentially the same.) Boxed answer: $\approx 0.257\ \mathrm{s}$.

questions.question: Same situation: ball with $m = 4\ \mathrm{g}$, $q = 3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$, projected vertically upward at $v_0 = 2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in a horizontal field $E = 10^4\ \mathrm{N/C}$ ($g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). What is the minimum speed of the ball during its motion?
questions.solution: Principle: the speed $v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2$ is minimal when $\frac{d(v^2)}{dt} = 2\vec{v}\cdot\vec{a} = 0$, i.e. when the velocity is perpendicular to the (constant) acceleration. Geometry then gives $v_{min} = v_0 \sin\alpha$ where $\sin\alpha = a_\perp/|a|$ with $a_\perp$ the component of $\vec{a}$ perpendicular to the initial (vertical) velocity: $a_\perp = a_x = qE/m = 7.5\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, $|a| = \sqrt{7.5^2 + 9.8^2} = 12.34\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. So $v_{min} = 2 \times 7.5/12.34 = 1.22\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Check: at $t^* = gv_0/|a|^2 = 0.1287\ \mathrm{s}$, $v = \sqrt{(7.5 \times 0.1287)^2 + (2 - 9.8 \times 0.1287)^2} = \sqrt{0.965^2 + 0.739^2} = 1.216\ \mathrm{m/s}$. (With $g = 10$: exactly $1.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$.) Boxed answer: $\approx 1.2\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

questions.question: Same situation: ball with $m = 4\ \mathrm{g}$, $q = 3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C}$, projected vertically upward at $v_0 = 2\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in a horizontal field $E = 10^4\ \mathrm{N/C}$ ($g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). Where is the ball when it moves slowest?
options: About $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ in the field direction and about $18\ \mathrm{cm}$ above the launch point
About $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ in the field direction and about $9\ \mathrm{cm}$ above the launch point
At the top of its vertical motion, directly above the launch point
questions.solution: Principle: the speed is minimal when $\vec{v} \perp \vec{a}$, at $t^* = \frac{g v_0}{a_x^2 + g^2} = \frac{9.8 \times 2}{7.5^2 + 9.8^2} = 0.1287\ \mathrm{s}$. Horizontal displacement: $x = \frac{1}{2}a_x t^{*2} = 3.75 \times 0.01657 = 0.062\ \mathrm{m} \approx 6\ \mathrm{cm}$ (in the direction of the electric force). Vertical displacement: $y = v_0 t^* - \frac{1}{2}g t^{*2} = 0.257 - 0.081 = 0.176\ \mathrm{m} \approx 18\ \mathrm{cm}$ above the launch point. (With $g = 10$: $x = 6.1\ \mathrm{cm}$, $y = 17.4\ \mathrm{cm}$ — same option.) Boxed answer: option B.

questions.question: An inclined plane of elevation angle $\alpha = 30^\circ$ stands on a horizontal surface. An object of mass $m = 4\ \mathrm{kg}$ is placed at the top of the incline; the mass can slide on the slope without friction. The incline is made to accelerate vertically (downward) at $a = 6\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, with $a < g$ ($g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$). What is the force exerted by the object on the slope?
questions.hint: Work in the frame of the accelerating incline and use the reduced effective gravity perpendicular to the slope.
questions.solution: In the non-inertial frame of the downward-accelerating incline, the effective gravity is $g_{\rm eff} = g - a = 9.8 - 6 = 3.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. The normal reaction is $N = m g_{\rm eff}\cos\alpha = 4 \times 3.8 \times \cos 30^\circ = 15.2 \times 0.866 \approx 13.2\ \mathrm{N}$. By Newton's third law the object presses on the slope with the same force, $13.2\ \mathrm{N}$, option (A).

questions.question: An object of mass $m = 1$ kg is set in motion in one dimension and has a position–time relationship $x = 2t^2 + t + 2$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds. Which of the following represents the force acting on the object?
questions.hint: Differentiate the position twice to get the acceleration, then apply Newton's second law.
questions.solution: $v = dx/dt = 4t + 1$ and $a = dv/dt = 4\ \text{m/s}^2$, constant. Newton's second law: $F = ma = (1\ \text{kg})(4\ \text{m/s}^2) = 4$ N. (The linear and constant terms in $x(t)$ contribute nothing to the acceleration.)

questions.question: The position of a particle of mass $m$ on the $xy$-plane is $\vec{r} = (x,y,z) = (r\cos\phi,\ r\sin\phi,\ 0)$, where $r$ and $\phi$ are functions of time $t$. Which of the following is the $z$-component of $\vec{l}$, where $\vec{l}$ is the angular momentum of the particle?
questions.hint: Use $l_z = m(x\dot{y} - y\dot{x})$ and differentiate $x = r\cos\phi$, $y = r\sin\phi$ with the product rule.
questions.solution: $l_z = m(x\dot{y} - y\dot{x})$. With $x = r\cos\phi$ and $y = r\sin\phi$: $\dot{x} = \dot{r}\cos\phi - r\dot{\phi}\sin\phi$ and $\dot{y} = \dot{r}\sin\phi + r\dot{\phi}\cos\phi$. Substituting, the $\dot{r}$ terms cancel: $l_z = m\left[r\cos\phi(\dot{r}\sin\phi + r\dot{\phi}\cos\phi) - r\sin\phi(\dot{r}\cos\phi - r\dot{\phi}\sin\phi)\right] = mr^2\dot{\phi}(\cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi) = mr^2\dot{\phi}$.

questions.question: A flat uniform disk of radius $2R$ has a hole of radius $R$ removed from the center. The resulting annulus is then cut in half along a diameter, and the remaining half-annulus has mass $M$. What is the moment of inertia of this shape about the axis of rotational symmetry of the original disk (through the center, perpendicular to the plane)?
questions.hint: Build the annulus from the full disk of radius $2R$ minus the disk of radius $R$, then note that cutting along a diameter simply halves the moment of inertia about the central axis.
questions.solution: The half-annulus has area $\frac{1}{2}\pi(4R^2 - R^2) = \frac{3\pi R^2}{2}$, so the full annulus has mass $2M$. For an annulus, $I = \frac{1}{2}m(r_{in}^2 + r_{out}^2)$: $I_{ann} = \frac{1}{2}(2M)(R^2 + 4R^2) = 5MR^2$. Cutting along a diameter through the center leaves the mass distribution symmetric about the central axis in the sense that each half carries exactly half the moment of inertia, so $I = 5MR^2/2 = \frac{5}{2}MR^2$.

questions.question: A horizontal beam of length 10 m and weight 200 N is attached to a wall (hinged). The far end is supported by a cable which makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the beam. A 500 N person stands 2 m from the wall. What is the tension in the cable?
questions.hint: Take torques about the hinge: only the vertical component $T\sin 60^\circ$ of the tension has a moment arm.
questions.solution: Torque equilibrium about the wall hinge: the beam's weight $200$ N acts at its center ($5$ m) giving $200 \times 5 = 1000$ N·m, and the person gives $500 \times 2 = 1000$ N·m, both tending to rotate the beam downward. The cable's vertical component $T\sin 60^\circ$ acts at $10$ m: $T\sin 60^\circ \times 10 = 1000 + 1000 = 2000$ N·m. Thus $T = \frac{2000}{10 \times 0.866} = 231$ N.

questions.question: Consider a flat uniform square of mass $M$ and side length $L$. A circle whose diameter equals the side length of the square, with the same center as the square, is cut out. What is the moment of inertia of the remaining shape about an axis through the center and perpendicular to the plane of the square?
questions.hint: Subtract: $I = I_{square} - I_{circle}$, with the circle's mass found from its area fraction $\pi/4$ of the square.
questions.solution: For the full square about a central perpendicular axis: $I_{sq} = \frac{1}{6}ML^2$. The cut-out circle has radius $L/2$ and mass $m_c = M\times\frac{\pi(L/2)^2}{L^2} = \frac{\pi M}{4}$, so $I_c = \frac{1}{2}m_c\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi M L^2}{32}$. The remaining shape: $I = \frac{ML^2}{6} - \frac{\pi ML^2}{32} = \left(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{\pi}{32}\right)ML^2$, with $M$ the original square's mass.

questions.question: A man jumps off a building 202 m high onto cushions having a total thickness of 2 m. If the cushions are crushed to a thickness of 0.5 m, what is the man's acceleration as he slows down (in units of $g$)?
questions.hint: He falls through $202 - 2 = 200$ m of air, then stops in the crushing distance $2 - 0.5 = 1.5$ m; equate kinetic energy to work done in each phase.
questions.solution: The man free-falls $h = 202 - 2 = 200$ m (from the roof to the top of the cushions), reaching $v^2 = 2gh$. He then stops over the crushing distance $d = 2 - 0.5 = 1.5$ m with constant deceleration $a$: $v^2 = 2ad$. Equating: $a = g\,h/d = g \times \frac{200}{1.5} \approx 133g$.

questions.question: A thin uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ is positioned vertically above an anchored frictionless pivot point and then allowed to fall to the ground. With what speed does the free end of the rod strike the ground?
questions.hint: The rod rotates about its end: use energy conservation with $I = ML^2/3$, then convert $\omega$ to the end speed via $v = \omega L$.
questions.solution: The center of mass drops by $L/2$, so $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = Mg\frac{L}{2}$ with $I = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$ about the pivot. Thus $\omega^2 = 3g/L$ and the free end strikes the ground at $v = \omega L = \sqrt{3gL}$.

questions.question: Two identical blocks are connected by a spring. The combination is suspended, at rest, with a string attached to the ceiling. The string breaks suddenly. What is the downward acceleration of the upper block immediately after the string breaks?
questions.hint: The spring force cannot change instantly; find the spring force while the system hangs at rest.
questions.solution: While hanging at rest, the spring is stretched by $mg$ (it supports the lower block), so it pulls the upper block downward with $mg$. Before the string breaks, the string tension is $2mg$, balancing the upper block's weight $mg$ plus the spring force $mg$. Immediately after the string breaks the tension vanishes but the spring force is unchanged: net downward force $= mg + mg = 2mg$, giving $a = 2g$.

questions.question: An object of mass $m$ is attached to the end of a massless rod of length $L$. The other end of the rod is attached to a frictionless pivot. The object is raised so that its height is $0.8L$ above the pivot. After the object is released from rest, what is the tension in the rod when it is horizontal?
questions.hint: Find the speed at the horizontal position from the $0.8L$ drop, then identify the radial force there.
questions.solution: Energy conservation from height $0.8L$ down to the horizontal position (height 0): $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.8\,mgL$, so $v^2 = 1.6\,gL$. When the rod is horizontal, gravity acts perpendicular to the rod (tangential), so the rod supplies the entire centripetal force: $T = mv^2/L = 1.6\,mg$.

questions.question: A sign consists of two uniform legs (each of weight $W$) joined at the top by a frictionless hinge, standing on a rough floor so that they form an inverted V. The coefficient of static friction between the ground and the legs is $\mu$. If $\theta$ is the opening angle between the two legs at the hinge, the maximum value of $\theta$ such that the sign will not collapse satisfies:
questions.hint: By symmetry each leg carries normal force equal to its own weight; balance the torques on one leg about the hinge using the leg's half-angle $\theta/2$ from the vertical.
questions.solution: Each leg (length $L$, weight $W$) makes angle $\theta/2$ with the vertical. Whole-sign equilibrium gives $2N = 2W$, so each floor contact carries $N = W$. Torques on one leg about the hinge: the weight acts at the midpoint with lever arm $\frac{L}{2}\sin(\theta/2)$ (splaying torque), while the normal force $N$ (lever arm $L\sin(\theta/2)$) and friction $f$ (lever arm $L\cos(\theta/2)$) restore it: $NL\sin(\theta/2) - fL\cos(\theta/2) - \frac{W L}{2}\sin(\theta/2) = 0$. With $N = W$ this gives $f = \frac{W}{2}\tan(\theta/2)$. No slipping requires $f \le \mu N = \mu W$, so the sign is stable for $\tan(\theta/2) \le 2\mu$; collapse begins at $\tan(\theta/2) = 2\mu$.
questions.figureNote: Two uniform legs hinged at the apex form an inverted V on a rough floor; θ is the angle between the legs at the hinge.

questions.question: A ring rolls down a plane surface, keeping pace with a block sliding on the same plane with angle of inclination $\theta$. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is given by:
questions.hint: "Keeping pace" means both have the same acceleration; find the rolling ring's acceleration first.
questions.solution: A ring rolling without slipping down the incline has $a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/mR^2}$ with $I = mR^2$, giving $a = \frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$. The sliding block must have the same acceleration: $g\sin\theta - \mu_k g\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$, so $\mu_k g\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$ and $\mu_k = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$.

questions.question: A cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a radially dependent density. The cylinder starts from rest and rolls without slipping down an inclined plane of height $H$. At the bottom of the plane its translational speed is $(8gH/7)^{1/2}$. What is the rotational inertia of the cylinder?
questions.hint: Write energy conservation $MgH = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I(v/R)^2$ and insert the given final speed.
questions.solution: Rolling without slipping means $\omega = v/R$. Energy conservation gives $MgH = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}Iv^2/R^2$. With $v^2 = 8gH/7$: $MgH = \frac{4}{7}MgH + \frac{1}{2}Iv^2/R^2$, so $\frac{1}{2}Iv^2/R^2 = \frac{3}{7}MgH$. Hence $I = \frac{6MgHR^2}{7v^2} = \frac{6MgHR^2}{8gH} = \frac{3}{4}MR^2$.

questions.question: Raindrops with a number density of $n$ drops per cubic meter and radius $r_0$ hit the ground with a speed $v_0$. The resulting pressure on the ground from the rain is $P_0$. If the number density is doubled, the drop radius is halved, and the speed is halved, the new pressure will be:
questions.hint: Pressure equals the rate of momentum delivery per area: $P \propto n \cdot m_{\text{drop}} \cdot v^2$, with $m_{\text{drop}} \propto r^3$.
questions.solution: Drops striking the ground are brought to rest, so the pressure is the momentum flux: $P = n\,m\,v^2$ with $m = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho$, i.e. $P \propto n\,r^3 v^2$. The scaling factor is $\frac{P_{\text{new}}}{P_0} = (2)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{2}{32} = \frac{1}{16}$, so $P_{\text{new}} = P_0/16$.

questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is placed on top of another block of mass $M$, which rests on a frictionless horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the two blocks is $\mu$. What is the minimum horizontal force that must be applied to the block of mass $M$ so that the upper block of mass $m$ just begins to slide?
questions.hint: Below the slipping threshold both blocks move together; static friction must supply $ma$ to the upper block, and it cannot exceed $\mu m g$.
questions.solution: While the blocks move together they share the acceleration $a = \dfrac{F}{M+m}$. The only horizontal force on the upper block is static friction, so $f = ma$ with $f \le \mu m g$, giving $a \le \mu g$. The upper block just begins to slide when $a = \mu g$, so the minimum applied force is $F_{\min} = (M+m)\mu g$.

questions.question: If a particle's motion is described by $t = \alpha x^2 + \beta x$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants and $x$ is the displacement, and if its velocity is $v$, then the particle's acceleration is proportional to:
questions.hint: Invert to get $v(x)$, then use $a = v\,\frac{dv}{dx}$.
questions.solution: Differentiating implicitly, $\dfrac{dt}{dx} = 2\alpha x + \beta$, so $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2\alpha x + \beta}$. Then $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$, and from $v = (2\alpha x+\beta)^{-1}$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -2\alpha(2\alpha x+\beta)^{-2} = -2\alpha v^2$. Hence $a = -2\alpha v^3$, i.e. the magnitude of the acceleration is proportional to $v^3$.

questions.question: A 2 kg block moving to the right with a speed of 4 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 6 kg block. If the collision is perfectly inelastic and the blocks stick together after the collision, what is the loss in kinetic energy?
questions.hint: Find the common final velocity from momentum conservation, then compare kinetic energies; or use $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}\mu_{\text{red}} v_{\text{rel}}^2$.
questions.solution: Momentum conservation gives the final speed $v = \dfrac{2 \times 4}{2+6} = 1$ m/s. Initial kinetic energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4^2) = 16$ J. Final kinetic energy: $K_f = \frac{1}{2}(8)(1^2) = 4$ J. Energy lost: $\Delta K = 16 - 4 = 12$ J. (Equivalently $\Delta K = \frac{1}{2}\mu_{\text{red}}v_{\text{rel}}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{12}{8}\cdot 16 = 12$ J.)

questions.question: A car of mass $m$ moves on a circular track of radius $r$ that is banked at an angle $\theta = 45^\circ$ with the horizontal. What is the maximum speed at which the car can negotiate the turn without skidding, given that the coefficient of static friction is $\mu$?
questions.hint: Use the banked-curve formula $v_{\max}^2 = rg\dfrac{\tan\theta + \mu}{1 - \mu\tan\theta}$ with $\tan 45^\circ = 1$; static friction (not kinetic) applies since the car does not skid.
questions.solution: On a banked track, at maximum speed friction acts down the slope. Resolving forces radially and vertically gives the standard result $v_{\max}^2 = rg\dfrac{\tan\theta + \mu}{1 - \mu\tan\theta}$. With $\theta = 45^\circ$, $\tan\theta = 1$, so $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(1+\mu)rg}{1-\mu}}$. The kinetic friction coefficient $\mu'$ is irrelevant because the car does not skid.

questions.question: A student starts from rest at the top of a large fixed frictionless hemispherical hill of radius $a = 7.5$ m and slides down its outside surface. At what vertical distance below the top of the hill does he lose contact with the surface? ($g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$)
questions.hint: He leaves the surface when the normal force vanishes; combine energy conservation with the radial equation of motion.
questions.solution: Let $\theta$ be the angular displacement from the top. Energy conservation gives $v^2 = 2ga(1-\cos\theta)$. Radially, $mg\cos\theta - N = \frac{mv^2}{a}$. Losing contact means $N=0$: $g\cos\theta = \frac{v^2}{a} = 2g(1-\cos\theta) \;\Rightarrow\; 3\cos\theta = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; \cos\theta = \frac{2}{3}$. The vertical drop is $h = a(1-\cos\theta) = a/3 = 7.5/3 = 2.5$ m (independent of $g$).

questions.question: A uniform rectangular plate of sides $a = 0.60$ m and $b = 0.80$ m (mass $M$) swings freely about a frictionless hinge at one corner, the hinge axis being horizontal and perpendicular to the plate. The plate is released from rest with its center of mass exactly above the hinge. Find the speed of the center of mass at the instant it passes exactly below the hinge. ($g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$)
questions.hint: About the corner, $I = M(a^2+b^2)/3$; the CM drops by the full corner-to-center distance doubled; then use $v_{cm} = \omega d$.
questions.solution: The hinge-to-CM distance is $d = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{a^2+b^2} = 0.50$ m, so the CM falls by $\Delta h = 2d = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} = 1.00$ m. By the perpendicular-axis and parallel-axis theorems, $I = \frac{M(a^2+b^2)}{12} + Md^2 = \frac{M(a^2+b^2)}{3}$ about the hinge. Energy conservation: $Mg\Delta h = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 \;\Rightarrow\; \omega^2 = \frac{6g}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$. Since $v_{cm} = \omega d$, $v_{cm}^2 = \omega^2\frac{a^2+b^2}{4} = \frac{3}{2}g\sqrt{a^2+b^2} = 1.5\times9.8\times1.00 = 14.7$ m$^2$/s$^2$, so $v_{cm} = 3.83$ m/s — remarkably independent of $M$.

questions.question: A bucket full of water rotates with angular velocity $\omega$, and the free surface of the water becomes a paraboloid. Considering the horizontal (centripetal) and vertical force components on a small packet of water at distance $x$ from the axis, the slope $dy/dx$ of the cross-section at that point is:
questions.solution: For a packet of mass $m$ at distance $x$, let $\theta$ be the angle of the surface with the horizontal and $N$ the normal force. Vertical equilibrium: $N\cos\theta = mg$. Horizontal: the normal's horizontal component provides the centripetal force, $N\sin\theta = m\omega^2 x$. Dividing: $\tan\theta = \frac{\omega^2x}{g}$. Since the surface slope $dy/dx = \tan\theta$, the slope is $\frac{\omega^2x}{g}$; integrating gives the parabola $y = \frac{\omega^2x^2}{2g} + $ const. Boxed: $\omega^2x/g$.

questions.question: Rotating-bucket $g$ meter: a laser at height $h$ above the surface point at $x = R/\sqrt2$ shines vertically down; the reflected ray returns to the laser's height a horizontal distance $d$ away, so the surface slope there is $m = \tan\left[\frac{1}{2}\arctan(d/h)\right]$, and the model gives $m = \omega^2R/(\sqrt2\,g)$, with $\omega$ found from the time for 20 revolutions. To extract $g$ from the $(20T, d)$ data table one should plot:
options: $m$ versus $\omega^2$; the slope equals $R/(\sqrt2\,g)$, so $g = R/(\sqrt2\times\text{slope})$
questions.solution: The model $m = \frac{R}{\sqrt2 g}\omega^2$ is linear in $\omega^2$ with zero intercept. So compute $m$ from each measured $d$ via $m = \tan[\frac12\arctan(d/h)]$, plot against $\omega^2 = (40\pi/20T)^2$, and fit a line through the origin: its slope is $k = R/(\sqrt2 g)$, hence $g = R/(\sqrt2 k)$. $d$ itself is not proportional to $\omega^2$ because $d = h\tan(2\theta)$ is a nonlinear function of the slope $m$; the small-angle shortcut $m \approx d/2h$ systematically distorts the large-deflection points. Boxed: B.

questions.question: In the rotating-bucket experiment ($h = 13$ cm, $R = 7.25$ cm) one data point gives a time of 23.48 s for 20 revolutions and $d = 40$ mm. Using $m = \tan\left[\frac{1}{2}\arctan(d/h)\right]$ and $m = \omega^2R/(\sqrt2\,g)$, calculate $g$ in m/s$^2$ from this point.
questions.solution: Angular velocity: $\omega = \frac{2\pi\times20}{23.48} = 5.351$ rad/s, so $\omega^2 = 28.63$ s$^{-2}$. Slope: $d/h = 0.040/0.13 = 0.3077$, so $m = \tan(0.29850/2) = \tan(0.14925) = 0.1504$. Then $g = \frac{\omega^2R}{\sqrt2\,m} = \frac{28.63\times0.0725}{1.4142\times0.1504} = 9.76$ m/s$^2$. Boxed: $g \approx 9.76$ m/s$^2$ (reference 9.7835 m/s$^2$, about 0.2% error).

questions.question: A bowling ball and a golf ball are dropped together from rest at height $h = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$; both radii are negligible compared to $h$. The bowling ball strikes the floor and rebounds perfectly elastically, then immediately collides with the still-descending golf ball. Just before this second collision the bowling ball moves up at $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ and the golf ball moves down at $v$. The line of centers at contact makes an angle $\alpha$ with the vertical (measured from the bowling ball's uppermost point). All collisions are perfectly elastic, there is no friction between the balls, and the bowling ball is so much more massive that the golf ball simply reflects elastically in the bowling ball's instantaneous rest frame. Take the collision to occur at ground level. The golf ball then flies freely and lands a distance $l$ away. Find the maximum possible landing distance $l_{\max}$, in meters, over all contact angles $\alpha$.
questions.hint: In the bowling ball's frame the golf ball's velocity reverses its normal component: $\vec{u}' = \vec{u} - 2(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\hat{n}$. Transform back, get $v_x$ and $v_y$, maximize the projectile range over $\alpha$.
questions.solution: Let $\hat{n} = (\sin\alpha, \cos\alpha)$ be the outward normal at contact (y up). In the bowling ball's frame the golf ball approaches with $\vec{u} = (0,-2v)$; elastic reflection off the massive ball reverses the normal component: $\vec{u}' = \vec{u} - 2(\vec{u}\cdot\hat{n})\hat{n} = (2v\sin 2\alpha,\ 2v\cos 2\alpha)$. Back in the lab frame (add the bowling ball's $+v$ upward): $v_x = 2v\sin 2\alpha$, $v_y = v(1+2\cos 2\alpha)$. The range (launched from ground level) is $l = 2v_xv_y/g = \frac{4v^2}{g}\sin 2\alpha\,(1+2\cos 2\alpha) = 8h\,f$ with $f = \sin c\,(1+2\cos c)$, $c = 2\alpha$. Maximizing: $df/dc = 0 \Rightarrow 3\cos^2 c + \cos c - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \cos c = (\sqrt{13}-1)/6 = 0.4343$, so $c = 64.2^\circ$, $\alpha = 32.1^\circ$, and $f = 1.6831$. Thus $l_{\max} = 8(2.0)(1.6831) \approx 26.9\ \mathrm{m}$ (i.e. $13.5\,h$).

questions.question: A shaking mammal is modeled as a cylinder of radius $R$ spinning at angular speed $\omega$ about its symmetry axis. Wet fur forms clumps of radius $r \ll R$; a clump is flung off when the required centripetal force $\sim \rho r^3 \omega^2 R$ (with water density $\rho$) exceeds the surface-tension hold $\sim \sigma r$, giving (up to numerical factors) $\omega^2 \approx \sigma/(\rho r^2 R)$. All mammal species have fur clumps of the same radius $r$ and bodies of the same average density, and a larger species is simply a scaled-up copy of a smaller one (all lengths, including $R$, scale by the same factor). If the shaking angular speed scales as $\omega \propto M^{n}$ with body mass $M$, find the exponent $n$.
questions.hint: Get the $R$-dependence of $\omega$ first, then link $R$ to $M$ using the fixed body density.
questions.solution: From $\omega^2 \approx \sigma/(\rho r^2 R)$ with $\sigma$, $\rho$ and $r$ the same for all species, $\omega \propto R^{-1/2}$. For scaled-up animals of fixed density, mass scales with volume: $M \propto R^3$, so $R \propto M^{1/3}$. Therefore $\omega \propto (M^{1/3})^{-1/2} = M^{-1/6}$, i.e. $n = -1/6 \approx -0.167$. Larger animals shake proportionally more slowly (e.g. a 20 g mouse at $\sim 30\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ versus a large dog at a few $\mathrm{rad/s}$), in agreement with observation.

questions.question: A stream of electrons is accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$ and falls on a metal that has an inner potential $φ$ binding electrons inside it (this is what prevents electrons from leaking out), so an electron of kinetic energy $eV$ outside has kinetic energy $e(V+φ)$ inside the metal. Taking the refractive index of the metal for the electrons as the ratio of de Broglie wavelengths, $n = \lambda_{out}/\lambda_{in}$, find $n$.
questions.solution: Principles: energy conservation for a charge ($KE = e\Delta V$) and $n$ defined as the ratio of de Broglie wavelengths. Outside the metal: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV \Rightarrow \lambda_{out} = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}$. Inside: $\frac{1}{2}mv_{in}^2 = e(V+φ) \Rightarrow \lambda_{in} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2me(V+φ)}}$. Hence $n = \frac{\lambda_{out}}{\lambda_{in}} = \sqrt{\frac{V+φ}{V}} > 1$: the electron wavelength shortens inside the metal, so the metal acts as an optically denser medium for electron waves (the basis of electron diffraction, as in Davisson–Germer).

questions.question: Muons, elementary particles with mean lifetime $\tau = 2.23\ \mu s$, are produced in cosmic-ray collisions in the atmosphere. Suppose $10^6$ muons are incident from a height of 15 km above the Earth's surface, but only $3.4\times10^4$ of them survive to sea level, the rest having decayed en route. Taking the speed of light as $3\times10^8$ m/s, by how much (in m/s) is their speed towards the Earth's surface slower than the speed of light? (Fast muons survive because of relativistic time dilation.)
questions.hint: Set the survival fraction $e^{-t/(\gamma\tau)}$ with flight time $t = 15000/(\beta c)$ and dilated lifetime $\gamma\tau$, then solve for $\beta$.
questions.solution: Radioactive decay gives $N/N_0 = e^{-t/(\gamma\tau)}$, so $t/(\gamma\tau) = \ln(10^6/3.4\times10^4) = 3.381$. With $t = 15000/(\beta c)$ and $\gamma\tau = \tau/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$: $\frac{15000}{\beta c\,\tau}\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 3.381$. Since $c\tau = 3\times10^8\times2.23\times10^{-6} = 669$ m, we get $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}/\beta = 3.381\times669/15000 = 0.1508$. Hence $1/\beta^2 = 1 + 0.1508^2 = 1.0227$, giving $\beta = 0.989$. The muons travel at about $0.989c$, i.e. $\Delta v = c(1-\beta) \approx 3.35\times10^6$ m/s slower than light.

questions.question: Although a photon has no rest mass it carries momentum $p = h/\lambda$ and so exerts pressure on a surface. Light of wavelength $\lambda$ strikes a perfectly reflecting surface at incidence angle $\theta$ measured from the surface, with $n$ photons striking each unit area of the surface per unit time. The light pressure on the surface is:
questions.solution: Principles: photon momentum $p = h/\lambda$; Newton's second law in momentum form; pressure = momentum delivered per unit area per unit time. Each photon arrives with momentum $p = h/\lambda$ at angle $\theta$ FROM the surface, so the component normal to the surface is $p\sin\theta$ (the tangential component of a perfectly reflected photon's momentum is unchanged; only the normal component reverses). Change of normal momentum per photon: $\Delta p_\perp = 2p\sin\theta = \dfrac{2h\sin\theta}{\lambda}$. Photons hitting unit area per unit time: $n$, so the momentum delivered per unit area per unit time is $P = n\,\Delta p_\perp = \dfrac{2nh\sin\theta}{\lambda}$. $\boxed{P = 2nh\sin\theta/\lambda}$

questions.question: Lily is in a spaceship moving at speed $0.5c$ with respect to a viewer at rest on Earth. Her friends James and Severus are also in their own spaceships. Lily watches Severus moving forward at $0.8c$ and James moving backward at $0.85c$ (both speeds relative to Lily). How fast, as a fraction of $c$, is James moving according to Severus?
questions.hint: Use the relativistic velocity transformation with $u_J = -0.85c$ and $u_S = +0.8c$ measured in Lily's frame.
questions.solution: Take the forward direction as positive. In Lily's frame $u_S = +0.8c$ and $u_J = -0.85c$. The relativistic velocity transformation into Severus's frame gives $u' = \frac{u_J - u_S}{1 - u_Ju_S/c^2} = \frac{-0.85c - 0.8c}{1 - (-0.85)(0.8)} = \frac{-1.65c}{1.68} = -0.982c$. So James recedes from Severus at $0.982c$.

questions.question: A charged pion decays in $10^{-8}$ s as measured in its own rest frame. In the laboratory it travels $3.91\times10^{-8}$ s in the detector before decaying. The pion's speed is most nearly
questions.hint: The lab lifetime is dilated: $\gamma = \Delta t/\Delta\tau$, then convert $\gamma$ to speed.
questions.solution: Time dilation gives $\gamma = \frac{\Delta t}{\Delta\tau} = \frac{3.91\times10^{-8}}{10^{-8}} = 3.91$. Then $\beta = \sqrt{1 - 1/\gamma^2} = \sqrt{1 - 1/15.29} = \sqrt{0.9346} = 0.967$. So $v = 0.967 \times 3.00\times10^8 = 2.90\times10^8$ m/s.

questions.question: An observer $O$ at rest midway between two sources of light at $x = 0$ and $x = 10$ m observes the two sources to flash simultaneously. A second observer $O'$ moves at constant speed parallel to the $x$-axis; according to $O'$, one source flashes 13 ns before the other. The speed of $O'$ relative to $O$ is
questions.hint: Use the Lorentz transformation for the time interval between two simultaneous events separated by $\Delta x = 10$ m.
questions.solution: In $O$'s frame the flashes are simultaneous ($\Delta t = 0$) with separation $\Delta x = 10$ m. The Lorentz transformation gives $\Delta t' = \gamma\left(\Delta t - \frac{v\,\Delta x}{c^2}\right)$, so $|\Delta t'| = \gamma\frac{v\,\Delta x}{c^2} = 13\,\text{ns}$. Thus $\gamma v = \frac{(13\times10^{-9})(3\times10^8)^2}{10} = 1.17\times10^8$ m/s, i.e. $\beta\gamma = 0.39$. Solving $\beta^2 = 0.39^2(1-\beta^2)$ gives $\beta = \frac{0.39}{\sqrt{1.1521}} = 0.363$, so $v \approx 0.36c$.

questions.question: A photon strikes an electron of mass $m$ that is initially at rest, creating an electron-positron pair. The photon is destroyed, and the positron and the two electrons move off at equal speeds along the initial direction of the photon. The energy of the photon was
questions.hint: Write both conservation laws with $\gamma$: $E_\gamma + mc^2 = 3\gamma mc^2$ and $E_\gamma/c = 3\gamma mv$, then eliminate $v$ and $\gamma$.
questions.solution: Let $E_\gamma$ be the photon energy and $\beta = v/c$ the common speed of the three final particles (each of mass $m$). Energy conservation: $E_\gamma + mc^2 = 3\gamma mc^2$. Momentum conservation: $E_\gamma/c = 3\gamma m\beta c$, i.e. $E_\gamma = 3\gamma mc^2 \beta$. Substituting $3\gamma mc^2 = E_\gamma + mc^2$ into the momentum equation gives $\beta = \frac{E_\gamma}{E_\gamma + mc^2}$. With $x = E_\gamma/mc^2$ we need $\beta^2 = 1 - 1/\gamma^2$ with $\gamma = (x+1)/3$: $\frac{x^2}{(x+1)^2} = 1 - \frac{9}{(x+1)^2}$, so $x^2 = (x+1)^2 - 9 \Rightarrow x = 4$. Hence $E_\gamma = 4mc^2$ (then $\gamma = 5/3$, $v = 0.8c$, and indeed $3\gamma mv = 4mc =$ photon momentum).

questions.question: An observer $O$ at rest midway between two sources of light at $x = 0$ m and $x = 10$ m observes the two sources to flash simultaneously. A second observer $O'$ moves at constant speed parallel to the $x$-axis; according to $O'$, one source flashes 13 ns before the other. The speed of $O'$ relative to $O$ is
questions.hint: Relativity of simultaneity: $\Delta t' = \gamma\,v\,\Delta x/c^2$ for events simultaneous in $O$'s frame.
questions.solution: In $O$'s frame the flashes are simultaneous ($\Delta t = 0$) with separation $\Delta x = 10$ m. The Lorentz transformation gives $|\Delta t'| = \gamma\frac{v\,\Delta x}{c^2} = 13\,\text{ns}$, so $\gamma v = \frac{(13\times10^{-9})c^2}{10} = 1.17\times10^8$ m/s, i.e. $\beta\gamma = 0.39$. Solving $\beta^2/(1-\beta^2) = 0.39^2$ yields $\beta = 0.363$, so $v \approx 0.36c$.

questions.question: A spherical ball of volume $V$ is moving at velocity $v = 0.8c$ relative to an observer on the ground. What is the volume of the ball as measured by the observer on the ground?
questions.hint: Length contraction acts only along the direction of motion; transverse dimensions are unaffected.
questions.solution: Only the dimension parallel to the motion contracts, by the factor $1/\gamma$ where $\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-0.64}} = \frac{5}{3}$. The transverse diameters are unchanged, so the measured volume is $V' = \frac{V}{\gamma} = \frac{3}{5}V$. Hence option (B).

questions.question: In 'Avengers: Infinity War', Thor has to hold open the star forge at Nidavellir. During the process, an intense beam of light falls on his back. Each second $5\times10^{30}$ photons hit him, each with a wavelength of 331 nm. What is the magnitude of the force exerted on Thor by the beam of light? (Assume all the photons are absorbed by Thor.)
questions.hint: Each absorbed photon transfers its momentum $h/\lambda$; force is the momentum delivered per second.
questions.solution: Each photon carries momentum $p = h/\lambda$. If $N$ photons are absorbed per second, the force is $F = \frac{Nh}{\lambda}$. With $N = 5\times10^{30}\ \text{s}^{-1}$, $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}$ J$\cdot$s and $\lambda = 331\times10^{-9}$ m: $F = \frac{(5\times10^{30})(6.63\times10^{-34})}{3.31\times10^{-7}} \approx 1.0\times10^{4}$ N. Hence option (C).

questions.question: An intense beam of light falls on Thor's back: each second $5\times10^{30}$ photons hit him, each of wavelength $331\,\mathrm{nm}$. Assuming all the photons are absorbed, what is the magnitude of the force exerted on Thor by the beam?
questions.solution: Principle: each absorbed photon transfers momentum $p = \frac{h}{\lambda}$ (de Broglie relation). Force equals momentum delivered per unit time: $F = \frac{N}{t}\cdot\frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{(5\times10^{30})(6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\cdot s})}{331\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}} = \frac{3.315\times10^{-3}}{3.31\times10^{-7}} \approx 1.0\times10^{4}\,\mathrm{N}$. Final answer: $\boxed{F \approx 10000\,\mathrm{N}}$

questions.question: A radioactive substance initially contains $N_0$ particles. Let $\Delta N$ be the number of particles that decay during the second one-third of the first half-life (i.e. between $t = T_{1/2}/3$ and $t = 2T_{1/2}/3$). Find $\Delta N/N_0$.
questions.solution: Principle: radioactive decay law $N(t) = N_0 2^{-t/T_{1/2}}$. At $t = T_{1/2}/3$: $N = N_0\,2^{-1/3} = 0.7937\,N_0$. At $t = 2T_{1/2}/3$: $N = N_0\,2^{-2/3} = 0.6300\,N_0$. The number decaying in that interval is $\Delta N = N_0(0.7937 - 0.6300) = 0.1637\,N_0$. Final answer: $\boxed{\Delta N/N_0 = 0.1637}$

questions.question: A radioactive isotope emits photons randomly and a detector registers them. When the detector is switched on for one minute, the probability that it detects at least one photon during that minute is 80%. In a new experiment the detector is kept on for five minutes. What is the probability that it detects at least one photon?
questions.solution: Principle: photon emissions in disjoint time intervals are statistically independent (Poisson statistics of radioactive decay), so non-detection probabilities multiply. From the first experiment, $P(0 \text{ photons in } 1\,\text{min}) = 1 - 0.80 = 0.2$. For five independent minutes, $P(0 \text{ in } 5\,\text{min}) = (0.2)^5 = 0.00032$. Therefore $P(\geq 1 \text{ photon}) = 1 - 0.00032 = 0.99968 = 99.968\%$. Note that $P(0) = 0.2^t$ decays exponentially with time, the same mathematics as the radioactive decay law $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$. Answer: $99.968\%$ (D).

questions.question: A photon has no mass but carries momentum $p$ along its propagation direction, related to its energy $E$ by $p = E/c$, where $c$ is the speed of light. A solar sail is a proposed method of spacecraft propulsion: sunlight shining on the sail exerts pressure that pushes it. Suppose the area of the sail is $A$ and $n$ photons strike per unit area per second. What is the maximum resultant force on the spacecraft due to the sunlight?
questions.hint: Maximum momentum transfer per photon happens on reflection — how much momentum does one reflected photon change?
questions.solution: Each photon carries momentum $p$. If a photon is absorbed it transfers $p$; if it is reflected elastically its momentum reverses, transferring $\Delta p = 2p$ — the maximum. The number of photons hitting the sail per second is $nA$, so the maximum force (rate of momentum transfer) is $F = (nA)(2p) = 2pnA$.

questions.question: A photon has no mass but carries momentum $p = E/c$ along its propagation direction. A solar sail of area $A$ is struck by sunlight carrying $n$ photons per unit area per second. What is the maximum resultant force that the sunlight can exert on the spacecraft?
questions.solution: The force is maximal when every photon is reflected straight back, reversing its momentum: each photon then transfers $\Delta p = p - (-p) = 2p$ to the sail. The sail intercepts $nA$ photons per second, so $F = \frac{\Delta p_{total}}{\Delta t} = (nA)(2p) = 2pnA$. (If the photons were merely absorbed, the force would be $pnA$ — option C.) Answer: (D). (Anomaly: option C was OCR-garbled; reconstructed as $pnA$.)

questions.question: Electrons in a cathode ray tube are accelerated through a potential difference of $20\ \mathrm{kV}$ and bombard a target in which the electrons have an average binding energy of $56\ \mathrm{eV}$. Estimate the wavelength of the X-ray photons produced (maximum photon energy).
questions.solution: Principle: energy of a photon $E = hc/\lambda$; an X-ray photon can carry at most the kinetic energy of one bombarding electron. Electron kinetic energy: $E_k = e\Delta V = 20000\ \mathrm{eV}$. Accounting for the binding energy that must first be spent: $E_\gamma \approx 20000 - 56 = 19944\ \mathrm{eV}$. Then $\lambda = hc/E_\gamma = 1240\ \mathrm{eV{\cdot}nm} / 19944\ \mathrm{eV} \approx 0.0622\ \mathrm{nm} = 62.2\ \mathrm{pm}$. (Even ignoring the $56\ \mathrm{eV}$ correction, $\lambda = 1240/20000 = 62.0\ \mathrm{pm}$; the source text's wording is garbled but the marked option corresponds to this value.) Boxed answer: $\approx 62\ \mathrm{pm}$ (option E).

questions.question: How fast must a 2 m stick be moving along its axis if its length is observed to be 1 m from the laboratory frame?
questions.hint: Apply $L = L_0\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$ with $L/L_0 = 1/2$.
questions.solution: Length contraction gives $L = L_0\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$. With $L/L_0 = 1/2$: $\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 1/2$, so $1 - \beta^2 = 1/4$ and $\beta = \sqrt{3}/2$. Thus $v = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}c \approx 2.6\times10^8$ m/s.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 4500 Å is incident on a Na surface for which the threshold wavelength of the photoelectrons is 5420 Å. Which of the following is the work function of sodium?
questions.hint: The work function is fixed by the threshold wavelength, not the incident one: $\phi = hc/\lambda_0$.
questions.solution: The work function is the photon energy at the threshold wavelength: $\phi = \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \frac{1240\ \text{eV·nm}}{542\ \text{nm}} = 2.29$ eV. (The incident 4500 Å photons carry $1240/450 = 2.76$ eV $> \phi$, so emission occurs and $K_{max} = 0.47$ eV — option (D) is the kinetic energy trap.)

questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, electromagnetic radiation is incident upon the surface of a metal. Which of the following is NOT a true statement about the photoelectric effect?
options: $\nu_0$ is characteristic of the cathode material.
Above the threshold frequency, the flux of electrons per second increases with the intensity of incident light.
The stopping potential $V_0$ is proportional to $\nu^2$.
The stopping potential is independent of the intensity.
questions.hint: Write Einstein's photoelectric equation for the stopping potential and check its frequency dependence.
questions.solution:
Einstein's equation gives $eV_0 = h
u - \phi$, so the stopping potential grows linearly with frequency $
u$, not as $
u^2$ — statement (D) is false. The rest are true: no emission (hence no current) below the threshold $
u_0$ (A); $
u_0 = \phi/h$ is set by the cathode material (B); above threshold the number of photoelectrons per second scales with the light intensity (C); and $V_0$ depends on frequency and material, not intensity (E).

questions.question: The $\mu$-meson (muon) has the same charge as the electron but a greater mass, $m_\mu = 207\,m_e$. Using Bohr theory, the radius of a $\mu$-mesonic atom (a nucleus of charge $Ze$ orbited by the $\mu^-$) compared to the radius of the corresponding hydrogen-like atom (same $Z$, orbited by an electron) is:
questions.hint: In the Bohr model $r_1 = \hbar^2/(m k Z e^2)$ — the radius scales inversely with the orbiting particle's mass.
questions.solution: Bor theory gives $r_1 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m k Z e^2}$ (from $mv^2/r = kZe^2/r^2$ with $mvr = \hbar$), so $r \propto 1/(mZ)$. With the same nuclear charge $Ze$ but the orbiting mass $207$ times larger: $r_\mu = r_H \frac{m_e}{m_\mu} = \frac{r_H}{207}$. The heavier muon orbits $207$ times closer to the nucleus.

questions.question: X-rays of wavelength 3.00 Å are incident on a substance. The scattered X-rays observed at $45.0^\circ$ have a different wavelength due to the Compton effect. Find the scattered wavelength.
questions.hint: Use the Compton shift $\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_ec}(1-\cos\theta)$ with $h/m_ec = 0.0243$ Å.
questions.solution: The Compton formula: $\lambda' - \lambda = \frac{h}{m_ec}(1-\cos\theta)$, with the electron Compton wavelength $h/m_ec = 0.02426$ Å. For $\theta = 45.0^\circ$: $\Delta\lambda = 0.02426\,(1 - 0.7071) = 0.02426 \times 0.2929 = 0.0071$ Å. So $\lambda' = 3.00 + 0.0071 = 3.007$ Å. The shift is always positive (longer wavelength) for scattering.

questions.question: The half-life of a radioactive nuclide is 60 hours. The fraction of original activity that will remain after 105 hours would be:
questions.hint: Count how many half-lives elapse in 105 hours; activity decays with the same half-life as the number of nuclei.
questions.solution: The activity decays as $A = A_0\,2^{-t/T_{1/2}}$. In 105 hours the number of elapsed half-lives is $t/T_{1/2} = 105/60 = 1.75$, so $A/A_0 = 2^{-1.75} = 2^{-7/4} \approx 0.297 \approx 0.3$, which corresponds to a fraction of about $1/3$.

questions.question: In the classic Fizeau experiment to verify the special theory of relativity, the speed of light in a moving liquid of refractive index $n$ is measured. If the speed of the liquid is $v$, then what is the measured speed of light in the laboratory frame?
questions.hint: This is relativistic velocity addition of $c/n$ (light in the liquid) and $v$ (the liquid's speed).
questions.solution: In the liquid's frame the light travels at $c/n$. Relativistic addition of the liquid's velocity $v$ gives $u = \frac{c/n + v}{1 + \frac{v}{cn}}$ — exactly the Fresnel-drag result Fizeau measured. Classical (Galilean) addition $c/n + v$ is only the $v \ll c$ approximation and would exceed the correct relativistic value.

questions.question: If the ionization energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV (electron volt), what is the ionization energy of positronium made out of an electron and a positron?
questions.hint: Bohr-level energies are proportional to the reduced mass of the two-body system.
questions.solution: The hydrogen ionization energy is the ground-state binding energy, $13.6\ \text{eV} \propto \mu$, the electron–proton reduced mass ($\approx m_e$). For positronium $\mu = \frac{m_e m_e}{m_e + m_e} = \frac{m_e}{2}$, so every level is half as deep: $E_{\text{ion}} = 13.6/2 = 6.8\ \text{eV}$.

questions.question: A tube of water is traveling at $c/2$ relative to the lab frame when a beam of light traveling in the same direction as the tube enters it. What is the speed of light in the water relative to the lab frame? The index of refraction of water is 4/3.
questions.hint: Use relativistic velocity addition with $u' = c/n$ (light in the water frame) and $v = c/2$.
questions.solution: In the water's rest frame the light travels at $u' = c/n = \frac{3}{4}c$. Adding the tube velocity $v = \frac{1}{2}c$ relativistically: $u = \frac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2} = \frac{\frac{3}{4}c + \frac{1}{2}c}{1 + \frac{3}{8}} = \frac{\frac{5}{4}c}{\frac{11}{8}} = \frac{10}{11}c \approx 0.91c$.

questions.question: If the Hubble constant were suddenly to become zero, what would happen to the Universe?
options: Shrink back to the original singularity.
The stars would collide with each other.
questions.hint: Hubble's law links recession speed directly to the value of $H_0$.
questions.solution: Hubble's law states $v = H_0 d$: the recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance through the Hubble constant. If $H_0$ becomes zero, every recession speed vanishes, so in this idealized picture the expansion stops immediately (subsequent evolution would then be governed only by mutual gravitational attraction).

questions.question: Two samples of radioactive nuclides have the same initial activity. If their half-lives are in the ratio 1:3, what is the ratio of the numbers of undecayed nuclei in the two samples after their respective mean lives?
questions.hint: Activity is $A = \lambda N$; after one mean life $\tau = 1/\lambda$ every sample loses the same fraction $1 - e^{-1}$.
