questions.solution: Because the sphere's density equals the water's, while it is fully submerged the buoyant force equals its weight $mg$, so the agent pulls with zero force and does no work — the depth $h$ never enters. Work is done only while the sphere emerges through the surface. When its centre is at height $y$ relative to the surface (from $-r$ to $+r$), the pull is $T = mg(1 - V_{sub}/V)$, with $V$ the sphere's volume. Hence $W = \int_{-r}^{r} mg\left(1-\dfrac{V_{sub}}{V}\right)dy = 2mgr - \dfrac{mg}{V}\int V_{sub}\,dy$. Writing $V_{sub}(y) = \int_{-r}^{-y}A(z)\,dz$ and swapping the integration order, $\int V_{sub}\,dy = \int A(z)(r+z)\,dz = rV$ (the odd part vanishes by symmetry). Therefore $W = 2mgr - mgr = mgr$ — option A, independent of $h$.

questions.question: Fariha has her baby weighed at an early childhood center every four weeks. The uncertainty in each measurement is $50\,\mathrm{g}$. At four weeks old the baby's weight is measured as $3.20\,\mathrm{kg}$; at eight weeks old it is measured as $4.05\,\mathrm{kg}$. The baby's weight gain in this four-week period, with its uncertainty, is therefore:
questions.hint: For a difference of two measurements, add the absolute uncertainties — do not combine relative ones, and do not invent extra precision in the central value.
questions.solution: The gain is the difference of the two readings: $\Delta w = 4.05 - 3.20 = 0.85\,\mathrm{kg}$. Each weighing carries an absolute uncertainty of $\pm50\,\mathrm{g} = \pm0.05\,\mathrm{kg}$. For a difference (or a sum) of two measurements, the absolute uncertainties add in the worst case: $\pm(0.05+0.05) = \pm0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$. (Adding relative uncertainties in quadrature would give about $\pm0.07\,\mathrm{kg}$, but at this level the linear worst-case rule is the intended treatment — and either way the matching listed choice uses $\pm0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$.) Relative uncertainties are only combined for products and quotients, not for differences. Hence the gain is $0.85\,\mathrm{kg} \pm 0.1\,\mathrm{kg}$ — option C. (Options C and E printed identically in the source; C is taken as the answer.)

questions.question: A $0.6\,\mathrm{kg}$ iron cylinder is attached to the end of a spring of stiffness $k = 64\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and a disc-shaped magnet of mass $0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$ sticks to the bottom of the cylinder. Initially the spring is unstretched; then the system is released and oscillates vertically, the magnet never falling off. What is the minimum magnetic attraction force between the magnet and the iron cylinder? ($g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
questions.hint: Separation is most likely at the highest point of the oscillation, where the required downward acceleration is largest — demand that the magnetic force still hold the magnet there.
questions.solution: Both bodies oscillate together with total mass $m_{tot} = 0.8\,\mathrm{kg}$. Released from the unstretched position, the amplitude equals the static extension: $A = m_{tot}g/k = 0.8\times9.8/64 = 0.1225\,\mathrm{m}$, and $\omega^{2} = k/m_{tot} = 80\,\mathrm{s^{-2}}$. The peak upward acceleration, at the top of the motion, is $\omega^{2}A = 80\times0.1225 = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}} = g$. For the magnet ($m_m = 0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$), gravity $m_m g$ acts down, the magnetic attraction $F_{mag}$ acts up, and the cylinder can only push it away (contact force $N \ge 0$, directed down on the magnet): $m_m a = m_m g + N - F_{mag}$. $N$ is smallest at the top ($a = -\omega^{2}A$); requiring $N \ge 0$ there gives $F_{mag} \ge m_m(g + \omega^{2}A) = 0.2\times19.6 = 3.92\,\mathrm{N} \approx 3.9\,\mathrm{N}$ — option A.

questions.question: Two conducting plates A and B are kept at a distance of $3\,\mathrm{mm}$. Plate A is at $+2\,\mathrm{V}$ and plate B at $0\,\mathrm{V}$. An electron starts to move from plate A with an initial velocity of magnitude $v$ (directed across the gap). Find $v$ such that when the electron reaches plate B, its speed becomes zero. ($e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $m_e = 9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$)
questions.hint: Use energy: the work done by the electric field on the electron equals the change in its kinetic energy; the plate spacing drops out.
questions.solution: The electric field points from A ($+2\,\mathrm{V}$) to B ($0\,\mathrm{V}$), so the negative electron is pushed back toward A and decelerates while travelling from A to B. Only the potential difference matters — the $3\,\mathrm{mm}$ separation is irrelevant. Energy conservation: $\tfrac{1}{2}m_e v^{2} = e\,\Delta V = e\times2\,\mathrm{V}$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2e\,\Delta V}{m_e}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times2}{9.1\times10^{-31}}} \approx 8.4\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, directed from A toward B, i.e. perpendicular to the plates. Among the listed options the closest value is $8.8\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ toward plate B — option E. Limit check: $v \propto \sqrt{\Delta V}$, so a larger voltage difference would demand a proportionally larger launch speed.

questions.question: A wooden block of density $0.6\,\mathrm{kg/L} = 600\,\mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$ floats in a large pool. It has a height of $40\,\mathrm{cm}$ and a square base of $80\,\mathrm{cm}\times80\,\mathrm{cm}$ (per the paper's English version). The block is fixed to the bottom of the pool by a vertical spring of unstretched length $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ and spring constant $k = 1440\,\mathrm{N/m}$. The water depth is $90\,\mathrm{cm}$. What is the height of the part of the block that is NOT under water? ($\rho_w = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
questions.hint: Balance three vertical forces on the block: weight, buoyancy from the submerged volume only, and the spring force (stretched beyond $50\,\mathrm{cm}$ it pulls downward).
questions.solution: Block mass: $m = 600\times(0.8\times0.8\times0.4) = 153.6\,\mathrm{kg}$, weight $= 1505.3\,\mathrm{N}$. Let $z$ be the height of the block's bottom above the pool bottom. The spring length is $z$, so for $z > 0.5\,\mathrm{m}$ it is stretched by $(z-0.5)$ and pulls the block down with $1440(z-0.5)$. The submerged depth is $x = 0.9 - z$, so the buoyant force is $\rho_w g\times0.64\,x = 6272x$. Vertical equilibrium: $6272(0.9-z) = 1505.3 + 1440(z-0.5)$, giving $7712\,z = 4859.5$ and $z = 0.630\,\mathrm{m}$ — indeed stretched ($z > 0.5$). The height above water is $z + 0.4 - 0.9 = 0.13\,\mathrm{m}$. Check: buoyancy $6272\times0.27 = 1693\,\mathrm{N}$ equals weight plus spring pull, $1505 + 187\,\mathrm{N}$.

questions.question: Using the equilibrium from the previous part (block bottom at $z_1 \approx 0.630\,\mathrm{m}$ above the pool bottom; water surface at $0.90\,\mathrm{m}$): at least how much work is required to raise the block (height $0.4\,\mathrm{m}$, base $0.8\times0.8\,\mathrm{m^{2}}$, mass $153.6\,\mathrm{kg}$, spring $k = 1440\,\mathrm{N/m}$ of unstretched length $0.5\,\mathrm{m}$) completely above the water surface, assuming the spring does not break? ($\rho_w = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$)
questions.hint: Add the gains in gravitational and spring potential energy, then subtract the work the decreasing buoyant force does on the block during the lift.
questions.solution: The block must rise from $z_1 = 0.630\,\mathrm{m}$ until its bottom reaches the surface, $z_2 = 0.9\,\mathrm{m}$ ($\Delta z = 0.270\,\mathrm{m}$). The minimum (quasi-static) work equals the gain of mechanical energy of block $+$ spring minus the work done by buoyancy. (1) Gravity: $mg\,\Delta z = 1505.3\times0.270 = 406\,\mathrm{J}$. (2) Spring: $\tfrac{1}{2}k\left[(z_2-0.5)^{2}-(z_1-0.5)^{2}\right] = 720\,(0.16-0.0169) = 103\,\mathrm{J}$. (3) Buoyancy does positive work as the submerged depth shrinks from $x_1 = 0.27\,\mathrm{m}$ to $0$: $\tfrac{1}{2}\rho_w g A_{base}x_1^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}\times6272\times0.27^{2} = 228\,\mathrm{J}$. Total: $W = 406 + 103 - 228 = 281\,\mathrm{J}$. Sanity check: lifting $154\,\mathrm{kg}$ through $27\,\mathrm{cm}$ alone would cost $407\,\mathrm{J}$; the buoyant force reduces this by about $228\,\mathrm{J}$, partly offset by the stretching spring.

questions.question: A ray of light passes from air into water of refractive index $n = 1.33$. What is the angle of incidence if, during refraction, the component of the light ray's velocity that is perpendicular to the boundary does not change?
questions.hint: Express both the unchanged-normal-component condition and Snell's law in terms of sines and cosines, then eliminate the refraction angle.
questions.solution: Let $\theta_i$ and $\theta_r$ be the angles of incidence and refraction. The velocity component normal to the boundary is $v\cos\theta$: in air $c\cos\theta_i$, in water $(c/n)\cos\theta_r$. The condition 'normal component unchanged' gives $\cos\theta_r = n\cos\theta_i$. Snell's law gives $\sin\theta_i = n\sin\theta_r$, i.e. $\sin\theta_r = \sin\theta_i/n$. Squaring and adding the two relations: $1 = n^2\cos^2\theta_i + \sin^2\theta_i/n^2$. Multiplying by $n^2$ and writing $\sin^2 = 1-\cos^2$: $n^2 = n^4\cos^2\theta_i + 1 - \cos^2\theta_i$, so $\cos^2\theta_i = (n^2-1)/(n^4-1) = 1/(n^2+1)$. For $n = 1.33$: $\cos\theta_i = 1/\sqrt{2.7689} = 0.601$, hence $\theta_i \approx 53^\circ$ (choice A). Check: $\sin\theta_i = 0.80$; then $\cos\theta_r = 1.33\times 0.601 = 0.80$, so $\theta_r = 37^\circ$ and $\sin\theta_r = 0.60 = 0.80/1.33$ — Snell's law is indeed satisfied.

questions.question: Two identical cylinder-shaped wooden billets, each of mass 45 kg, lie in a water-filled channel with vertical walls. They have the same size and material, touch each other and both walls; one billet is completely submerged while only half of the other is immersed. Friction is negligible everywhere. What is the density of the wood? Take $\rho_{\mathrm{water}} = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
questions.hint: Balance vertical forces on each billet separately; the walls act horizontally, and the two billets push each other along the vertical line joining their centres.
questions.solution: Vertical frictionless walls can only push perpendicular to themselves, i.e. horizontally, so they contribute no vertical force. Two equal cylinders that touch each other and both walls are stacked one directly above the other (each spans the channel width), so the contact force $N$ between them acts along the line of centres — vertically. Let each billet have volume $V$ and the wood density $\rho$. Upper billet (half immersed): $\rho Vg = \rho_w (V/2) g + N$, so $N = (\rho - \rho_w/2)Vg$. Lower billet (fully immersed): $\rho_w Vg = \rho Vg + N$, so $N = (\rho_w - \rho)Vg$. Equating the two expressions for $N$: $\rho - \rho_w/2 = \rho_w - \rho \Rightarrow 2\rho = 1.5\,\rho_w \Rightarrow \rho = 750\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ (choice C). The 45 kg masses and the channel width are distractors — only the submerged fractions matter. Consistency: $N > 0$ requires $\rho_w/2 < \rho < \rho_w$, which holds.

questions.question: The turns of a uniform spring of relaxed length $l = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ and force constant $k = 500\ \mathrm{N/m}$ almost touch each other. A light glue is applied evenly between every adjacent turn; the glue breaks when stretched by a force exceeding $F_b = 100\ \mathrm{N}$. The spring is placed on a frictionless horizontal floor and pulled from one end, the pulling force being gradually increased to $F = 200\ \mathrm{N}$. What does the length of the spring become?
questions.hint: On a frictionless floor the tension is not uniform — it must accelerate the mass behind it, growing linearly from the free end to the pulled end.
questions.solution: The floor is frictionless, so the whole spring (mass $M$) accelerates at $a = F/M$. The tension at distance $x$ from the free end has to accelerate only the part of mass $Mx/l$, so $T(x) = (Mx/l)(F/M) = Fx/l$: zero at the free end, $F$ at the pulled end. Glue snaps wherever $T > F_b$: $Fx/l > 100$ gives $x > lF_b/F = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$. A piece of spring of natural length $dx$ has stiffness $kl/dx$, so a tension $T$ stretches it by $T\,dx/(kl)$. Each junction breaks exactly when the tension across it first reaches $F_b$, i.e. at local strain $F_b/(kl) = 100/500 = 0.2$; once broken, the glue exerts no force, so that stretch is frozen while the coils are still dragged along by the wire. Final extension: intact half ($0 \le x \le 0.5\ \mathrm{m}$): $\Delta l_1 = \int_0^{0.5} \frac{(Fx/l)\,dx}{kl} = \frac{Fl}{8k} = \frac{200}{8\times500} = 0.05\ \mathrm{m}$; broken half ($0.5$ to $1.0\ \mathrm{m}$): frozen strain $0.2 \times 0.5\ \mathrm{m} = 0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. Total extension $0.15\ \mathrm{m}$, so the length becomes $1.15\ \mathrm{m}$ (choice C).

questions.question: A perfectly spherical elastic balloon of diameter $0.2\ \mathrm{m}$ is filled with hydrogen gas at sea level, then rises to an altitude where the atmospheric pressure is $0.65\ \mathrm{atm}$. The temperature stays the same. What is the balloon's diameter at that altitude?
questions.hint: At fixed temperature $PV$ is constant, but the diameter scales as the cube root of the volume ratio.
questions.solution: An elastic balloon with negligible wall tension always has the same pressure inside as outside, so the gas expands isothermally as the external pressure falls. Boyle's law: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = V_1(P_1/P_2) = V_1/0.65 = 1.538\,V_1$. For a sphere $V \propto d^3$, so the diameter grows only as the cube root of the volume ratio: $d_2 = d_1(1/0.65)^{1/3} = 0.2 \times 1.154\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.23\ \mathrm{m}$ (choice B). Sanity check: a 35% pressure drop raises the volume by about 54% but the diameter by only about 15% — cube roots grow slowly, so answers like $0.32\ \mathrm{m}$ (which would need roughly triple the volume) are far too large.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ and charge $q$ levitates at a distance $R$ from a fixed charge $Q$ of the same sign: the Coulomb repulsion exactly balances the particle's weight, $k_e qQ/R^2 = mg$. The particle is now given a slight displacement along the line joining the charges, toward $Q$, and released. Determine the period of the resulting small oscillation (variations of $g$ with height are negligible).
questions.hint: Expand the Coulomb force to first order in the small displacement about equilibrium; the coefficient of the displacement acts as the effective spring constant.
questions.solution: At the equilibrium separation, $k_e qQ/R^2 = mg$. Displace the particle toward $Q$ by a small $\xi$; the separation becomes $R-\xi$ and the electric force $k_e qQ/(R-\xi)^2 \approx (k_e qQ/R^2)(1 + 2\xi/R) = mg(1+2\xi/R)$, using the binomial expansion to first order. The net force is then $mg(1+2\xi/R) - mg = (2mg/R)\,\xi$, directed back toward $R$ — a restoring force proportional to the displacement. Newton's second law gives $m\ddot{\xi} = -(2mg/R)\,\xi$: simple harmonic motion with $\omega^2 = 2g/R$. Eliminating $g$ via the equilibrium condition $g = k_e qQ/(mR^2)$: $\omega^2 = 2k_e qQ/(mR^3)$, hence $T = 2\pi\sqrt{mR^3/(2k_e qQ)}$ (choice B). Note that a displacement away from $Q$ weakens the repulsion below $mg$, so there is no restoring force in that direction — the oscillation corresponds to the inward displacement.

questions.question: Different amounts of water at different temperatures are mixed: 1 litre at $10^\circ$C, 2 litres at $20^\circ$C, 3 litres at $30^\circ$C, 4 litres at $40^\circ$C, 5 litres at $50^\circ$C, 6 litres at $60^\circ$C, 7 litres at $70^\circ$C, 8 litres at $80^\circ$C and 9 litres at $90^\circ$C. What is the common temperature of the mixture if heat losses to the surroundings are negligible?
questions.hint: Weight each temperature by the amount of water carrying it, not by the number of samples - think $Q = mc\Delta T$ per litre.
questions.solution: Use conservation of energy: the heat released by the warm samples equals the heat absorbed by the cool ones. Since every sample is water, $Q_i = m_i c\,T_i$ with $m_i \propto V_i$ (same density) and the same specific heat $c$, so the final temperature is the volume-weighted mean: $T_f = \frac{\sum_i V_i T_i}{\sum_i V_i} = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^{9} n\cdot(10n)\,^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\sum_{n=1}^{9} n}$. Here $\sum_{n=1}^{9} n^2 = \frac{9\cdot10\cdot19}{6} = 285$ and $\sum n = 45$, giving $T_f = \frac{10\times 285}{45} = 63.3^\circ$C, i.e. option D. The plain average $50^\circ$C (option C) would be correct only if all volumes were equal; here the larger volumes are the warmer ones, so they dominate and pull the final temperature above the average. Sanity check: the result must lie between $10^\circ$C and $90^\circ$C and closer to the warm side, which $63^\circ$C is.

questions.question: A steel ball of volume $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ is sinking vertically downward at a speed of $1\,\mathrm{cm/s}$ in a closed jar completely filled with honey of density $2\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. What is the momentum of the honey?
questions.hint: Ask where the honey has to go when the ball makes room for itself - the jar is closed and already full.
questions.solution: The jar is closed and completely full of incompressible honey, so wherever the ball moves down, honey must move up to occupy the space the ball vacates. Each second the ball sweeps through a volume $V = 1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$; exactly this volume of honey, of mass $\rho_h V = 2\,\mathrm{g}$, is effectively transferred from below/around the ball to above it. Formally, the honey's centre of mass shifts so that its total momentum is $p_{\mathrm{honey}} = \rho_h V_{\mathrm{ball}}\,v = 2\times1\times1 = 2\,\mathrm{g\cdot cm/s}$. Direction: the honey flows upward while the ball sinks, so the honey's momentum points vertically upward, opposite to the ball's velocity - if 'downward' were taken as positive it would be $-2$ (option C is the direction trap). Note the answer is independent of the steel ball's mass: the rest of the momentum bookkeeping is carried by the forces between honey, jar and table.

questions.question: A heavy, flexible, inelastic chain of length $L$ hangs almost symmetrically over a light pulley that can rotate about a fixed horizontal axis (friction negligible, pulley small compared with $L$). Released from rest, the chain slips off. What is the speed of the chain at the moment it leaves the pulley? (The original options carried square-root signs that were lost in digitisation; they are reconstructed here.)
questions.hint: Track the centre of mass: how far does it drop between the symmetric hang and the moment the chain slips off?
questions.solution: Use energy conservation: the light pulley exerts only normal forces, which do no work, and the chain is inelastic, so mechanical energy is conserved. Let the chain have mass $m$. Initially it hangs almost symmetrically: each half has length $L/2$ with its centre of mass $L/4$ below the pulley, so measuring potential energy from the pulley, $U_i = -mg\,L/4$. At the instant the last link leaves the pulley, the whole chain hangs on one side with its centre of mass $L/2$ below the pulley: $U_f = -mg\,L/2$. The lost potential energy $mgL/4$ becomes kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{4}mgL$, hence $v = \sqrt{gL/2} \approx 0.71\sqrt{gL}$ - option A. The distractor $\sqrt{gL}$ results from assuming the centre of mass falls by $L/2$ (forgetting the initial symmetric hang), and $\sqrt{2gL}$ from free-fall of the full length.

questions.question: A large rocky planet was formed from eight small rocky planets, each of radius $R$. The small planets and the new large planet all have the same density, and initially the small planets were so far apart that they did not interact. The energy required to blast a planet of mass $m$ and radius $r$ apart is $\dfrac{3Gm^2}{5r}$, where $G$ is a constant. How many times as much energy is required to blast the large planet apart as to blast all of the eight small planets apart?
questions.hint: Same density means the merged planet's radius grows as the cube root of the volume ratio.
questions.solution: All planets share the same density $\rho$, so mass scales with radius cubed. The big planet contains eight small-planet volumes, hence its mass is $M = 8m$ and its radius is $R_{\mathrm{big}} = 8^{1/3}R = 2R$. The given blasting energy is $E = \frac{3Gm^2}{5r}$. One small planet: $E_s = \frac{3Gm^2}{5R}$, so all eight together require $8E_s = \frac{24Gm^2}{5R} = 4.8\,Gm^2/R$. The big planet: $E_b = \frac{3G(8m)^2}{5(2R)} = \frac{3\cdot64}{10}\frac{Gm^2}{R} = 19.2\,Gm^2/R$. The ratio is $\frac{E_b}{8E_s} = \frac{19.2}{4.8} = 4$ - option D. Although the big planet carries all the mass, the blasting energy per unit mass falls as $1/r$, so doubling the radius halves the specific binding energy; that is why the answer is 4, not 8.

questions.question: A vast region has a uniform horizontal electric field of strength $E = 10^4\,\mathrm{N/C}$. At one point of this region a small metal ball of mass $m = 4\,\mathrm{g}$, carrying a positive charge $q = 3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$, is projected vertically upward with speed $v_0 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). (a) What is the magnitude of the ball's displacement from the launch point at the instant its speed again equals $v_0$?
questions.hint: Treat horizontal and vertical motions independently; the speed is the Pythagorean combination of the two components.
questions.solution: The two directions decouple. Horizontal: $a_x = qE/m = (3\times10^{-6}\times10^4)/0.004 = 7.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Vertical: $a_y = -g = -10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The speed returns to $v_0$ when $v_x^2 + v_y^2 = v_0^2$: $(7.5t)^2 + (2-10t)^2 = 4$. Expanding, the constant $4$ cancels: $156.25t^2 - 40t = 0$, giving $t = 0.256\,\mathrm{s}$ besides $t = 0$. Then $x = \frac{1}{2}a_xt^2 = 0.246\,\mathrm{m}$ along the field and $y = v_0t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0.184\,\mathrm{m}$ upward, so $|\Delta\vec{r}| = \sqrt{0.246^2 + 0.184^2} \approx 0.31\,\mathrm{m}$. Cross-check via work-energy: zero net work means $qEx = mgy$, and indeed $0.03\times0.246 \approx 0.04\times0.184$. The ball rises only $0.18\,\mathrm{m}$ while the electric force has already dragged it $0.25\,\mathrm{m}$ sideways.

questions.question: A vast region has a uniform horizontal electric field of strength $E = 10^4\,\mathrm{N/C}$. At one point a small metal ball of mass $m = 4\,\mathrm{g}$, carrying a positive charge $q = 3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$, is projected vertically upward with speed $v_0 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). (b) How much time elapses after launch until the ball's speed again equals $v_0$?
questions.hint: Solve $v_x^2 + v_y^2 = v_0^2$ for $t$ - one root is the trivial $t = 0$.
questions.solution: With $a_x = qE/m = 7.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and $a_y = -g$, the speed squared is $v^2(t) = (7.5t)^2 + (2-10t)^2$. Setting $v^2 = v_0^2 = 4\,\mathrm{m^2/s^2}$: $56.25t^2 + 4 - 40t + 100t^2 = 4 \Rightarrow t(156.25t - 40) = 0$. The non-trivial root is $t = 40/156.25 = 0.256\,\mathrm{s}$. Physically: the vertical component first falls to zero at $t = 0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ (apex) and then reverses, while $v_x$ keeps growing; the total speed is back to $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ shortly after the apex, once the growing horizontal component has replaced the lost vertical one. (With $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ the result is $0.257\,\mathrm{s}$ - identical to two significant figures.)

questions.question: A vast region has a uniform horizontal electric field of strength $E = 10^4\,\mathrm{N/C}$. At one point a small metal ball of mass $m = 4\,\mathrm{g}$, carrying a positive charge $q = 3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$, is projected vertically upward with speed $v_0 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). (c) What is the minimum speed of the ball during its motion?
questions.hint: Minimum speed occurs where the net acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity.
questions.solution: Minimise $v^2(t) = (7.5t)^2 + (2-10t)^2 = 156.25t^2 - 40t + 4$. Setting $\mathrm{d}(v^2)/\mathrm{d}t = 312.5t - 40 = 0$ gives $t = 0.128\,\mathrm{s}$ - exactly half the time found in part (b), as expected for the vertex of a parabola midway between its roots $t=0$ and $t=0.256\,\mathrm{s}$. There $v_x = 7.5\times0.128 = 0.96\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $v_y = 2 - 10\times0.128 = 0.72\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so $v_{\min} = \sqrt{0.96^2 + 0.72^2} = \sqrt{1.44} = 1.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Interpretation: the speed is minimum exactly when the velocity is perpendicular to the constant net acceleration $\vec{a} = (7.5, -10)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ ($\vec{a}\cdot\vec{v} = 0$); before that instant the acceleration still slows the ball, afterwards it speeds it up. (With $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ one gets $1.22\,\mathrm{m/s}$.)

questions.question: A vast region has a uniform horizontal electric field of strength $E = 10^4\,\mathrm{N/C}$. At one point a small metal ball of mass $m = 4\,\mathrm{g}$, carrying a positive charge $q = 3\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{C}$, is projected vertically upward with speed $v_0 = 2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (take $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; the speed is minimum at $t = 0.128\,\mathrm{s}$ after launch, when the velocity is perpendicular to the net acceleration). (d) Where is the ball, relative to the launch point, when it moves slowest? Give the horizontal displacement along the field and the height above the launch point.
questions.hint: Insert the time of the speed minimum into the two kinematic equations for $x(t)$ and $y(t)$.
questions.solution: From part (c) the slowest instant is $t = 0.128\,\mathrm{s}$. The position components follow from the two independent motions: $x = \frac{1}{2}a_xt^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times7.5\times(0.128)^2 = 0.061\,\mathrm{m}$ along the field, and $y = v_0t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 2\times0.128 - 5\times(0.128)^2 = 0.174\,\mathrm{m}$ above the launch point. The displacement ratio $y/x \approx 2.8$ shows the ball is still climbing almost vertically while drifting sideways along $\vec{E}$. Its velocity there is $(0.96, 0.72)\,\mathrm{m/s}$, i.e. $1.2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at $36.9^\circ$ above the horizontal - perpendicular to $\vec{a} = (7.5, -10)\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, as required at the speed minimum. (With $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$: $x = 0.062\,\mathrm{m}$, $y = 0.176\,\mathrm{m}$.)

questions.question: A heating element is built into a boiler containing 10 L of water. Its power is so small that it cannot bring the water to its boiling point. After the water has been heated as long as possible (steady state reached), the heating is switched off, and during the first minute afterwards the water temperature falls by $1^\circ$C. What is the power rating of the heating element if the water equivalent of the boiler is 3 kg? (Take $c_{water} = 4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}$.)
questions.hint: At steady state the element's power exactly equals the rate of heat leakage — and the cooling in the first minute after switch-off tells you that leakage rate.
questions.solution: In the steady state the water temperature no longer rises, so every joule supplied per second by the element is lost to the surroundings: $P = \dot{Q}_{loss}$. When heating stops, the water is at the same temperature, so heat initially keeps leaking at the same rate $P$; the observed fall of $1^\circ$C in the first minute therefore measures that leak rate: $P = (m_{water} + m_{eq})\,c\,\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$. Here $m_{water} = 10$ kg (10 L of water), the water equivalent is $m_{eq} = 3$ kg, and $\Delta T/\Delta t = 1/60$ K/s. So $P = 13 \times 4200 \times \frac{1}{60} \approx 9.1\times10^2$ W $\approx 900$ W (using $c = 4186$ gives 907 W). Concept used: energy balance (first law) — the steady-state input power equals the heat-loss rate, which the cooling just after switch-off reveals. Answer A.

questions.question: A body fully immersed in water can be kept in equilibrium by an upward force of 1.5 N; when it is fully immersed in glycerine (density $1260\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$), the force needed is only 1 N. Find the volume and density of the body. (Density of water $1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.)
questions.hint: Write the force balance for each liquid and subtract the two equations — the weight and $g$ both drop out.
questions.solution: Use Archimedes' principle (buoyancy = weight of displaced liquid) and static equilibrium. With an upward applied force $F$: $mg = \rho_{liq} V g + F$ in each liquid. Subtracting the water equation ($F = 1.5$ N) from the glycerine equation ($F = 1$ N) eliminates $mg$: $(\rho_g - \rho_w)\,Vg = 1.5 - 1.0 = 0.5$ N, so $Vg \times 260 = 0.5$ and $Vg = 1/520$ (SI), i.e. $V \approx 1.96\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^3} \approx 0.20$ L with $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Then from the water balance $\rho V g = 1000\,Vg + 1.5$, giving $\rho = 1000 + \frac{1.5}{Vg} = 1000 + 1.5\times520 = 1780\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$, closest to option E (1800 kg/m^3). Note $g$ cancels out of $\rho$. Consistency check: the holding force is smaller in the denser glycerine, so the body must be denser than both liquids and sink in each — as assumed.

questions.question: A spring (usable in both compression and extension) of natural length $\ell$ is compressed to a length $d < \ell/2$ by a force $F_1$. The spring is then cut in half, and the two identical halves, held side by side (in parallel), are compressed again to length $d$. Into how many equal pieces should a spring with $\ell = 10d$ be cut so that the total force $F_n$, exerted when all the pieces are held in parallel and compressed to length $d$, is maximum?
questions.hint: A spring's stiffness scales inversely with its length — write the total parallel force as a function of the number of pieces and maximize it.
questions.solution: Use Hooke's law $F = k\,\Delta x$ together with the scaling rule $k \propto 1/L$: cutting a spring of constant $k$ into $n$ equal pieces gives each piece constant $nk$ and natural length $\ell/n$. Compressed to length $d$, each piece is shortened by $(\ell/n - d)$ and exerts $F_{piece} = nk(\ell/n - d) = k(\ell - nd)$. With $n$ pieces in parallel the total force is $F_n = n\,k(\ell - nd) = kd\;n(10-n)$ for $\ell = 10d$. This is a downward-opening parabola in $n$, maximal at $n = 5$: $F_5 = 25\,kd$, while $F_4 = F_6 = 24\,kd$. Constraint check: each piece must remain longer than $d$ to be compressed down to $d$, i.e. $\ell/n > d \Rightarrow n < 10$, which rules out $n = 10$ (where the force would vanish anyway). Answer C.

questions.question: A ball of mass $m$ is dropped from rest from the top of a very high tower. The ball is subject to gravity and a drag force $F = -\alpha v^2$ (opposing the motion), where $\alpha$ is a constant. Eventually the ball reaches a constant velocity (terminal velocity) when the total force on it is zero; you can show that in this case $v_T = mg/\alpha$. If instead the ball is thrown downwards with an initial speed of $2v_T$, what is its terminal velocity?
options: It never reaches a terminal velocity
questions.hint: Ask what force balance defines the terminal speed — does the way the motion started enter that equation?
questions.solution: Terminal velocity is defined by the force balance, not by the initial speed: it is the speed at which the drag exactly cancels the weight, $mg = \alpha v_T^2$. This balance involves only $m$, $g$ and $\alpha$, so it is the same whatever the launch conditions. Thrown down at $2v_T$, the drag is $\alpha(2v_T)^2 = 4mg$, larger than the weight, so the net force is upward and the ball decelerates. As $v$ decreases, the drag $\alpha v^2$ decreases too, so the deceleration fades and the speed approaches $v_T$ asymptotically without overshooting. Hence $v_T$ is an attractor of the motion: from any initial speed (above or below it) the ball tends to the same terminal velocity. Answer B.

questions.question: One end of a very thin, negligible-mass rod of length $R = 0.64$ m is attached to a horizontal axle; a small sphere of mass $m = 5$ g and charge $Q = 6\times10^{-7}$ C ($Q > 0$) is fixed to the other end. The whole structure sits in a uniform electric field of strength $E = 2\times10^5$ V/m directed vertically downward, and the rod is initially horizontal. The sphere is given a vertically downward initial speed $v_0$, swings through $3/4$ of a complete circle (ending at the top of the circle, where the rod is vertical and the sphere's velocity is horizontal), at which instant the rod jams and the sphere is released from it. What must $v_0$ be so that the sphere then flies as a projectile exactly back through its initial position? (Take $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$.)
questions.hint: Replace $g$ by an effective downward acceleration that includes the electric force, then chain energy conservation around the 3/4 circle with the projectile's 'equal horizontal and vertical drops' condition.
questions.solution: Both forces on the sphere — weight $mg = 0.005\times9.8 = 0.049$ N and electric force $QE = 6\times10^{-7}\times2\times10^5 = 0.12$ N — point vertically downward and are constant, so replace $g$ by an effective gravity $g_{eff} = g + QE/m = 9.8 + 24 = 33.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$. Phase 1 (3/4 circle from axle height up to the top, height $R$): energy conservation gives $\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv_1^2 + m g_{eff} R$, where $v_1$ is the (horizontal) speed at the top. Phase 2 (projectile from the top): to pass exactly through the initial position it must travel horizontal distance $R$ while falling height $R$, so $t = \sqrt{2R/g_{eff}}$ and $v_1 = R/t = \sqrt{g_{eff}R/2} \approx 3.29$ m/s. Substituting: $v_0^2 = \frac{g_{eff}R}{2} + 2g_{eff}R = \frac{5}{2}g_{eff}R = 2.5\times33.8\times0.64 \approx 54.1\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}$, so $v_0 \approx 7.35$ m/s with $g = 9.8$ (7.38 m/s with $g = 10$) $\approx 7.4$ m/s. The rigid rod can pull as well as push, so the sphere stays on the circle until the designed release.

questions.question: Continuing the electric-rod problem (rod length $R = 0.64$ m, effective gravity $g_{eff} = g + QE/m = 33.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$): using the result of the previous part, the sphere is released at the top of the circle, where its velocity is horizontal with magnitude $v_1 = \sqrt{g_{eff}R/2} \approx 3.3$ m/s, and it flies as a projectile back through its initial position (at axle height, a horizontal distance $R$ from the release point). What angle does the sphere's velocity make with the horizontal as it passes its initial position?
questions.hint: At release the velocity is purely horizontal; track how each component has grown by the time the sphere falls back to axle height, then take the ratio.
questions.solution: Projectile motion, starting from the top with purely horizontal velocity. Horizontal component (constant): $v_x = v_1 = \sqrt{g_{eff}R/2} \approx 3.29$ m/s. Vertical component: the sphere starts with zero vertical velocity and falls height $R$ in $t = \sqrt{2R/g_{eff}} \approx 0.195$ s, so $v_y = g_{eff}t = \sqrt{2g_{eff}R} \approx 6.58$ m/s. Therefore $\tan\theta = \frac{v_y}{v_x} = \frac{\sqrt{2g_{eff}R}}{\sqrt{g_{eff}R/2}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$, a pure number — the angle is independent of $R$, $m$, $Q$, $E$ and even $g$. Hence $\theta = \arctan 2 \approx 63.4^\circ$ below the horizontal: as it passes its starting point the sphere is moving forward and steeply downward. Units check: both components are in m/s, so their ratio is dimensionless.

questions.question: Using the result $v_0 \approx 7.4$ m/s from part (a) (same electric-rod setup: rod $R = 0.64$ m, effective gravity $g_{eff} = g + QE/m = 33.8\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, sphere released at the top with horizontal speed $v_1 = \sqrt{g_{eff}R/2}$ and landing at its initial position at axle height): find the ratio of the sphere's speed when it passes its initial position to its initial speed $v_0$.
questions.hint: Both forces acting on the sphere are conservative and the start and end points are at the same height — what is the net work over the loop?
questions.solution: Shortest route — energy conservation. Gravity and the uniform electric field are both constant, conservative forces, and the sphere starts and finishes at the same height (its initial position is at axle level), so the net work done on it over the whole trip is zero and its speed on return equals $v_0$: the ratio is 1. Component check: $v_f^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2 = \frac{g_{eff}R}{2} + 2g_{eff}R = \frac{5}{2}g_{eff}R = v_0^2$ — the energy $m g_{eff} R$ invested in climbing to the top of the circle is exactly returned during the projectile fall back down to axle height. Note the direction of the velocity has changed (now $\arctan 2 \approx 63^\circ$ below the horizontal), but its magnitude is unchanged.

questions.question: A Gaussian wave has the form $\psi(x,t) = A\,e^{-a(bx+ct)^2}$, where $a$, $b$, $c$ are positive constants. What is the speed and direction of propagation of the wave?
questions.hint: Track a point where the wave has a fixed value and see how it must move as time passes — then check which options even have units of speed.
questions.solution: A rigid profile $\psi = f(bx+ct)$ translates without changing shape: a point of constant displacement satisfies $bx+ct = \text{const}$, so $b\,dx + c\,dt = 0$ and $dx/dt = -c/b$. The wave therefore propagates in the $-x$ direction with speed $c/b$. Now test the options dimensionally: $(bx+ct)$ must be dimensionless, so $[b] = L^{-1}$ and $[c] = T^{-1}$, and $a(bx+ct)^2$ being dimensionless makes $a$ a pure number. Then $a/b$ is a length, $a/c$ a time, $ab^2/c$ a time per length squared and $b/c$ a time per length — none of these is a speed. The correct magnitude $c/b$ appears nowhere among A-D, so the answer is (E) None. Moral: a quick units check (only $c/b$ even has the dimensions of velocity) settles this instantly.

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment the slits are separated by $a$ and the screen is at distance $D$. A thin transparent sheet of thickness $t$ and refractive index $\mu$ is placed in front of one of the slits. It is observed that the central maximum gets shifted by a distance equal to $n$ fringe widths. If the wavelength of the light used is $\lambda$, then $t$ will be:
questions.hint: Ask what extra optical path the sheet inserts, and how many fringe widths that shift is worth.
questions.solution: Concept: a sheet of thickness $t$ and index $\mu$ in one arm adds an extra optical path $(\mu-1)t$ to that arm. At a point $y$ from the old centre the geometric path difference is $ay/D$, so the new central maximum (zero total path difference) sits at $y_0$ with $(\mu-1)t = ay_0/D$, i.e. the whole pattern shifts by $y_0 = (\mu-1)tD/a$. The fringe width is $\beta = \lambda D/a$, so the shift expressed in fringe widths is $n = y_0/\beta = (\mu-1)t/\lambda$. Solving gives $t = n\lambda/(\mu-1)$. Note that $a$ and $D$ cancel — the shift measured in fringe widths depends only on the sheet and the wavelength — which immediately rules out options A, B, C and E. Answer (D).

questions.question: A string is clamped at both the ends and it is vibrating in its 4th harmonic. The equation of the corresponding stationary wave is $Y = 0.3\sin(0.157x)\cos(200\pi t)$ (all quantities in SI units). The length of the string is:
questions.hint: Read the wave number from the sine factor to get the wavelength, then count how many half-wavelengths the 4th harmonic contains.
questions.solution: For a string fixed at both ends the spatial factor $\sin(kx)$ must vanish at $x = 0$ and $x = L$, and the $n$-th harmonic occupies $n$ half-wavelengths: $L = n\lambda/2$. Comparing with $Y = 0.3\sin(0.157x)\cos(200\pi t)$, the wave number is $k = 0.157\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, so $\lambda = 2\pi/k = 6.283/0.157 \approx 40$ m. For the 4th harmonic, $L = 4\lambda/2 = 2\lambda = 80$ m. Consistency check from the time factor: $\omega = 200\pi$ rad/s gives $f = 100$ Hz and wave speed $v = \omega/k \approx 4000$ m/s $= f\lambda$, as it must. Answer (B) 80 m.

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment the two slits are spaced $d = 0.1\ \mathrm{mm}$ apart. When the screen is at a distance $l = 1\ \mathrm{m}$, the first bright maximum is displaced $y = 2\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the central maximum. What is the wavelength of the light?
questions.hint: At the first bright fringe the path difference is exactly one wavelength; be careful with the angstrom conversion.
questions.solution: At the first bright fringe the path difference equals one wavelength: $y = \lambda l/d$, so $\lambda = yd/l$. Using $y = 2$ cm $= 2.0\times10^{-2}$ m (the Bengali version's value; the English text's '2 mm' conflicts and would give 2000 Å, which is not among the options), $d = 0.1$ mm $= 1.0\times10^{-4}$ m and $l = 1$ m: $\lambda = (2.0\times10^{-2})(1.0\times10^{-4})/1 = 2.0\times10^{-6}$ m. Since 1 Å $= 10^{-10}$ m, $\lambda = 2.0\times10^{-6}/10^{-10} = 2\times10^{4}$ Å $= 20000$ Å. Watch the conversion trap in option D: $5\times10^{-7}$ Å is only $5\times10^{-17}$ m. Answer (E).

questions.question: Two long, straight, parallel conductors carry currents $I_1 = 1.5\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_2 = 2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ in the same direction. Conductor 1 passes through the origin and conductor 2 is parallel to it at a distance $x = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$ in the $+\hat{x}$ direction. What is the force per unit length exerted on the second conductor by the first?
questions.hint: Field of a long wire at distance $x$, then $F = IL\times B$ — and remember what parallel currents do.
questions.solution: Ampere's force law between parallel currents. The field of wire 1 at the position of wire 2 has magnitude $B = \mu_0 I_1/(2\pi x)$ and circles around wire 1, so at wire 2 it is perpendicular to both the wire and $\hat{x}$. The force per unit length on wire 2 is $F/L = I_2 B = \mu_0 I_1 I_2/(2\pi x)$. Direction: parallel currents attract, so wire 2 is pulled toward wire 1, i.e. in the $-\hat{x}$ direction. Hence $\vec{F}/L = -\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi x}\,\hat{x}$. Magnitude check: $(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1.5)(2.0)/(2\pi\times0.10) = 6.0\times10^{-6}$ N/m. Options C-E have the wrong powers of $\pi$; option B has the wrong sign. Answer (A).

questions.question: How fast must a 2 m stick be moving along its axis if its length is observed to be 1 m from the laboratory frame?
questions.hint: Relate the contracted length to the Lorentz factor.
questions.solution: Length contraction gives $L = L_0\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$. With $L_0 = 2$ m and $L = 1$ m: $1 - v^2/c^2 = (1/2)^2 = 1/4$, so $v = c\sqrt{1 - 1/4} = (\sqrt{3}/2)c \approx 0.866c$. Answer (C). (Special relativity is outside the Category-C syllabus, so this item is flagged out of the in-syllabus bank.)

questions.question: The position of a particle is $P = (1.0\ \mathrm{m},\ 1.0\ \mathrm{m})$ in standard Cartesian coordinates. What is the position of this particle with respect to a frame whose axes are rotated by $30^\circ$ (counterclockwise) about the same origin?
questions.hint: The new coordinates are the projections of P on the rotated axes; P makes $45^\circ$ with the old $x$-axis.
questions.solution: Rotating the axes by $\theta$ leaves the point fixed but changes its components: $x' = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta$ and $y' = -x\sin\theta + y\cos\theta$ (the projections of $\vec{r}$ on the new axes). With $x = y = 1.0$ m and $\theta = 30^\circ$: $x' = 0.866 + 0.5 = 1.366 \approx 1.37$ m and $y' = -0.5 + 0.866 = 0.366 \approx 0.37$ m. Invariance check: $\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2} = \sqrt{1.866 + 0.134} = \sqrt{2} = |\vec{r}|$, as a rotation must leave the magnitude unchanged. Option (C) corresponds to rotating the axes the other way (or rotating the vector instead of the frame). Answer (B).

questions.question: Two different quantities of the same fluid are mixed in the laboratory. The mass $m_1$ of the hotter sample is twice the mass $m_2$ of the cooler one, and the initial temperature $T_1$ of the hotter sample is twice the initial temperature $T_2 = 30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ of the other. Find the equilibrium temperature (no heat exchange with the surroundings).
questions.hint: Write 'heat lost by the hot sample = heat gained by the cold one'; the common specific heat cancels.
questions.solution: Calorimetry — energy conservation: heat lost by the hot sample equals heat gained by the cold one. Both samples are the same fluid, so the specific heat $c$ is common and cancels: $m_1 c(T_1 - T) = m_2 c(T - T_2)$. With $m_1 = 2m_2$ and $T_1 = 2T_2 = 60^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $2m_2(60 - T) = m_2(T - 30)$, so $120 - 2T = T - 30$, giving $3T = 150$ and $T = 50^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Sanity check: the result lies between 30 °C and 60 °C and is pulled toward the hot temperature because the hot sample has twice the mass. Answer (C).

questions.question: An ideal gas expands adiabatically so that its volume doubles from $V_0$ to $2V_0$. Taking $\gamma = 5/3$ (monatomic gas), what happens to the initial temperature $T_0$?
questions.hint: Use the adiabatic temperature–volume relation; note that $2^{2/3} \approx 1.59$.
questions.solution: For a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas, $TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{const}$. Hence $T = T_0\left(V_0/2V_0\right)^{\gamma-1} = T_0\,2^{-(\gamma-1)}$. With $\gamma = 5/3$: $T = T_0\,2^{-2/3} = T_0/2^{2/3} = T_0/1.59 \approx 0.63\,T_0$. Physically the gas cools because it does work on the surroundings with no heat input (first law with $Q = 0$: $W = -\Delta U$). Option (A) quotes the reciprocal factor 1.59 but calls it a rise — an adiabatic expansion must always cool the gas. Answer (E).

questions.question: A sign consists of two identical uniform legs (each of mass $m$ and length $L$) joined at the top by a frictionless hinge; the feet rest on the ground, forming an inverted V (an A-frame). $\theta$ is the angle between the two legs at the hinge. The coefficient of static friction between the ground and each leg is $\mu$. Which of the following gives the maximum value of $\theta$ such that the sign will not collapse?
questions.hint: Take torques on one leg about the hinge — the frictionless hinge exerts no torque — and see how the needed friction grows with the splay angle.
questions.solution: By symmetry each foot carries a normal force $N = mg$ (the total weight is $2mg$). Consider one leg and take torques about the hinge — the frictionless hinge transmits no torque. With half-angle $\theta/2$, the foot is a horizontal distance $L\sin(\theta/2)$ and a vertical distance $L\cos(\theta/2)$ from the hinge. Torque balance for the leg: $NL\sin(\theta/2) = mg\,(L/2)\sin(\theta/2) + f\,L\cos(\theta/2)$, which gives $f = (mg/2)\tan(\theta/2)$: the wider the stance, the more friction is demanded of the feet. The sign just holds when $f = \mu N = \mu mg$, so $(mg/2)\tan(\theta/2) = \mu mg$, i.e. $\tan(\theta/2) = 2\mu$. Answer (E).

questions.question: A capacitor is constructed from two square metal plates of area $L^2$ separated by a distance $d$. The space between the plates is completely filled by two dielectric layers parallel to the plates: one half of the gap (thickness $d/2$) is filled with a substance of dielectric constant $\kappa_1$ and the other half with a substance of dielectric constant $\kappa_2$. Calculate the capacitance of the device, assuming that the free-space capacitance is $C_0$.
questions.hint: Dielectric slabs stacked along the gap act like series capacitors; slabs side-by-side would act in parallel.
questions.solution: Two dielectric layers stacked along the gap behave as two capacitors in series (the same charge passes through both interfaces). Each layer has thickness $d/2$, so $C_1 = \kappa_1\varepsilon_0 A/(d/2) = 2\kappa_1 C_0$ and $C_2 = 2\kappa_2 C_0$, where $C_0 = \varepsilon_0 A/d = \varepsilon_0 L^2/d$. Series combination: $1/C = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 = \dfrac{1}{2C_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{\kappa_1} + \dfrac{1}{\kappa_2}\right)$, hence $C = \dfrac{2C_0\kappa_1\kappa_2}{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}$. Limit checks: $\kappa_1 = \kappa_2 = \kappa$ gives $C = \kappa C_0$ (uniform dielectric) and $\kappa_2 \to \infty$ gives $C = 2\kappa_1 C_0$ (a conducting layer halves the gap) — both correct. Answer (D). (Option E would hold if the two dielectrics split the plate area side-by-side instead of stacking along the gap.)

questions.question: Suppose the position of a particle of mass $m$ in the $xy$-plane is $\boldsymbol{r} = (x, y, z) = (r\cos\phi,\ r\sin\phi,\ 0)$, where $r$ and $\phi$ are functions of time $t$. Which of the following is the $z$-component of $\boldsymbol{l}$, where $\boldsymbol{l}$ is the angular momentum of the particle?
questions.hint: Compute the cross product — or note that only the tangential velocity component $r\dot{\phi}$ can contribute.
questions.solution: Angular momentum is $\boldsymbol{l} = m\,\boldsymbol{r}\times\boldsymbol{v}$ with $l_z = m(xv_y - yv_x)$. Differentiating the position: $v_x = \dot{r}\cos\phi - r\dot{\phi}\sin\phi$ and $v_y = \dot{r}\sin\phi + r\dot{\phi}\cos\phi$. Then $xv_y - yv_x = r\cos\phi(\dot{r}\sin\phi + r\dot{\phi}\cos\phi) - r\sin\phi(\dot{r}\cos\phi - r\dot{\phi}\sin\phi) = r^2\dot{\phi}(\cos^2\phi + \sin^2\phi) = r^2\dot{\phi}$. So $l_z = mr^2\dot{\phi}$: only the tangential velocity component $r\dot{\phi}$ contributes, because the radial component $\dot{r}$ is parallel to $\boldsymbol{r}$ and produces no moment. Check: uniform circular motion ($r$ constant) gives the familiar $L = mr^2\omega$. Answer (B).

questions.question: The velocity of a body as a function of time $t$ is given by $v(t) = \dfrac{\alpha}{3t} + \beta t^2 + \gamma e^{-\sigma t^3}$. What are the dimensions of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \sigma$ respectively?
questions.hint: Every term must individually have the dimensions of velocity, and an exponential's argument must be dimensionless.
questions.solution: Each added term in a velocity equation must separately have the dimensions of velocity, $[LT^{-1}]$, and the argument of an exponential must be dimensionless. (i) $\alpha/(3t)$: $[\alpha]/T = LT^{-1}$ gives $[\alpha] = [M^0L^1T^0]$. (ii) $\beta t^2$: $[\beta]T^2 = LT^{-1}$ gives $[\beta] = [M^0L^1T^{-3}]$. (iii) $\gamma$ multiplies the exponential, so $[\gamma] = [M^0L^1T^{-1}]$; and $\sigma t^3$ must be dimensionless, so $[\sigma] = [M^0L^0T^{-3}]$. Only option (A) satisfies all four conditions. (Note the exponent must contain $t^3$: with a plain $t$, $\sigma$ would have dimension $T^{-1}$, which no option offers.) Answer (A).

questions.question: The total number of turns and the cross-sectional area of a solenoid are fixed, but its length $L$ is varied by adjusting the separation between windings. The self-inductance of the solenoid will be proportional to:
questions.hint: Write the solenoid field in terms of the turn density $N/L$ and build up the flux linkage.
questions.solution: Self-inductance is flux linkage per unit current. Inside a long solenoid the field is $B = \mu_0 (N/L) I$, with $N$ the total number of turns and $L$ the length. The flux linkage through the coil is $NBA = \mu_0 N^2 A I / L$, so the inductance is $L_{\mathrm{ind}} = \mu_0 N^2 A / L$. With $N$ and $A$ fixed, $L_{\mathrm{ind}} \propto 1/L$: stretching the solenoid over a longer length thins out the turn density, weakens the field for a given current, and lowers the inductance. Answer (D) $1/L$.

questions.question: In a simple AC circuit involving only a resistor $R = 50\ \Omega$ and a voltage source $V$, find the linear frequency of the generator if $V = 0.50\,V_m$ at time $t = 1/720\ \mathrm{s}$ (assume $V = 0$ at $t = 0$; $V_m$ is the peak voltage).
questions.hint: Ask at what phase angle a sine wave first reaches half of its peak.
questions.solution: With $V = 0$ at $t = 0$ the source voltage is $V = V_m\sin(2\pi f t)$; the resistance is a red herring — it does not affect the source waveform. The condition gives $\sin(2\pi f/720) = 0.5$. The first time after $t = 0$ that the sine reaches half its peak corresponds to the angle $\pi/6$: $2\pi f/720 = \pi/6$, so $f = 60$ Hz. Check: at $f = 60$ Hz the period is $T = 1/60$ s, and $t = 1/720$ s $= T/12$, so the phase is $2\pi/12 = \pi/6$ and $\sin(\pi/6) = 0.5$. (The next solution, $5\pi/6$, would give $f = 300$ Hz, which is not offered; option A confuses $\omega = 120\pi$ rad/s with $f$.) Answer (C) 60 Hz.

questions.question: A light, uniform, ideal spring has one end fixed; a mass attached to the other end oscillates with angular frequency $\omega$. Now the other end of the spring is also fixed, and the spring is cut in half, with the mass attached between the two half-springs (each half connects the mass to one of the fixed ends). The new angular frequency of the oscillations is:
questions.hint: How does the constant of half a spring compare with that of the whole, and do the two halves aid or oppose each other?
questions.solution: The spring constant of a uniform spring scales inversely with its length — half the coils means twice the stiffness — so each half-spring has $k' = 2k$, where $k$ is the original constant and $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$. In the new arrangement both halves attach the mass to fixed supports, so they act in parallel: displacing the mass stretches one half and compresses the other, and the two restoring forces add. Hence $k_{\mathrm{eff}} = 2k + 2k = 4k$ and the new angular frequency is $\omega' = \sqrt{k_{\mathrm{eff}}/m} = \sqrt{4k/m} = 2\omega$. Answer (D).

questions.question: A spring of relaxed length $l_1$ and spring constant $k_1$ is placed 'in parallel' with a spring of relaxed length $l_2$ and spring constant $k_2$ (both stretched between the same pair of end plates). A force $F$ is applied to each end. The combination acts like a single spring with spring constant $k$ and relaxed length $l$, where:
questions.hint: At a common end-to-end length each tension is constant times (length minus its own natural length), and the tensions add.
questions.solution: In a parallel arrangement both springs span the same end-to-end length, say $\ell$. Each spring's tension is its constant times its own extension: $T_1 = k_1(\ell - l_1)$ and $T_2 = k_2(\ell - l_2)$. The total tension is $T = T_1 + T_2 = (k_1+k_2)\ell - (k_1l_1 + k_2l_2) = (k_1+k_2)(\ell - l)$, so $k = k_1 + k_2$ and the effective relaxed length is the stiffness-weighted mean $l = (k_1l_1 + k_2l_2)/(k_1+k_2)$ — each natural length weighted by its own spring constant. Checks: identical springs ($k_1 = k_2$, $l_1 = l_2$) give $l = l_1$; letting $k_2 \to \infty$ (a rigid rod of length $l_2$) forces $l \to l_2$, as it must. Answer (B).

questions.question: A flat uniform disk of radius $2R$ has a concentric hole of radius $R$ removed from its center, leaving an annulus. The annulus is then cut in half along a diameter. The remaining half-annulus has mass $M$. What is the moment of inertia of this shape about the axis of rotational symmetry of the original disk (the axis through the center, perpendicular to the plane of the disk)?
questions.hint: Cutting a body in half removes mass but relocates none of it — how must the moment of inertia of each half compare with that of the whole annulus?
questions.solution: Use $I=\int r^2\,dm$ about the symmetry axis. For a uniform annulus with inner radius $R$, outer radius $2R$ and mass $m$: $I=\frac{1}{2}m(R_1^2+R_2^2)=\frac{1}{2}m(R^2+4R^2)=\frac{5}{2}mR^2$. The half-annulus has mass $M$, so the full annulus would have mass $2M$. Cutting the annulus in half does not move any mass element — every element keeps its distance from the central axis — so the two halves share the moment of inertia equally: $I_{\text{half}}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{5}{2}(2M)R^2=\frac{5}{2}MR^2$. Direct check: the half-annulus area is $\frac{1}{2}\pi(4R^2-R^2)=\frac{3\pi R^2}{2}$, so $\sigma=\frac{2M}{3\pi R^2}$, and $I=\sigma\pi\int_R^{2R}r^3\,dr=\frac{2M}{3\pi R^2}\cdot\pi\frac{15R^4}{4}=\frac{5}{2}MR^2$. Since all the mass lies between $R$ and $2R$ from the axis, $I>MR^2$, consistent with $2.5\,MR^2$.

questions.question: Light is incident at nearly normal incidence on a prism of apex angle $\alpha$ made of a material of refractive index $n_r$; the light comes from, and finally returns to, a surrounding medium of refractive index $n_i$. Using the small-angle approximation, the angle of deviation equals:
questions.hint: Snell's law works from either side of a surface — write it at both faces and remember the internal angles add up to the apex angle.
questions.solution: Apply Snell's law at each refracting surface with $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ for small angles. First surface: $n_i i_1 = n_r r_1$. Second surface: $n_r r_2 = n_i i_2$. Prism geometry ties the internal angles to the apex angle: $r_1+r_2=\alpha$. The total deviation is the sum of the bendings at the two surfaces: $\delta=(i_1-r_1)+(i_2-r_2)$. Substituting $i_1=\frac{n_r}{n_i}r_1$ and $i_2=\frac{n_r}{n_i}r_2$ gives $\delta=\frac{n_r}{n_i}(r_1+r_2)-(r_1+r_2)=\left(\frac{n_r}{n_i}-1\right)\alpha$. Limiting check: for a prism in air ($n_i=1$) this reduces to the familiar thin-prism result $\delta=(n_r-1)\alpha$, confirming the algebra; and if $n_r=n_i$ there is no bend, $\delta=0$, as expected.

questions.question: Two springs of spring constants $k_1$ and $k_2$ are connected in series (one after the other) and stretched by pulling the free end, so the same tension acts through both springs. What is the ratio of their stored potential energies, $U_1/U_2$?
questions.hint: In a series connection it is the tension, not the extension, that is the same for both springs.
questions.solution: Springs in series carry the same force $F$ (force balance on the massless junction between them). Write the spring energy in force form: with $x=F/k$, $U=\frac{1}{2}kx^2=\frac{F^2}{2k}$. So for equal forces the softer spring (smaller $k$) stretches more and stores more energy: $\frac{U_1}{U_2}=\frac{F^2/(2k_1)}{F^2/(2k_2)}=\frac{k_2}{k_1}$. Limiting check: if $k_2\to\infty$ (effectively rigid), $U_2\to0$ and the ratio $U_1/U_2$ grows without bound like $k_2$ — exactly what option C predicts. The common trap is assuming equal extensions (that is the parallel case); in series it is the force that is common.

questions.question: Which of the following represent(s) traveling wave(s)? (Here $A$, $a$, $b$, $k$, $\omega$ are positive constants and $v$ is a speed.)
questions.hint: Ask whether the whole expression can be written as a function of a single combination like $(x\mp vt)$ — that is the fingerprint of a traveling wave.
questions.solution: A traveling wave keeps its shape while its profile moves: the function must depend on position and time only through a single combination such as $(x\mp vt)$ or $(kz-\omega t)$, so that surfaces of constant phase travel at constant speed. (B) $e^{-i(kz-\omega t)}$ is the complex representation of a plane wave traveling in $+z$ — its phase $kz-\omega t$ is exactly of that form, so it is a traveling wave. (C) $\frac{A}{r}\cos(kr\mp\omega t)$ (with $\omega=kv$) has phase $kr\mp\omega t$; setting it constant gives $r=r_0\pm vt$ — spherical phase fronts expanding or contracting at speed $v$. The $1/r$ amplitude decay conserves the energy flux of the spreading wave but does not stop it from being a traveling wave. (A) contains the mixed term $t\,x^3$: it cannot be rewritten as $f(x\mp vt)$, so the waveform distorts in time and it is not a traveling wave. Hence both (B) and (C) qualify.

questions.question: An object of mass $m=1$ kg is set in motion in one dimension and has a position–time relationship $x = 2t^2 + t + 2$, where $x$ is in meters and $t$ in seconds. Which of the following represents the force acting on the object?
questions.hint: Force comes from acceleration — differentiate the position twice and ignore the terms that vanish.
questions.solution: Differentiate the position twice to get the acceleration: $v=\frac{dx}{dt}=4t+1$ m/s, then $a=\frac{dv}{dt}=4$ m/s$^2$, a constant. Newton's second law gives $F=ma=1\times4=4$ N. Note that the linear term $t$ and the constant term $2$ in $x(t)$ contribute nothing to the acceleration — only the $2t^2$ term matters, since $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}(2t^2)=4$. Because the acceleration is constant, the force is constant in time (not just on average). Units check: kg$\cdot$m/s$^2$ = N. Answer: 4 N.

questions.question: An infinitely long wire along the z-axis is composed of positive charges with linear charge density $+\lambda$ which are at rest, and negative charges with linear charge density $-\lambda$ moving with speed $v$ in the $z$ direction (both densities as measured in the lab frame). Determine the magnitude of the electric field $E$ at points a distance $r$ outside the wire.
questions.hint: Count the total charge enclosed by a coaxial Gaussian cylinder — motion of charge does not change how much charge is there.
questions.solution: Apply Gauss's law, $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=Q_{\text{encl}}/\epsilon_0$, with a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $r$ and length $L$. The enclosed charge is the algebraic sum of both charge species contained in the cylinder: $Q_{\text{encl}}=(+\lambda)L+(-\lambda)L=0$, because both linear densities are specified in the lab frame — the frame in which we evaluate the field. Gauss's law cares only about the enclosed charge at that instant, not about whether the charges are moving; the motion sets up a current and hence a magnetic field $\vec B$ circling the wire, but no net charge and therefore no electric field. By the cylindrical symmetry, $E$ would have to be uniform on the Gaussian surface, so $E\cdot 2\pi r L=0$ and $E=0$. The distractors tempt you to fold the speed $v$ into the electric field.

questions.question: A wire 100 cm in length carries a current of 1.0 A in a region where a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 100 T points in the x-direction. If $\theta=45^\circ$ is the angle between the wire and the x-axis, what is the magnetic force on the wire?
questions.hint: Use the $BIL\sin\theta$ magnitude formula, and remember to convert centimeters to meters.
questions.solution: The force on a straight current-carrying wire in a uniform field is $\vec F=I\vec L\times\vec B$, with magnitude $F=BIL\sin\theta$. Convert the length to SI: $L=100\text{ cm}=1.00$ m. Then $F=100\ \text{T}\times1.0\ \text{A}\times1.00\ \text{m}\times\sin45^\circ=100\times0.7071=70.7$ N. The negative options cannot be chosen: the sign depends on the sense of the current (which end the current enters), which the problem does not specify, so only the magnitude 70.7 N is determined. Sanity check: if the wire were parallel to $\vec B$ ($\theta=0$) the force would vanish, and it is maximal ($100$ N) at $\theta=90^\circ$; $45^\circ$ gives $1/\sqrt2$ of the maximum.

questions.question: A horizontal beam of length 10 m and weight 200 N is hinged to a wall. Its far end is supported by a cable that makes an angle of 60° with the beam, running from the far end up to the wall. A 500 N person stands on the beam 2 m from the wall (figure: hinge at the wall, beam weight acting at its midpoint, person between the hinge and the far end, cable attached at the far end). What is the tension in the cable?
questions.hint: Take torques about the hinge; only the component of the tension perpendicular to the beam turns it.
questions.solution: Static equilibrium: take torques about the hinge so the unknown hinge reaction drops out. The beam's weight 200 N acts at its center, 5 m from the wall; the person's 500 N acts 2 m from the wall; the tension acts at 10 m, and only its component perpendicular to the beam, $T\sin60^\circ$, has a moment arm. Torque balance (counterclockwise = clockwise): $T\sin60^\circ\times10 = 200\times5 + 500\times2 = 1000+1000 = 2000$ N$\cdot$m. Hence $T=\dfrac{2000}{10\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{200}{0.866}\approx231$ N. The horizontal component $T\cos60^\circ$ acts along the beam's line toward the hinge and contributes no torque about it. Order-of-magnitude check: the cable's moment arm is the largest, so $T$ (231 N) is smaller than the total load (700 N) — consistent.

questions.question: Consider a flat uniform square of mass $M$ and side length $L$. A circle is cut out of the square; the circle has a diameter equal to the side length $L$ and the same center as the square. What is the moment of inertia of the remaining shape about an axis through the center and perpendicular to the plane of the square?
questions.hint: Treat the hole as negative mass: subtract the disk's moment of inertia from the square's, all about the same central axis.
questions.solution: Use superposition about the same central perpendicular axis: $I_{\text{remaining}}=I_{\text{square}}-I_{\text{disk}}$. The square has $I=\frac{1}{6}ML^2$. The circle's area is $\pi(L/2)^2=\frac{\pi L^2}{4}$ against the square's $L^2$, so (uniform sheet) its mass is $m=\frac{\pi}{4}M$. A uniform disk of mass $m$ and radius $L/2$ has $I=\frac{1}{2}m(L/2)^2=\frac{\pi M}{4}\cdot\frac{L^2}{8}=\frac{\pi}{32}ML^2$. Therefore $I_{\text{remaining}}=\left(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{\pi}{32}\right)ML^2\approx(0.167-0.098)ML^2=0.069\,ML^2$. Sanity check: the hole removes about 78% of the area (it sits right at the center, where mass contributes least), so the result must be positive but far below $\frac{1}{6}ML^2$ — and it is.

questions.question: What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at the center of a circular ring of radius $r$ that carries a current $I$?
questions.hint: Apply Biot–Savart at the center: every element contributes equally and perpendicular to the loop.
questions.solution: Use the Biot–Savart law, $d\vec B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\frac{d\vec l\times\hat r}{r^2}$. At the center of the ring every current element is perpendicular to its position vector ($\sin90^\circ=1$) and lies at the same distance $r$, and all contributions point the same way (perpendicular to the loop, by the right-hand rule). So the magnitudes simply add: $B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r^2}\oint dl=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r^2}(2\pi r)=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$. Option B, $\mu_0 I/2\pi r$, is the field of a long straight wire — a classic mix-up; option A is wrong because a current loop certainly produces a field at its center (this is how an electromagnet coil works).

questions.question: Three cubical blocks of the same volume are made of wood, styrofoam and plastic. When the plastic block is placed in water, half of its volume is submerged. If the wooden block is placed in water with the plastic block on top, the wooden block is just fully submerged. Similarly, if the styrofoam block is placed in oil (density $0.7\,\rho_{\text{water}}$) with the plastic block on top, the styrofoam block is just fully submerged. What is the ratio of the density of wood to the density of styrofoam, $\rho_w/\rho_s$?
questions.hint: Write weight = buoyant force for each floating situation; the just-submerged condition means the whole volume displaces fluid.
questions.solution: Floating equilibrium: buoyant force = total weight. Plastic alone in water, half submerged: $\rho_p=0.5\,\rho_{\text{water}}$. Wood with plastic on top, wood just fully submerged in water: $(\rho_w+\rho_p)V=\rho_{\text{water}}V\Rightarrow\rho_w=0.5\,\rho_{\text{water}}$. Styrofoam with plastic on top, just fully submerged in oil: $(\rho_s+\rho_p)V=0.7\,\rho_{\text{water}}V\Rightarrow\rho_s=0.2\,\rho_{\text{water}}$. Hence $\rho_w/\rho_s=0.5/0.2=2.5$. (Excluded from the bank: buoyancy is outside the listed topic set.)

questions.question: A particle has potential energy $U = k r^n$, where $r=|\vec r|$ is the distance from the origin and $k$, $n$ are constants. Calculate the vector force due to this potential energy.
questions.hint: Force is minus the gradient of the potential — differentiate with respect to $r$ and convert the unit vector $\hat r$ into $\vec r/r$.
questions.solution: A conservative force is the negative gradient of the potential: $\vec F=-\nabla U=-\frac{dU}{dr}\hat r$, since $U$ depends only on $r$. Here $\frac{dU}{dr}=kn\,r^{\,n-1}$, and the radial unit vector is $\hat r=\vec r/r$. Therefore $\vec F=-kn\,r^{\,n-1}\frac{\vec r}{r}=-kn\,r^{\,n-2}\,\vec r$. Checks: for $n=2$ ($U=kr^2$, a 3D spring), $\vec F=-2k\,\vec r$ — a linear restoring force toward the origin, and the exponent $n-2=0$ correctly leaves no extra $r$ factor; the minus sign is essential because the force must point down the potential gradient (toward lower $U$), which rules out options C, D and E.

questions.question: A man jumps off a building 202 m high onto cushions having a total thickness of 2 m. If the cushions are crushed to a thickness of 0.5 m while stopping him, what is the man's (average) acceleration as he slows down, expressed in units of $g$?
questions.hint: Connect the two stages through the landing speed: $v^2$ from the free fall equals $v^2$ in the crushing stage.
questions.solution: Free fall: he drops through $h=202-2=200$ m (building height minus the cushion thickness) before touching the cushions, arriving with speed $v$ given by $v^2=2gh$. Stopping: the cushions crush from 2 m to 0.5 m, so he decelerates over $d=2-0.5=1.5$ m with (constant) deceleration $a$: $v^2=2ad$. Eliminating $v^2$: $a=g\,\dfrac{h}{d}=g\times\dfrac{200}{1.5}\approx133g$. Order-of-magnitude check: the stopping distance (1.5 m) is roughly $133$ times smaller than the fall height (200 m), so the deceleration must be roughly $133$ times $g$ — the short crushing distance is what makes the landing violent.

questions.question: An object orbits a star in an elliptical orbit. Its distance from the star is $2a$ at aphelion (farthest point) and $a$ at perihelion (closest point). Determine the ratio of the object's speed at perihelion to its speed at aphelion.
questions.hint: No torque acts about the star, so compare angular momenta at the two ends of the ellipse where velocity is perpendicular to the radius.
questions.solution: Gravity is a central force, so it exerts no torque about the star and the object's angular momentum is conserved throughout the orbit: $m v_p r_p = m v_a r_a$. At perihelion and aphelion the velocity is exactly perpendicular to the radius vector, so this product form applies directly. Hence $\dfrac{v_p}{v_a}=\dfrac{r_a}{r_p}=\dfrac{2a}{a}=2$ — the object moves twice as fast at the close point as at the far point. This is precisely Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times): near perihelion the shorter radius is compensated by a proportionally larger speed. Limiting check: for a circular orbit ($r_p=r_a$) the ratio is 1, as the formula gives.

questions.question: Which of the following does the Hall effect relate to?
options: The behavior of waves in regularly spaced lattices, known as constructive interference
The generation of a voltage when a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field
The consequences of Coulomb's inverse-square law
questions.hint: The Hall effect is what happens to moving charges in a wire when a magnetic field pushes them sideways.
questions.solution: In the Hall effect, a magnetic field applied perpendicular to a current-carrying conductor pushes the drifting charge carriers sideways through the magnetic Lorentz force $q\vec v\times\vec B$. Charges pile up on one edge of the strip until the resulting transverse electric field exactly balances the magnetic force on subsequent carriers. The steady charge separation is a measurable transverse (Hall) voltage across the conductor — the working principle of Hall probes used to measure magnetic fields, and historically the evidence that currents in metals are carried by negative charges. This matches option B. Options A, C and D describe wave interference in lattices, electrostatics, and dielectric behavior respectively — none involves the combination of current plus magnetic field.

questions.question: Consider a system of particles, each of mass $m$, at temperature $T$, which follow the classical Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics. What is the average speed of the particles?
questions.hint: Remember the ordering: most probable speed < mean speed < rms speed for the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.
questions.solution: The mean speed follows from averaging $v$ over the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution, $\langle v\rangle=\int v f(v)\,dv=\sqrt{\frac{8kT}{\pi m}}$. It sits between the most probable speed $\sqrt{2kT/m}$ (option E) and the rms speed $\sqrt{3kT/m}$ (option A), since the distribution's long tail pulls the mean above the peak. (Excluded from the bank: statistical distributions go beyond the syllabus's ideal-gas basics.)

questions.question: A 100 g mass attached to a spring moves on a horizontal frictionless table in simple harmonic motion with amplitude 16 cm and period 2 s ($x$ in cm, $t$ in s). The mass is released from rest at $t=0$ at $x=-16$ cm. Which of the following is the displacement as a function of time?
questions.hint: Fix the angular frequency from the period first, then choose the phase so that the particle starts at rest at the negative extreme.
questions.solution: Write the SHM solution as $x=A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ with $A=16$ cm and $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ rad/s. Released from rest at $x=-16$ cm means the mass starts at the negative extreme, where the velocity is momentarily zero: at $t=0$, $x=-A$, which requires $\cos\varphi=-1$, i.e. $\varphi=\pi$. Hence $x=16\cos(\pi t+\pi)$ cm (equivalently $-16\cos\pi t$ cm); the 100 g mass is irrelevant to the kinematics. Test each option at $t=0$: (A) and (B) give $x=+16$ cm — wrong extreme; (C) starts correctly but has $\omega=\pi/2$, i.e. period $T=4$ s; (D) gives $+16$ cm at $t=0$ and $T=1$ s. Only (E) matches both the initial condition and the 2 s period.

questions.question: By the early 1900s the two major theories of physics were Maxwell's equations and Newton's laws. The transformation from a lab reference frame to a moving reference frame was done by the Galilean transformation ($x' = x - vt$, $t' = t$). Which of the major theories is invariant under these transformation equations?
options: Neither Maxwell's equations nor Newton's laws
Both Maxwell's equations and Newton's laws
questions.hint: Ask what the Galilean velocity addition $u' = u - v$ does to the fixed speed $c$ appearing in Maxwell's equations.
questions.solution: Under the Galilean transformation $x' = x - vt$, $t' = t$, velocities transform as $u' = u - v$; differentiating again gives $a' = a$ because $v$ is constant. Masses and forces are unchanged, so $F = ma$ keeps exactly the same form in every inertial frame: Newton's laws are Galilean invariant. Maxwell's equations, however, contain the fixed wave speed $c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$. Under $u' = u - v$ the measured speed of light would become $c - v$ or $c + v$ in a moving frame, so the equations would change form — they are NOT invariant under Galilean transformations (they are invariant under Lorentz transformations instead). This very conflict motivated Einstein's 1905 relativity paper. Hence only Newton's laws are invariant: choice D.

questions.question: A massless cable of diameter 2.54 cm is tied horizontally between two trees 18.0 m apart. A tightrope walker stands at the center of the cable, giving it a tension of 7300 N. The cable stretches and makes an angle of 1.50° with the horizontal. What is the Young's modulus of the material of the cable?
questions.solution: Out of syllabus (elasticity), but for reference: stress $= T/A = 7300/\pi(0.0127)^2 = 1.44\times10^{7}$ Pa; each half of the cable stretches from 9.0 m to $9.0/\cos 1.50^\circ$ m, so the strain $= 1/\cos 1.50^\circ - 1 = 3.43\times10^{-4}$; $Y = 1.44\times10^{7}/3.43\times10^{-4} \approx 4.2\times10^{10}$ N/m$^2$ (E).

questions.question: A long, insulating cylindrical rod has a radius $R$ and carries a uniform volume charge density $\rho$. A uniform external electric field $E$ exists in the direction of its axis. The rod moves in the direction of its axis at speed $v$. What is the magnetic field $B$ at the surface of the rod?
questions.hint: Turn the moving charge density into a current (charge per unit length times speed), then apply Ampère's law on a loop around the rod.
questions.solution: The moving charge density constitutes an electric current. The charge per unit length of the rod is $\lambda = \rho\pi R^2$, so the current passing any fixed point is $I = \lambda v = \rho\pi R^2 v$. Apply Ampère's law, $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_{\rm enc}$, on a circle of radius $R$ coaxial with the rod: symmetry makes $B$ azimuthal and constant on the loop, so $B(2\pi R) = \mu_0\rho\pi R^2 v$ and $B = \mu_0 R\rho v/2$. The steady axial electric field contributes no displacement-current term and has no azimuthal effect, so it is a distractor. Note: options A and C are printed identically in the source scan; the correct value $\mu_0 R\rho v/2$ is recorded here as choice A.

questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor consists of two discs of radius $R$ separated by a distance $d \ll R$. The capacitor carries charge $Q$, and is being charged by a small, constant current $I$. What is the magnetic field $B$ just inside the edge of the capacitor?
questions.hint: Inside the gap the changing electric flux behaves like a uniform current density; enclose the whole disc with an Amperian loop at the rim.
questions.solution: While charging, $dQ/dt = I$, so the field between the plates, $E = Q/(\varepsilon_0\pi R^2)$, changes at the rate $dE/dt = I/(\varepsilon_0\pi R^2)$. In the gap there is no conduction current, so use the Ampère–Maxwell law $\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\, d\Phi_E/dt$: the changing electric flux acts as a displacement current of uniform density $J_d = \varepsilon_0\, dE/dt = I/(\pi R^2)$. An Amperian circle of radius $R$ just inside the rim encloses $J_d\pi R^2 = I$, giving $B(2\pi R) = \mu_0 I$, i.e. $B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi R)$ — exactly the same as the field just outside the wire, so $\vec{B}$ is continuous across the edge of the capacitor. Answer B.

questions.question: In an experiment to determine the speed of sound, a student measured the distance that a sound wave traveled to be $(75.0 \pm 2.0)$ cm, and found the time it took the sound wave to travel this distance to be $(2.15 \pm 0.10)$ ms. Assume the uncertainties are Gaussian. How should the computed speed of sound be recorded?
questions.hint: Convert to SI, divide for the speed, then combine the two fractional uncertainties in quadrature.
questions.solution: Best estimate: $v = d/t = (0.750\ \text{m})/(2.15\times10^{-3}\ \text{s}) = 348.8$ m/s. For a quotient of independent Gaussian variables the fractional uncertainties add in quadrature: $\sigma_v/v = \sqrt{(\sigma_d/d)^2 + (\sigma_t/t)^2} = \sqrt{(2.0/75.0)^2 + (0.10/2.15)^2} = \sqrt{(0.0267)^2 + (0.0465)^2} = 0.0536$. Thus $\sigma_v = 0.0536 \times 348.8 = 18.7 \approx 19$ m/s; the time uncertainty dominates. (Adding the two absolute errors linearly would overestimate the error, while using only the larger one would underestimate it.) Rounded to matching significant figures the result is $(349 \pm 19)$ m/s — choice E.

questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor consists of two discs of radius $R$ separated by a distance $d \ll R$. The capacitor carries charge $Q$, and is being charged by a small, constant current $I$. What is the power $P$ delivered to the capacitor?
questions.hint: Power is the rate of change of the stored energy $Q^2/2C$, and only $Q$ changes with time.
questions.solution: The power delivered equals the rate at which the capacitor's stored energy grows. For a parallel-plate disc capacitor $C = \varepsilon_0\pi R^2/d$ and $U = Q^2/(2C)$, so $P = dU/dt = (Q/C)(dQ/dt) = QI/C = IQd/(\varepsilon_0\pi R^2)$. Equivalently, the source pushes current $I$ against the instantaneous plate voltage $V = Q/C = Qd/(\varepsilon_0\pi R^2)$, and $P = IV$ gives the same result. Limiting checks: $P$ grows linearly with the accumulated charge $Q$ (the voltage rises as the capacitor fills), and it vanishes as $d \to 0$ where $C \to \infty$ — both physically sensible. Answer D.

questions.question: A beam of muons is maintained in a circular orbit by a uniform magnetic field. Neglect energy loss due to electromagnetic radiation. The mass of the muon is $1.88\times10^{-28}$ kg, its charge is $-1.602\times10^{-19}$ C, and its half-life is 1.523 µs. The speed of the muons is much less than the speed of light.
