It is found that half of the muons decay during each full orbit. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field?
questions.hint: Set the cyclotron period $2\pi m/|q|B$ equal to the half-life.
questions.solution: 'Half decay during each full orbit' fixes the period: after one orbit of duration $T$ the surviving fraction is $2^{-T/t_{1/2}}$, which equals $1/2$ exactly when $T = t_{1/2} = 1.523\ \mu$s. For a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field, $|q|vB = mv^2/r$ gives the cyclotron period $T = 2\pi m/(|q|B)$, which is independent of $v$ and $r$ (valid since $v \ll c$). Solving for $B$: $B = 2\pi m/(|q|T) = 2\pi(1.88\times10^{-28})/(1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.523\times10^{-6}) = 4.84\times10^{-3}\ \text{T} \approx 4.85$ mT. The negative sign of the muon charge only reverses the sense of circulation, not the magnitude. Answer C.

questions.question: Light is incident on a prism of apex angle $\alpha = 60^\circ$ at an angle of incidence $\theta_{i1} = 30^\circ$. The prism is made of a substance of refractive index $n_r = 1.5$ and is surrounded by a near vacuum ($n = 1$). Determine the net angle of deviation of the light due to passage through the prism.
questions.hint: Refract in, use the prism geometry $\theta_3 = \alpha - \theta_2$, check the critical angle at the second face, then refract out.
questions.solution: Trace the ray with Snell's law at both faces. First face: $\sin\theta_2 = \sin 30^\circ/1.5 = 1/3$, so $\theta_2 = 19.47^\circ$ (bent toward the normal). Prism geometry links the interior angles: at the second face the ray strikes at $\theta_3 = \alpha - \theta_2 = 60^\circ - 19.47^\circ = 40.53^\circ$. Before the exit refraction, check total internal reflection: the critical angle is $\theta_c = \arcsin(1/1.5) = 41.81^\circ$. Since $\theta_3 < \theta_c$ the ray just manages to escape. Exit face: $\sin\theta_4 = 1.5\sin 40.53^\circ = 0.9748$, so $\theta_4 = 77.1^\circ$. The net deviation is the sum of the two bendings: $\delta = (\theta_1 - \theta_2) + (\theta_4 - \theta_3) = \theta_1 + \theta_4 - \alpha = 30^\circ + 77.1^\circ - 60^\circ \approx 47^\circ$. Answer D.

questions.question: A block on a ramp is given an initial velocity $v_0$ upward along the ramp. It slides up the ramp over a duration $t_u$, traveling some distance, and then slides downward for a time $t_d$ until it returns to its original position. What is $t_d$ in terms of $t_u$? The height of the incline is 0.6 times its length and the coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.5.
questions.hint: The same distance is covered each way; find both accelerations with friction reversing direction, then use $d = \frac{1}{2}at^2$ on each leg.
questions.solution: Height = 0.6 $\times$ length means $\sin\theta = 0.6$ and $\cos\theta = 0.8$. Kinetic friction always opposes the velocity, so the two legs have different accelerations. Uphill, gravity and friction both point down the slope: $a_{\rm up} = g(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta) = g(0.6 + 0.5\times0.8) = g$. Downhill, friction points up the slope: $a_{\rm down} = g(\sin\theta - \mu\cos\theta) = g(0.6 - 0.4) = 0.2g$. The block covers the same distance $d$ on each leg, being at rest at the turn-around point and at the return: $d = \frac{1}{2}a_{\rm up}t_u^2 = \frac{1}{2}a_{\rm down}t_d^2$. Therefore $t_d = t_u\sqrt{a_{\rm up}/a_{\rm down}} = \sqrt{1/0.2}\,t_u = \sqrt{5}\,t_u$. Answer C; the descent takes longer because friction no longer helps gravity slow the block.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is placed at the center of a hemispherical shell of radius $R$ and surface density of mass $\sigma$. What is the gravitational force of the shell on the particle?
questions.hint: Integrate ring by ring; symmetry keeps only the axial component $\propto \sin\theta\cos\theta$, and the $R$'s cancel.
questions.solution: Slice the hemisphere into rings at polar angle $\theta$ from the symmetry axis. A ring has area $dA = 2\pi R\sin\theta\cdot R\,d\theta$ and mass $dm = \sigma\,dA$; every element of it lies at distance $R$ from the particle and attracts it with $dF = Gm\,dm/R^2$ along the joining line. Symmetry cancels all transverse components, leaving only the axial projection $dF\cos\theta$: $F = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{Gm\sigma}{R^2}\,2\pi R^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta = 2\pi Gm\sigma\left[\frac{\sin^2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \pi Gm\sigma$, directed along the symmetry axis toward the shell. Remarkably the radius $R$ drops out — only the surface mass density $\sigma$ matters. Answer E. (Choices A-D are garbled in the source scan; the clean printed option $\pi Gm\sigma$ is correct.)

questions.question: A wheel of radius $R$ is rolling without slipping with angular velocity $\omega$. For point A on the wheel at an angle $\theta$ with respect to the vertical — measured from the downward vertical, i.e. from the ground contact point (the original figure showed the angle drawn at the wheel's center) — what is the magnitude of its velocity with respect to the ground?
questions.hint: Add the center's velocity and the tangential rotational velocity as vectors, then simplify with the half-angle identity $1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)$.
questions.solution: Rolling without slipping is the superposition of the center's translation, $v_c = \omega R$, and rotation about the center, which gives every rim point a tangential speed $\omega R$ relative to the center. With $\theta$ measured from the downward vertical (contact point), the rotational velocity of A is $\omega R(-\cos\theta\,\hat{x} + \sin\theta\,\hat{y})$, so the total velocity is $\vec{v} = \omega R(1-\cos\theta)\hat{x} + \omega R\sin\theta\,\hat{y}$ and $|\vec{v}|^2 = (\omega R)^2[(1-\cos\theta)^2 + \sin^2\theta] = 2(\omega R)^2(1-\cos\theta)$. Using $1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ gives $|\vec{v}| = 2\omega R|\sin(\theta/2)|$. Checks: at the contact point ($\theta = 0$) the point is instantaneously at rest; at the top ($\theta = 180^\circ$) it moves at $2\omega R$. Answer B.

questions.question: Find the potential energy per ion for an infinite one-dimensional ionic string of charges of magnitude $e$ and alternating sign. Let the distance between adjacent ions be $s$.
questions.hint: Write the alternating series over neighbor distances and use $\sum(-1)^n/n = -\ln 2$.
questions.solution: Place a $+e$ ion at the origin. The $n$-th neighbor on each side sits at distance $ns$ and carries charge $(-1)^n e$ (opposite sign for odd $n$). The potential energy of this ion in the field of all the others is $u = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2\,\frac{e(-1)^n e}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 ns} = \frac{e^2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 s}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n}$, where the factor 2 counts the two ions at $\pm ns$. The alternating harmonic series sums to $-\ln 2$, so $u = -\frac{e^2\ln 2}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 s}$ — finite and negative, so the chain is bound; the alternating signs are essential, since like charges alone would give a divergent positive energy (choice D). (Counting each pair only once gives half this value per ion; the paper's options match the convention used here.) Answer A.

questions.question: A cube of sides 2 cm is moving along the $y$-direction with a speed of 6 m/s in the presence of a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T along the $z$-direction. What is the electric potential difference between the two planes (faces) perpendicular to the $x$-axis?
questions.hint: Balance $qvB$ against $qE$ to find the internal field, then multiply by the side length along $x$.
questions.solution: A charge co-moving with the cube feels $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$; with $\vec{v} = v\hat{y}$ and $\vec{B} = B\hat{z}$, the product $\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = vB\,\hat{x}$ drives positive charge toward one $x$-face. The separated charge builds an electric field until the electric and magnetic forces balance: $qE = qvB$, i.e. $E = vB = 6\times0.1 = 0.6$ V/m (this is a Hall effect in the moving conductor). The two faces perpendicular to the $x$-axis are separated by the cube side $\ell = 0.02$ m, so the potential difference is $\Delta V = E\ell = 0.6\times0.02 = 0.012\ \text{V} = 12$ mV. Answer D.

questions.question: Two planets A and B have masses $m_A = 2m_B$. They orbit a star in circular orbits of radii $r_A = 3r_B$. Let $E_i$ and $L_i$ respectively be the kinetic energy and the magnitude of the angular momentum of planet $i$. Which of the following is true?
questions.hint: Use $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, then compare $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $mvr$ for the two planets.
questions.solution: For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ — the orbital speed is set by the radius, not by the planet's mass. Kinetic energy: $E = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{GMm}{2r}$, hence $E_A/E_B = (m_A/m_B)(r_B/r_A) = 2\times\frac{1}{3} = 2/3$, so $E_A < E_B$. Angular momentum magnitude: $L = mvr = m\sqrt{GMr}$, hence $L_A/L_B = (m_A/m_B)\sqrt{r_A/r_B} = 2\sqrt{3} > 1$, so $L_A > L_B$. The heavier, more distant planet moves slower (less kinetic energy) but carries more angular momentum thanks to its larger mass and orbit radius. Answer E.

questions.question: Raindrops with number density $n$ (drops per m$^3$) and radius $r_0$ strike the ground with speed $v_0$, producing a pressure $P_0$ on the ground. If instead the number density is doubled, the drop radius is halved and the impact speed is halved, the new pressure will be …
questions.hint: Count how many drops hit each square metre per second, then multiply by the momentum a single drop delivers.
questions.solution: Rain pressure is a momentum-flux problem: in one second, all drops inside a column of height $v$ above 1 m$^2$ of ground hit that area, i.e. $nv$ drops. Each drop of radius $r$ has mass $m=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho$ and delivers momentum $mv$, so the pressure is $P=(nv)(mv)=n\frac{4}{3}\pi\rho\, r^3v^2$. Now scale each factor: number density $n\to 2n$ gives $\times 2$; radius $r_0\to r_0/2$ gives $r^3\to r_0^3/8$, i.e. $\times\frac{1}{8}$; speed $v_0\to v_0/2$ gives $v^2\to v_0^2/4$, i.e. $\times\frac{1}{4}$. Total factor: $2\times\frac{1}{8}\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{16}$, so $P_{\text{new}}=P_0/16$. Note the radius enters as the cube (mass) and the speed as the square — that is why the pressure drops so sharply.

questions.question: An inertial frame $K'$ moves with velocity $0.8c$ relative to the inertial frame $K$ along the $xx'$ axes. A particle in $K$ has velocity $\vec v = (0.5,\ \sqrt{3}/2)\,c$. What is the velocity of the particle in $K'$?
questions.hint: Requires the relativistic velocity-addition formulas, which are beyond this syllabus.
questions.solution: Out of syllabus (kept for reference). Relativistic velocity transformation with $V=0.8c$: $u_x'=\frac{u_x-V}{1-u_xV/c^2}=\frac{0.5c-0.8c}{1-0.5\times0.8}=-0.5c$, and $u_y'=\frac{u_y}{\gamma(1-u_xV/c^2)}$ with $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.64}=5/3$, giving $u_y'=\frac{(\sqrt{3}/2)c}{(5/3)(0.6)}=0.866c$. Then $|\vec v\,'|=\sqrt{0.5^2+0.866^2}\,c=c$, directed at $\tan^{-1}(0.866/-0.5)=120^\circ$ from the $+x$ axis.

questions.question: A group of skydivers performs a stunt: they jump off an aircraft individually and meet together in the sky while freely falling. Skydiver B was initially below skydiver A. What can skydiver A do if she wants to catch up with skydiver B?
options: Skydiver A should hunch her body in order to increase the gravitational force acting on her.
Skydiver A should stretch out her body in order to increase the gravitational force acting on her.
Skydiver A should hunch her body in order to reduce the air resistance acting on her.
Skydiver A should stretch out her body in order to reduce the air resistance acting on her.
There is nothing A can do about this.
questions.hint: Both divers feel the same gravity — ask which posture lets her fall faster at terminal velocity.
questions.solution: Weight cannot be changed by posture: $W=mg$ depends only on mass and $g$, so options A and B rest on a false premise. What posture changes is the drag force $F_d=\frac{1}{2}\rho C_d A v^2$, where $A$ is frontal area and $C_d$ a shape factor. A falling diver approaches terminal velocity when $mg=\frac{1}{2}\rho C_d A v_t^2$, so $v_t=\sqrt{2mg/(\rho C_d A)}$. Hunching into a compact ball reduces both $A$ and $C_d$, raising $v_t$; stretching does the opposite. With a higher terminal speed than B, A can fall faster than B and close the vertical gap. Hence hunch to reduce air resistance — option C.

questions.question: A pendulum of length $L$ oscillates inside a box. A person holds the box and gently shakes it vertically with frequency $\nu$, at a fixed amplitude and for a fixed time. The resulting amplitude of the pendulum is maximum when $\nu$ satisfies …
options: There will be no significant effect of the value of $\nu$ on the pendulum amplitude.
questions.hint: Vertical shaking modulates $g$ in time instead of pushing the bob — at what multiple of the natural frequency does a parametric drive pump best?
questions.solution: A vertical shake never pushes the bob sideways, so there is no direct forcing term; instead the pivot acceleration $\ddot y=A\omega^2\cos\omega t$ adds to (or subtracts from) $g$, giving $\ddot\theta+\left[\frac{g}{L}+\frac{A\omega^2}{L}\cos\omega t\right]\theta=0$ — a parametrically driven (Mathieu-type) oscillator whose 'stiffness' $g/L$ oscillates in time. A parametric drive pumps energy fastest at twice the natural frequency (principal parametric resonance): $\omega=2\omega_0=2\sqrt{g/L}$, exactly like pumping a playground swing by standing and squatting twice per period. Hence $\nu=\omega/2\pi=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{4g/L}$ — option A. Option C, $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g/L}$, would be the resonance for horizontal shaking, not vertical.

questions.question: A wire of length $2L$ is made by joining two wires A and B of equal length $L$ but different radii $r$ and $2r$, made of the same material. It vibrates at a frequency such that the joint of the two wires forms a node. If the number of antinodes in wire A is $p$ and that in wire B is $q$, then the ratio $p:q$ is …
questions.hint: Same tension and material: how does wave speed depend on thickness, and how many half-wavelengths then fit in each equal length at a common frequency?
questions.solution: Both segments share the same tension $T$ (they are one joined string), but the mass per unit length is $\mu=\rho\pi r^2$, so wire B (radius $2r$) has $\mu_B=4\mu_A$ and wave speed $v_B=\sqrt{T/\mu_B}=v_A/2$. Both are driven at the same frequency $f$, so the wavelengths satisfy $\lambda_B=v_B/f=\lambda_A/2$. With a node at the joint (and nodes at the outer ends), each segment holds an integer number of half-wavelengths, and the number of antinodes equals that number: $p=2L/\lambda_A$ and $q=2L/\lambda_B=2p$. Therefore $p:q=1:2$ — the thinner, faster wire A accommodates half as many half-wavelengths in the same length.

questions.question: Two wires are bent into semicircles of radius $a$ and joined at the ends of a horizontal diameter, forming a complete circle. The leads attached at the left and right junctions carry a total current $I$, entering at the left junction, so the upper semicircle (resistance $2R$) and the lower semicircle (resistance $R$) are connected in parallel between the junctions. Here $\hat z$ represents the direction out of the plane of the paper. The magnetic field at the centre of the circle is …
questions.hint: The arcs are in parallel, so divide the current inversely with resistance; then superpose the two opposing semicircle fields.
questions.solution: The two arcs are in parallel, so the same potential difference drives both and the current splits inversely with resistance: $I_{\text{upper}}=I\cdot R/(R+2R)=I/3$ and $I_{\text{lower}}=2I/3$. The field at the centre of a semicircular arc of radius $a$ is $B=\mu_0 I/(4a)$ — half of a full loop's $\mu_0 I/2a$. With the current entering on the left, the lower-arc current flows left$\to$right along the bottom (counterclockwise), giving $+\hat z$; the upper-arc current flows over the top (clockwise), giving $-\hat z$. The two fields oppose, so $B=\frac{\mu_0}{4a}\left(\frac{2I}{3}-\frac{I}{3}\right)=\frac{\mu_0 I}{12a}$ out of the page. The resistances matter only through the current split; each arc's field depends solely on the current it carries.

questions.question: A Carnot cycle is run in reverse as a refrigeration cycle (counterclockwise on the $PV$ diagram) between a hot reservoir at $T_H$ and a cold reservoir at $T_C$. If the efficiency is computed as for an engine, $e=\frac{\text{net work done by the gas}}{\text{heat absorbed by the gas}}$, the result is …
questions.hint: In reverse, which reservoir supplies heat to the gas — and what sign does the net work done by the gas have?
questions.solution: Run in reverse, the working substance absorbs $Q_C$ isothermally at $T_C$ (refrigeration — heat is taken from the cold side) and rejects $Q_H$ at $T_H$, with the Carnot ratio $Q_H/Q_C=T_H/T_C$. The net work done BY the gas over the cycle is $W=Q_C-Q_H<0$: work is put IN, not extracted. Feeding this into the engine definition, $e=W/Q_{\text{absorbed}}=\frac{Q_C-Q_H}{Q_C}=1-\frac{Q_H}{Q_C}=1-\frac{T_H}{T_C}$, which is negative because $T_H>T_C$. The negative value is the physics: a refrigerator consumes work rather than producing it, so engine efficiency is not the right figure of merit — the coefficient of performance $Q_C/W_{\text{in}}$ is used instead. Option A is the efficiency of the same cycle run forward as an engine.

questions.question: The pressure wave $P=0.01\sin[1000t-3x]\ \text{N m}^{-2}$ corresponds to the sound produced by a vibrating blade on a day when the atmospheric temperature is $0^\circ$C. On some other day when the temperature is $T$, the speed of the sound produced by the same blade at the same frequency is found to be 336 m/s. What is the approximate value of $T$?
questions.hint: Read $\omega$ and $k$ off the phase $1000t-3x$, then use $v\propto\sqrt{T}$ with absolute temperature.
questions.solution: From the wave equation the angular frequency is $\omega=1000$ rad/s and the wavenumber $k=3$ m$^{-1}$, so on the $0^\circ$C day the speed is $v_1=\omega/k=1000/3\approx333.3$ m/s. The same blade means the same frequency, so only the speed changes. For sound in an ideal gas, $v=\sqrt{\gamma RT/M}\propto\sqrt{T}$ with $T$ in kelvin. Hence $T_2=T_1\left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^2=273\text{ K}\times\left(\frac{336}{333.3}\right)^2=273\times1.016\approx277.5$ K, i.e. $277.5-273\approx4.5^\circ$C — closest to $4^\circ$C (option A). The speed changes only slightly because $v$ grows as the square root of absolute temperature.

questions.question: Body 1 ($m_1=10$ kg) hangs vertically from a weightless rope that passes over a weightless, frictionless pulley at the edge of a frictionless horizontal table and is tied to body 2 ($m_2=15$ kg) resting on the table; a second weightless rope ties body 2 to body 3 ($m_3=20$ kg), also on the table. A horizontal force $F=50$ N is applied at the far end of body 3, pulling it away from the pulley. What is the tension $T_2$ in the rope connecting bodies 2 and 3?
questions.hint: Find the common acceleration of the entire chain first, then apply Newton's second law to block 3 alone.
questions.solution: Treat the whole chain ($m_1+m_2+m_3=45$ kg, all moving together) as one system: along the line of motion the driving force is $m_1g$ toward the pulley and $F$ opposes it, so $a=\frac{m_1g-F}{45}=\frac{98.1-50}{45}\approx1.07$ m/s$^2$ toward the pulley. Now isolate body 3 alone: it is pulled toward the pulley by $T_2$ and away from it by $F$, so $T_2-F=m_3a$ and $T_2=50+20\times1.07\approx71.4$ N (with $g=9.8$ m/s$^2$: 71.3 N). Note $T_2>F$: this rope must both overcome $F$ and accelerate 20 kg. The other rope has $T_1=m_1(g-a)\approx87.4$ N — a listed distractor, but that is $T_1$, not $T_2$.

questions.question: A car has a maximum acceleration $a_0$ and a minimum acceleration $-a_0$ (i.e. maximum deceleration of magnitude $a_0$). The shortest possible time for the car to begin at rest and arrive at rest at a point a distance $d$ away is …
questions.hint: Use the maximum allowed acceleration the entire way — where must braking start for a symmetric rest-to-rest run?
questions.solution: The time-optimal profile pushes the acceleration limit the whole way: accelerate at $+a_0$ over the first half of the distance, then brake at $-a_0$ over the second half (any gentler phase wastes time). For one half, $d/2=\frac{1}{2}a_0t_1^2$ gives $t_1=\sqrt{d/a_0}$; by symmetry the braking half takes the same time, so $T=2\sqrt{d/a_0}$ — option E. Cross-check with the velocity–time graph: it is a triangle of peak speed $v_{\max}=a_0t_1=\sqrt{a_0d}$ at mid-distance, and the area gives $d=\frac{1}{2}v_{\max}T$, so $T=2d/\sqrt{a_0d}=2\sqrt{d/a_0}$, the same result.

questions.question: A spaceship travelling at $1.50\times10^8$ m/s leaves the Earth in the year 2050 with John on board. John leaves his twin brother James behind on Earth and goes to a star 25 light-years away; upon arrival he immediately returns. On return, what is the difference in their ages?
questions.hint: Requires relativistic time dilation, which is beyond this syllabus.
questions.solution: Out of syllabus (kept for reference). $v=0.5c$, so $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-0.25}=1.1547$. In the Earth frame the round trip covers $2\times25=50$ light-years at $0.5c$, taking $50/0.5=100$ years — James ages 100 years. John's proper time is the dilated $100/\gamma=100\times0.866=86.6$ years. The age difference is $100-86.6\approx13.4$ years, matching option E (13.3 years).

questions.question: A 3.0 cm thick layer of oil of density $\rho_0=800$ kg/m$^3$ floats above water of density $\rho_w=1000$ kg/m$^3$. A solid cylinder floats with $1/3$ of its volume in the water, $1/3$ in the oil and $1/3$ in the air. Additional oil is poured in until the cylinder floats only in oil. What fraction of the cylinder is then in the oil?
questions.hint: Requires Archimedes' principle, which is outside the listed syllabus for this category.
questions.solution: Out of syllabus (kept for reference). The initial float fixes the cylinder's density: $\rho_{\text{cyl}}Vg=\rho_w\frac{V}{3}g+\rho_0\frac{V}{3}g$, so $\rho_{\text{cyl}}=\frac{1000+800}{3}=600$ kg/m$^3$. Floating wholly in oil: $\rho_{\text{cyl}}Vg=\rho_0 fVg$, giving $f=600/800=3/4$ (option B). The 3.0 cm layer thickness only ensures the oil is deep enough.

questions.question: If the absolute temperature of a blackbody is increased by a factor of 3, the energy radiated per second per unit area …
questions.hint: Requires blackbody radiation laws, which are beyond this syllabus.
questions.solution: Out of syllabus (kept for reference). By the Stefan–Boltzmann law the radiated power per unit area is $P/A=\sigma T^4$, so raising the absolute temperature by a factor of 3 raises the output by $3^4=81$ (option E).

questions.question: A proton moves in the $+z$ direction after being accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$. The proton then passes through a region with a uniform electric field $E$ in the $+x$ direction and a uniform magnetic field $B$ in the $+y$ direction, but the proton's trajectory is not affected. If the experiment were repeated using a potential difference of $2V$, the proton would then be …
questions.hint: Ask which of the two forces grows with speed — and in which direction does $\hat z\times\hat y$ point?
questions.solution: This is a velocity selector. The accelerating gap gives $qV=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so $v=\sqrt{2qV/m}$. Inside the fields, the electric force is $qE$ along $+x$, while the magnetic force is $q\vec v\times\vec B=q(v\hat z)\times(B\hat y)=-qvB\,\hat x$ (since $\hat z\times\hat y=-\hat x$). With the original $V$ the beam passes straight, so the forces balance: $qE=qvB$. Doubling $V$ raises the speed to $v'=\sqrt{2}\,v$, so the magnetic force grows to $\sqrt{2}\,qE$ while the electric force stays $qE$. The net force is therefore along $-x$: the proton is deflected in the $-x$ direction. No $y$-force arises, since $\vec v\times\vec B$ has no $y$ component.

questions.question: An infinite slab of insulating material with dielectric constant $K$ and permittivity $\epsilon=K\epsilon_0$ is placed in a uniform electric field of magnitude $E_0$, the field being perpendicular to the surface of the material. The magnitude of the electric field inside the material is …
questions.hint: It is the normal component of $D=\epsilon E$, not of $E$ itself, that is continuous across the dielectric surface.
questions.solution: With no free charge on the slab surface, the normal component of the electric displacement $D=\epsilon E$ is continuous across the boundary: $\epsilon_0E_0=K\epsilon_0E_{\text{in}}$, hence $E_{\text{in}}=E_0/K$ (option A). Physically, the external field polarizes the dielectric; the bound surface charges produce an internal field opposing $E_0$, leaving only the fraction $1/K$ of it. Sanity checks: $K=1$ returns $E_0$ (no dielectric effect), and a large $K$ strongly suppresses the internal field. Option D inverts the logic — $D$ itself equals $\epsilon_0E_0$ inside and outside, and $D=\epsilon E_{\text{in}}$, not $E_{\text{in}}=\epsilon E_0$.

questions.question: Two capacitors $C_1$ and $C_2$ are connected in parallel and their combined equivalent capacitance is measured as 18 μF. When they are combined in series their equivalent capacitance is 4 μF. What are the individual capacitances?
questions.hint: Turn the parallel and series results into the sum and the product of the two capacitances, then solve the resulting quadratic.
questions.solution: In parallel, capacitances add: $C_1 + C_2 = 18\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. In series, $1/C = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2$, so $C_1C_2/(C_1+C_2) = 4\,\mu\mathrm{F}$, which gives the product $C_1C_2 = 4 \times 18 = 72\,\mu\mathrm{F}^2$. The two capacitances are therefore the roots of $x^2 - 18x + 72 = 0$. The discriminant is $18^2 - 4\cdot 72 = 324 - 288 = 36$, so $x = (18 \pm 6)/2 = 12$ or $6\,\mu\mathrm{F}$. Check: $12 + 6 = 18$ and $12 \times 6/(12+6) = 72/18 = 4$, as required — option (C).

questions.question: A ring rolls without slipping down a plane surface inclined at angle $\theta$, keeping pace with (i.e. having the same acceleration as) a block that slides down the same plane. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the plane is:
questions.hint: First compute the ring's rolling acceleration using $I = mR^2$, then demand that the sliding block match it.
questions.solution: A rolling body on an incline accelerates with $a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/(mR^2)}$. For a ring $I = mR^2$, so $a_{\text{ring}} = \frac{g\sin\theta}{2}$. 'Keeping pace' means the sliding block has this same acceleration. For the block, kinetic friction $\mu_k mg\cos\theta$ acts up the slope, so $a = g\sin\theta - \mu_k g\cos\theta$. Setting the accelerations equal: $g\sin\theta - \mu_k g\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$, which gives $\mu_k\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$, i.e. $\mu_k = \frac{1}{2}\tan\theta$ — option (D).

questions.question: Five positive charges, each of magnitude $q$, are arranged symmetrically (equally spaced, $72^\circ$ apart, like the vertices of a regular pentagon) around the circumference of a circle of radius $r$. What is the magnitude of the electric field at the center of the circle? Here $k = 1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$.
questions.hint: The field is a vector: add the five equal contributions component by component and exploit the equally spaced directions.
questions.solution: Use superposition plus symmetry. Each charge alone would give a field of magnitude $E_1 = kq/r^2$ at the center, directed radially away from that charge. The five field vectors point in five directions equally spaced by $72^\circ$. Equal vectors arranged at equal angular intervals around a point cancel: taking an axis through one charge, the net component along it is $E_1\sum_{n=0}^{4}\cos(2\pi n/5) = 0$, and likewise perpendicular to it (the five unit vectors form a closed regular pentagon when placed head-to-tail). So the net field at the center is exactly zero. The tempting distractor $5kq/r^2$ treats the field as a scalar; electric fields are vectors, and for a symmetric ring the vector sum, not the arithmetic sum, is what counts. The same argument gives zero for any number $N \ge 2$ of equal, equally spaced charges on a circle.

questions.question: A positive charge $Q$ is located at a distance $L$ above an infinite conducting plane that is grounded (held at zero potential), as shown in the figure (a point charge above a horizontal conducting plane). What is the total charge induced on the plane?
questions.hint: Ask what single 'image' charge placed below the plane would make the plane a zero-potential surface — the total induced charge equals it.
questions.solution: Use the method of images plus Gauss' law. The grounded plane can be replaced, for the field above it, by an image charge $-Q$ a distance $L$ below the plane: this pair makes the plane a $V=0$ equipotential, which is exactly the grounding condition, so by uniqueness it reproduces the true field. The induced surface charge follows from Gauss' law applied to a pillbox on the surface ($\sigma = \varepsilon_0 E_\perp$); integrating $\sigma$ over the whole plane yields exactly the image charge, $q_{\text{ind}} = -Q$, independent of $L$. Physically: field lines leaving $Q$ either escape to infinity or terminate on the plane, and the lines that terminate carry exactly the charge $-Q$, which is drawn up from ground onto the plane. The magnitude is fixed by charge bookkeeping, not by the distance $L$.

questions.question: An ideal monatomic gas expands quasi-statically to twice its initial volume. If the process is isothermal, the work done by the gas is $W_i$; if the process is adiabatic, the work done by the gas is $W_a$. Which of the following is true?
questions.hint: Sketch the isotherm and the adiabat through the same initial point on a $P$-$V$ diagram: which curve stays higher as $V$ doubles?
questions.solution: In both processes the gas expands, so $\int P\,dV > 0$: both works are positive, eliminating options (B) and (D). On a $P$-$V$ diagram drawn from the same initial state, the isotherm ($P \propto 1/V$) lies above the adiabat ($P \propto V^{-\gamma}$ with $\gamma = 5/3 > 1$ for a monatomic gas), because the expanding adiabatic gas does work at the expense of its internal energy and cools, while the isothermal gas keeps its temperature by absorbing heat. The work is the area under the curve up to $2V$, so $W_i > W_a > 0$. Numerically: $W_i = nRT\ln 2 \approx 0.693\,nRT$, while $W_a = nC_V(T_i - T_f) = \frac{3}{2}nRT_i\left(1 - 2^{-2/3}\right) \approx 0.555\,nRT_i$, confirming $0 < W_a < W_i$.

questions.question: A thin uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ stands vertically with its lower end attached to an anchored, frictionless pivot (figure: a vertical rod hinged at its bottom point), and is then allowed to fall to the ground. With what speed does the free (upper) end of the rod strike the ground?
questions.hint: Use energy conservation about the pivot — and make sure the moment of inertia you insert is the one about the end of the rod, not its center.
questions.solution: Apply conservation of energy with rotation about the fixed pivot. The center of mass drops from height $L/2$ to ground level, so the loss in potential energy is $MgL/2$, which becomes rotational kinetic energy: $Mg\frac{L}{2} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, with the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its end $I = \frac{1}{3}ML^2$. Solving, $\omega^2 = \frac{MgL}{I} = \frac{3g}{L}$, and the free end, a distance $L$ from the pivot, moves with $v = \omega L = \sqrt{3gL}$. Check the distractors: using $I = ML^2/12$ (about the center of mass) instead of about the pivot wrongly gives $\sqrt{12gL}$, and treating the rod as a point mass falling freely through $L$ gives $\sqrt{2gL}$ — the rod's tip actually moves faster than $\sqrt{2gL}$ because most of the mass stays near the pivot while the tip sweeps a circle of the full radius $L$.

questions.question: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ is incident on a series of three polarizing filters. The axis of the second filter is oriented at $45^\circ$ to that of the first, while the axis of the third filter is oriented at $90^\circ$ to that of the first. What is the intensity of the light transmitted through the third filter?
questions.hint: Halve the intensity for the unpolarized light, then apply Malus's law at each subsequent filter.
questions.solution: After the first polarizer, unpolarized light is halved to $I_0/2$ and becomes polarized along the first axis. Malus's law then gives $\frac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{I_0}{4}$ after the second filter (now polarized at $45^\circ$), and $\frac{I_0}{4}\cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{I_0}{8}$ after the third. The intermediate $45^\circ$ filter is what allows light to pass the crossed $(0^\circ, 90^\circ)$ pair at all. Excluded from the bank: polarization and Malus's law are outside the Category-C syllabus.

questions.question: Two identical blocks, each of mass $m$, are connected by a light spring. The combination hangs at rest from a ceiling by a string attached to the upper block (figure: string from ceiling to upper block, spring from upper block down to lower block, all vertical). The string breaks suddenly. What is the downward acceleration of the upper block immediately after the string breaks?
questions.hint: Find the spring's tension while the system hangs at rest, then remember that a spring's force cannot jump instantly when the string is cut.
questions.solution: First find the spring force before the string breaks. The lower block hangs in equilibrium under gravity $mg$ down and the spring force $F_s$ up, so the spring is stretched with $F_s = mg$. A spring force cannot change instantaneously, because the spring's extension needs time to change — unlike a string tension, which vanishes the moment the string breaks. Immediately after the break, the forces on the upper block are its weight $mg$ downward plus the spring pull $F_s = mg$ still downward (the stretched spring pulls the upper block toward the lower block), with the string tension gone. Net force: $2mg$ downward, so $a = 2g$. Meanwhile the lower block still has $mg$ down and $mg$ up from the spring, so its acceleration is momentarily zero — the two blocks briefly accelerate differently.

questions.question: A tube of water is traveling at $c/2$ relative to the lab frame when a beam of light traveling in the same direction as the tube enters it. What is the speed of the light in the water relative to the lab frame? The index of refraction of water is $4/3$.
questions.hint: This needs the relativistic velocity-addition formula, not simple addition.
questions.solution: Relativistic velocity addition gives $u = \frac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2}$ with $u' = c/n = \frac{3}{4}c$ (light speed in the water's rest frame) and $v = \frac{1}{2}c$: $u = \frac{\frac{3}{4}c + \frac{1}{2}c}{1 + \frac{3}{8}} = \frac{\frac{5}{4}c}{\frac{11}{8}} = \frac{10}{11}c$. This is the Fizeau drag effect. Excluded from the bank: special relativity is outside the Category-C syllabus.

questions.question: A segment of wire carrying current $I$ is bent into a circular arc of radius $R$ subtending angle $\theta$ (figure: a circular arc whose two straight leads lie along radial lines, with point P at the center of the circle of which the arc is a part). What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at P?
questions.hint: Every arc element sits at the same distance $R$ from P — integrate the constant Biot–Savart contribution over the arc length $R\theta$.
questions.solution: Use the Biot–Savart law, $d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}$. Every element of the arc lies at the same distance $R$ from P, and $d\vec{\ell}$ is perpendicular to $\hat{r}$, so each element contributes $dB = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}\,d\ell$ in the same direction (perpendicular to the plane of the arc). Integrating over the arc length $\ell = R\theta$ gives $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R^2}(R\theta) = \frac{\mu_0 I\theta}{4\pi R}$. Limiting checks: $\theta = 2\pi$ (full circle) gives $B = \mu_0 I/2R$, the standard full-loop result, and $\theta \to 0$ gives zero field. The straight lead wires, running along radial directions, contribute nothing because $d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r} = 0$ for every element along them.

questions.question: Two identical springs, each with spring constant $k$, are connected to identical blocks of mass $M$ on a frictionless horizontal surface in two ways (Figure 1: both springs attach the block to a wall side by side, in parallel; Figure 2: the two springs connect the wall to the block end-to-end, in series). The ratio of the oscillation period for the parallel arrangement (Figure 1) to the period for the series arrangement (Figure 2) is
questions.hint: Find the effective spring constant of each arrangement first: same displacement for parallel, same tension for series.
questions.solution: Reduce each arrangement to one effective spring constant, then use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{M/k_{\text{eff}}}$. Parallel: both springs undergo the same displacement $x$, so their restoring forces add: $F = kx + kx = 2kx$, giving $k_{\text{par}} = 2k$ and $T_{\text{par}} = 2\pi\sqrt{M/(2k)}$. Series: both springs carry the same tension and their extensions add: $x = F/k + F/k = 2F/k$, giving $k_{\text{ser}} = k/2$ and $T_{\text{ser}} = 2\pi\sqrt{2M/k}$. The ratio is $\frac{T_{\text{par}}}{T_{\text{ser}}} = \sqrt{\frac{M/2k}{2M/k}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$. Intuition check: the parallel combination is stiffer, so it oscillates faster (shorter period); the series combination is softer and oscillates slower — the ratio must come out well below 1, consistent with $1/2$.

questions.question: An astronomer observes a very small moon orbiting a planet and measures the moon's minimum and maximum distances from the planet's center and the moon's maximum orbital speed. Which of the following CANNOT be calculated from these measurements?
questions.hint: Which quantity cancels out of every orbital equation, no matter how you combine gravity and motion?
questions.solution: Test each quantity with conservation laws. (E) The semimajor axis follows directly: $a = (r_{\min} + r_{\max})/2$. (C) Angular momentum is conserved and speed is greatest at closest approach, so $r_{\min}v_{\max} = r_{\max}v_{\min}$ gives the minimum speed. (B) Conservation of energy, $\frac{1}{2}v_{\max}^2 - \frac{GM}{r_{\min}} = \frac{1}{2}v_{\min}^2 - \frac{GM}{r_{\max}}$, now has only one unknown, the planet's mass $M$, so $M$ follows. (D) Kepler's third law, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{a^3/GM}$, then yields the period. (A) The moon's own mass appears on both sides of every orbital equation — in $\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}$ it cancels — so it can never be extracted from the orbit alone. A small 'test particle' moon probes only the mass of the central body, not its own.

questions.question: A cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ has a radially dependent (non-uniform) density. It starts from rest and rolls without slipping down an inclined plane of height $H$ (figure: cylinder on an incline whose upper end is at height $H$). At the bottom of the plane its translational speed is $v = (8gH/7)^{1/2}$. What is the rotational inertia of the cylinder about its axis?
questions.hint: Split $MgH$ between $\frac{1}{2}Mv^2$ and $\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$, using $v = \omega R$ for rolling without slipping.
questions.solution: Rolling without slipping means $v = \omega R$. Energy conservation from top to bottom gives $MgH = \frac{1}{2}Mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}M\left(\frac{8gH}{7}\right) + \frac{1}{2}I\frac{8gH}{7R^2}$. The translational term uses $\frac{4}{7}MgH$, leaving $\frac{3}{7}MgH$ for rotation: $\frac{1}{2}I\frac{8gH}{7R^2} = \frac{3}{7}MgH$, so $I = \frac{3}{7}MgH \cdot \frac{14R^2}{8gH} = \frac{3}{4}MR^2$. Sanity check: a uniform solid cylinder has $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$ and reaches the bottom with $v = \sqrt{4gH/3} \approx \sqrt{1.33\,gH}$; here $v = \sqrt{1.14\,gH}$ is smaller, which requires a larger moment of inertia — and indeed $\frac{3}{4} > \frac{1}{2}$, consistent with mass concentrated toward the rim.

questions.question: A three-dimensional harmonic oscillator is in thermal equilibrium with a temperature reservoir at temperature $T$. What is the average total energy of the oscillator?
questions.hint: Count the independent quadratic energy terms (kinetic and potential) and give each $\frac{1}{2}kT$.
questions.solution: By the equipartition theorem, each independent quadratic term in the energy carries $\frac{1}{2}kT$ on average. A three-dimensional harmonic oscillator has three kinetic and three potential quadratic terms, so $\langle E \rangle = 6 \times \frac{1}{2}kT = 3kT$. Excluded from the bank: equipartition beyond ideal-gas basics is outside the Category-C syllabus.

questions.question: A gaseous mixture of $O_2$ (molecular mass 32 u) and $N_2$ (molecular mass 28 u) is maintained at constant temperature. What is the ratio $\frac{v_{\text{rms}}(O_2)}{v_{\text{rms}}(N_2)}$ of the root-mean-square speeds of the two kinds of molecules?
questions.hint: At equal temperature the rms speed depends only on molecular mass — and keep track of where the square root sits.
questions.solution: From kinetic theory, $\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$, so the rms speed of an ideal-gas molecule is $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m}$, set by the temperature and the molecular mass alone. At the same temperature, $\frac{v_{\text{rms}}(O_2)}{v_{\text{rms}}(N_2)} = \sqrt{\frac{m_{N_2}}{m_{O_2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{28\,\text{u}}{32\,\text{u}}} = \sqrt{\frac{7}{8}} \approx 0.94$. The ratio must be less than 1 because the heavier $O_2$ molecules move more slowly on average than the lighter $N_2$ molecules at the same temperature — this immediately rules out option (C), which exceeds 1, and option (A), which forgets the square root that the $v \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$ relation requires.

questions.question: An object of mass $m$ is attached to the end of a massless rod of length $L$ whose other end is attached to a frictionless pivot (figure: rod pivoted at one end with the bob at the other end). The object is raised so that its height is $0.8L$ above the pivot and released from rest. What is the tension in the rod at the moment the rod swings through the horizontal position?
questions.hint: Get $v^2$ from energy conservation first, then ask which forces have a radial component when the rod is horizontal.
questions.solution: First get the speed from energy conservation. The bob falls from height $0.8L$ above the pivot down to the pivot's level (rod horizontal), losing $\Delta U = 0.8\,mgL$, so $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.8\,mgL$ and $v^2 = 1.6\,gL$. In the horizontal position the bob is beside the pivot, so its weight is perpendicular to the rod — purely tangential — and contributes nothing radially. The rod tension alone must supply the centripetal force: $T = \frac{mv^2}{L} = 1.6\,mg$. General check: released from rest at height $h$ above pivot level, the horizontal-position tension is $T = \frac{mv^2}{L} = \frac{2mgh}{L}$; with $h = 0.8L$ this gives $1.6\,mg$. The formula correctly gives $T = 0$ when the bob is released from the horizontal position itself ($h = 0$), and grows linearly with $h$ for higher releases, so $1.6\,mg$ sits sensibly between those limits.

questions.question: Raindrops with a number density of $n$ drops per cubic meter and radius $r_0$ hit the ground with speed $v_0$. The resulting average pressure on the ground from the rain is $P_0$. If instead the number density is doubled, the drop radius is halved, and the impact speed is halved, what is the new pressure? (Each drop is brought to rest on impact; the drops have water density $\rho$.)
questions.hint: The pressure equals (number of drops hitting one square meter per second) times (momentum each drop delivers) — find how each factor scales.
questions.solution: Treat the rain as a momentum flux (impulse per unit area). In time $\Delta t$, all drops within a height $v_0\Delta t$ above $1\,\text{m}^2$ of ground hit it: $n v_0 \Delta t$ drops, each of mass $m = \rho\frac{4}{3}\pi r_0^3$. Each drop delivers momentum $m v_0$ as it is brought to rest, so the average force per unit area — the pressure — is $P_0 = n v_0 \cdot m v_0 = \frac{4}{3}\pi\rho\, n\, r_0^3 v_0^2$. Hence $P \propto n\, r^3 v^2$. Applying the changes: $n \to 2n$, $r \to r_0/2$, $v \to v_0/2$ multiplies the pressure by $2 \times (1/2)^3 \times (1/2)^2 = 2 \times \frac{1}{8} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{16}$. The new pressure is $P_0/16$. Note the strong $r^3$ dependence: halving the radius alone removes a factor of 8, which dominates the change.

questions.question: A 20 H inductor is connected in series with a 10 $\Omega$ resistor and a source of constant EMF (figure: a series $L$-$R$ circuit with battery and switch, switch closed at $t = 0$). At what time (in seconds) is the rate of dissipation of energy (Joule heat) in the resistance equal to the rate at which magnetic energy is being stored in the inductor?
questions.hint: Both rates depend only on the instantaneous current — ask when the current has grown to half its final value.
questions.solution: The build-up current in an $L$-$R$ circuit is $i(t) = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R}\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$ with time constant $\tau = L/R = 20/10 = 2$ s. The Joule heating rate is $P_R = i^2R$. The rate of magnetic energy storage is $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{1}{2}Li^2\right) = Li\frac{di}{dt}$, which by the loop equation $\mathcal{E} = iR + L\frac{di}{dt}$ equals $i(\mathcal{E} - iR)$. Setting the two rates equal: $i^2R = i(\mathcal{E} - iR) \Rightarrow i = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{2R}$ — the equality occurs exactly when the current has reached half its final value. Then $1 - e^{-t/\tau} = \frac{1}{2}$ gives $t = \tau\ln 2 = 2\ln 2 \approx 1.39$ s. Note that $L$ and $R$ enter only through $\tau$, so the answer is independent of the source voltage.

questions.question: The propagation of sound in a gas may be modeled as adiabatic in nature. For an ideal gas with three degrees of freedom, by what factor does the sound speed change when the pressure is doubled at constant density?
questions.hint: Write the adiabatic sound speed in terms of $P$, $\rho$ and $\gamma$, then ask which of those quantities actually changes.
questions.solution: Newton–Laplace: sound travels with $v = \sqrt{B_{\text{ad}}/\rho} = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$, because the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave are fast enough that heat flow is negligible (adiabatic). The adiabatic index $\gamma = (f+2)/f$ depends only on the number of degrees of freedom $f$; with $f = 3$, $\gamma = 5/3$, and it does not change when the pressure changes. Holding the density $\rho$ fixed and doubling $P$ gives $v' = \sqrt{2\gamma P/\rho} = \sqrt{2}\,v$: the speed increases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. Physically, higher pressure at the same density means a stiffer medium (larger restoring force per unit mass), and the wave speed grows as the square root of the stiffness. Note that even the isothermal formula $v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$ gives the same $\sqrt{2}$ factor, so the conclusion is robust.

questions.question: In the classic Fizeau experiment to verify the special theory of relativity, the speed of light in a moving liquid of refractive index $n$ is measured. If the speed of the liquid is $v$, what is the measured speed of light in the laboratory frame?
questions.hint: This requires the relativistic velocity-addition formula, not Galilean addition.
questions.solution: Relativistic velocity addition of the light speed in the liquid's rest frame $u' = c/n$ and the liquid speed $v$ gives the lab-frame value $u = \frac{u' + v}{1 + u'v/c^2} = \frac{c/n + v}{1 + \frac{(c/n)v}{c^2}} = \frac{c/n + v}{1 + v/(cn)}$. The $1 + v/(cn)$ denominator is the relativistic correction that makes Fizeau's drag experiment agree with special relativity rather than with simple Galilean addition. Excluded from the bank: special relativity is outside the Category-C syllabus.

questions.question: Using the linearization $\ln V = b\,\ln P + \ln A$ and the data $(P, V)$ = (1.1, 2.05), (1.9, 4.4), (3.1, 7.95), (4.05, 13.1), (5.02, 20.3), determine the exponent $b$ and the coefficient $A$ - for example by drawing the best straight line through the points $(\ln P, \ln V)$ and reading off its slope and intercept, or equivalently by a least-squares fit.
questions.hint: Convert every data point to $(\ln P, \ln V)$ and fit the best straight line through the five points.
questions.solution: Convert the data to $(x, y) = (\ln P, \ln V)$: $x = 0.0953, 0.6419, 1.1314, 1.3987, 1.6134$ and $y = 0.7178, 1.4816, 2.0732, 2.5726, 3.0106$. A least-squares fit gives the slope $b = \dfrac{\sum xy - 5\bar x\bar y}{\sum x^2 - 5\bar x^2} = \dfrac{11.821 - 9.621}{6.261 - 4.764} = \dfrac{2.200}{1.497} \approx 1.47$, and the intercept $\ln A = \bar y - b\bar x = 1.9712 - 1.4700\times0.9761 = 0.536$, so $A = e^{0.536} \approx 1.71$. Reading slope and intercept off a hand-drawn graph gives the same values within a few per cent ($b \approx 1.4$ to $1.5$, $A \approx 1.6$ to $1.8$). Sanity check: $AP^b$ at $P = 3.1$ predicts $1.71\times3.1^{1.47} \approx 9.0$ against the measured $7.95$ - about 10% scatter, which is normal for real data.

questions.question: In the power-law flow relation $V = AP^b$, the exponent $b$ characterizes how the flowed volume responds to the pressure difference (the fit to the data of the previous part gives $b \approx 1.5$). For a Newtonian fluid in the laminar viscous (Hagen-Poiseuille) regime, the flow rate is directly proportional to the pressure difference. What is the value of $b$ in that ideal linear regime, and what does the fitted $b \approx 1.5$ therefore indicate about this flow?
questions.hint: In the linear viscous regime $V \propto \Delta P$ - what exponent does direct proportionality correspond to?
questions.solution: Hagen-Poiseuille laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid gives a volume flow rate $\dot V = \dfrac{\pi R^4\Delta P}{8\eta L}$ - linear in the pressure difference, so $V \propto P^1$ and $b = 1$. The exponent therefore acts as a diagnostic of the flow physics: $b = 1$ signals a purely linear, viscosity-dominated response, while any departure of $b$ from 1 quantifies non-linear hydrodynamic behaviour. The fitted value $b \approx 1.5$ means the flowed volume increases much faster than linearly with the applied pressure difference, so this fluid does not obey the simple Poiseuille law - its pressure-flow characteristic is strongly non-linear. Measuring $b$ from the slope of a log-log plot is thus a quick experimental way to identify the flow regime without knowing $A$ in advance.

questions.question: In an adiabatic process involving an ideal gas, the gas expands and does $500\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on its surroundings. What is the change in the internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas?
questions.hint: Apply the first law with $Q=0$; be careful about the sign of the work done by the gas.
questions.solution: Use the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = Q - W_{\text{by}}$, where $W_{\text{by}}$ is the work done by the gas on its surroundings. The process is adiabatic, so no heat enters or leaves: $Q = 0$. The gas expands and does $+500\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on the surroundings, so $\Delta U = 0 - 500\ \mathrm{J} = -500\ \mathrm{J}$. Physically, the gas spends internal energy to push the surroundings out with no heat input, so its internal energy (and temperature) must drop — exactly the cooling seen in adiabatic expansion. Quick check: if the gas were compressed adiabatically instead, the sign of the work would reverse and $\Delta U$ would be positive, consistent with heating by compression.

questions.question: A stationary siren emits sound waves of frequency $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$. An observer moves directly away from the siren with a speed of $34\ \mathrm{m/s}$, and the speed of sound in air is $340\ \mathrm{m/s}$. What is the apparent frequency heard by the observer?
questions.hint: For a receding observer the effective wave speed relative to the observer is reduced; only $v_o$, not the source speed, enters.
questions.solution: This is the Doppler effect for sound with a stationary source and a receding observer. Moving away, the observer meets fewer wave crests per second, so $f' = f\,(v - v_o)/v$, with $v = 340\ \mathrm{m/s}$ the sound speed and $v_o = 34\ \mathrm{m/s}$ the observer's speed (positive when receding). Thus $f' = 500 \times (340-34)/340 = 500 \times 306/340 = 450\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Sanity checks: receding motion must lower the pitch, so $f' < 500\ \mathrm{Hz}$; the shift factor is $1 - v_o/v = 1 - 34/340 = 0.9$, giving $0.9 \times 500 = 450\ \mathrm{Hz}$. In the extreme limit $v_o = v$, the observer rides along with the wave crests and $f' = 0$, confirming the formula.

questions.question: A satellite orbits a planet in an elliptical orbit. At which point in the orbit is its angular momentum (about the planet) maximum?
options: At the point of closest distance (perihelion/perigee).
At the point of farthest distance (aphelion/apogee).
At the point of average distance.
Always — it is the same at every point of the orbit.
questions.hint: Ask whether gravity exerts any torque about the planet's center.
questions.solution: The only force on the satellite is the planet's gravity, a central force directed along the line joining satellite and planet. The torque about the planet's center is $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = 0$ because $\vec{F}$ is parallel to $\vec{r}$. With zero torque, the angular momentum $\vec{L}$ is conserved: it has the same magnitude and direction at every point of the ellipse. This is exactly the content of Kepler's second law — the radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so near perigee the satellite moves faster precisely in proportion to the smaller distance ($L = mrv$ for transverse motion). A common trap is to answer perigee, confusing maximum speed with maximum angular momentum: $v$ is largest there but $r$ is smallest, and the product stays constant.

questions.question: A block of mass $m$ is placed on top of another block of mass $M$, which rests on a frictionless horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the two blocks is $\mu$. What is the minimum horizontal force that must be applied to the block of mass $M$ so that the upper block of mass $m$ just begins to slide?
questions.hint: Find the acceleration at which the friction needed to carry the top block reaches its maximum static value, then scale up to the total mass.
questions.solution: Draw free-body diagrams. While the two blocks move together, the common acceleration is $a = F/(M+m)$. The only horizontal force on the upper block is the static friction $f$ from the lower block, so $f = ma$. Static friction cannot exceed $\mu m g$, hence the blocks move together only while $a \le \mu g$. The upper block is on the verge of sliding when $a = \mu g$, which requires $F = (M+m)\mu g$ — choice E. Any larger force makes the friction needed to accelerate $m$ exceed $\mu m g$ and the top block slips. Sanity check: even for a very light top block ($m \ll M$) the threshold exceeds $\mu g M$, because the lower block must also transmit enough friction to accelerate $m$ itself — that is the extra $\mu g m$ term.

questions.question: A particle of mass $M$ moves in the potential $V(x) = A\,(1 - \cos(kx))$, where $A$ and $k$ are constants. What is its time period for small oscillations about the stable equilibrium point?
questions.hint: Expand $\cos(kx)$ for small $x$ and read off the effective spring constant from $F \approx -V''(0)x$.
questions.solution: The minimum of $V$ is at $x = 0$. For small oscillations about a potential minimum, linearize the restoring force: $F = -dV/dx = -Ak\sin(kx) \approx -Ak^2 x$. This is Hooke's law with effective spring constant $k_{\text{eff}} = Ak^2$, so $\omega^2 = k_{\text{eff}}/M = Ak^2/M$ and $T = 2\pi/\omega = 2\pi\sqrt{M/(Ak^2)}$ — choice A. Dimensional check: $A$ is an energy ($\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$) and $k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, so $Ak^2$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}} = \mathrm{N/m}$, a proper spring constant, and $\sqrt{M/(Ak^2)}$ is a time. In general, for any smooth potential, small oscillations about a minimum $x_0$ satisfy $T = 2\pi\sqrt{M/V''(x_0)}$; here $V''(0) = Ak^2$.

questions.question: The motion of a particle is described by $t = \alpha x^2 + \beta x$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are constants and $x$ is the displacement. If the particle's velocity is $v$, the particle's acceleration is proportional to which of the following?
questions.hint: Invert the relation to get $v(x)$, then use $a = v\,(dv/dx)$.
questions.solution: Differentiate the given relation with respect to $x$: $dt/dx = 2\alpha x + \beta$, so the velocity is $v = dx/dt = 1/(2\alpha x + \beta)$. The acceleration is $a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = (dv/dx)\,v$ by the chain rule. Now $dv/dx = -2\alpha(2\alpha x + \beta)^{-2}$. Since $(2\alpha x + \beta) = 1/v$, we get $dv/dx = -2\alpha v^2$, and therefore $a = -2\alpha v^3$: the acceleration is proportional to $v^3$ (the constant factor $-2\alpha$ is fixed), choice C. The chain rule through $x$ is the key step — the motion is non-uniform, so you cannot divide $v$ by $t$ directly. As a check, larger $v$ means smaller $2\alpha x + \beta$, i.e. small $x$, where the speed changes fastest, consistent with $a$ growing steeply like $v^3$.

questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor of plate area $A$ and plate separation $d$ is connected to a battery of emf $E$ and remains connected. The plates are moved apart at a constant speed $v$, so that $d$ increases at the rate $v$. To what quantity is the rate of change of the energy stored in the capacitor proportional?
questions.hint: At constant voltage write $U = \tfrac12 C E^2$ with $C = \epsilon_0 A/d$ and differentiate with respect to time.
questions.solution: Because the battery stays connected, the voltage across the capacitor is fixed at $E$. The stored energy is $U = \tfrac{1}{2}CE^2$ with $C = \epsilon_0 A/d$, so $U = \epsilon_0 A E^2/(2d)$. Differentiate with respect to $d$ and multiply by $dd/dt = v$: $dU/dt = -\epsilon_0 A E^2 v/(2d^2)$. The magnitude of the rate of change of stored energy is therefore proportional to $\epsilon_0 A v/d^2$, with the constant factor $E^2/2$ — choice B. Physically the capacitance falls as $1/d$, so at fixed voltage the stored energy falls too: the plates attract each other, so pulling them apart requires external work, while the battery takes energy back as charge returns through the wire. Dimension check: $\epsilon_0 A/d$ is a capacitance ($\mathrm{F}$), so $\epsilon_0 A v/d^2$ has units $\mathrm{F/s}$, and multiplying by the constant $E^2$ (units $\mathrm{V^2}$) gives $\mathrm{J/s}$ as required.

questions.question: The diameter of the Moon is $3474.8\ \mathrm{km}$, and the distance between the Earth and the Moon is $3.844 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{km}$. What will be the diameter of the image of the Moon formed by a convex mirror of focal length $7.6\ \mathrm{m}$?
questions.hint: The Moon is effectively at infinity; the image lands at the focal plane and the magnification is about $f/|u|$.
questions.solution: A convex mirror has a virtual focus, so $f = -7.6\ \mathrm{m}$, and the object distance is $u = -3.844 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m}$. The mirror equation $1/v + 1/u = 1/f$ gives $1/v = -1/7.6 + 1/(3.844\times10^{8}) \approx -0.13158\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, so $v \approx -7.6\ \mathrm{m}$: the image is virtual, standing $7.6\ \mathrm{m}$ behind the mirror. The magnification is $m = -v/u = 7.6/(3.844\times10^{8}) \approx 1.98\times10^{-8}$ (positive, hence erect). The image diameter is $3.4748\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m} \times 1.98\times10^{-8} \approx 6.87\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 6.9\ \mathrm{cm}$ — choice A. Shortcut worth remembering: for a very distant object ($|u| \gg f$) a mirror forms an image essentially at its focal plane with linear magnification $m \approx f/|u|$, so the image size is set by the focal length alone.

questions.question: A small body of mass $M$ hangs from a long, massless string of length $L$ and cross-sectional area $A$. When the body is pulled slightly downward from its equilibrium position and then released, it executes simple harmonic motion with angular frequency $\omega$ (the string stretches elastically). What is the Young's modulus of the material of the string?
questions.hint: Treat the stretched string as a spring with $k = YA/L$ and use $\omega^2 = k/M$.
questions.solution: Gravity merely shifts the equilibrium position; the restoring force for a small extra displacement $y$ comes from the elastic stretching of the string. By Hooke's law for a wire, the string behaves like a spring of stiffness $k = YA/L$, where $Y$ is Young's modulus. The vertical mass–spring system then has $\omega^2 = k/M = YA/(ML)$. Solving, $Y = ML\omega^2/A$ — choice B. Reasonableness: a longer or thinner string (larger $L$, smaller $A$) is softer, so for the same measured $\omega$ the material must be stiffer — consistent with $Y \propto L\omega^2/A$. Note that the motion is along the string (stretching and relaxing, a longitudinal spring-like oscillation), not a pendulum swing, so the pendulum formula $\omega = \sqrt{g/L}$ does not apply.

questions.question: A uniform wire of resistance $20\ \Omega$ is bent into the shape of a circle. A $1.5\ \mathrm{V}$ battery is connected across two points on the ring such that the circumference is divided in the ratio $3:1$. What is the ratio of the currents flowing through the two parts of the ring?
questions.hint: Resistance scales with arc length; the two arcs sit in parallel across the same voltage.
questions.solution: For a uniform wire, resistance is proportional to length. The two arcs therefore have resistances $R_1 = (3/4)\times 20 = 15\ \Omega$ and $R_2 = (1/4)\times 20 = 5\ \Omega$. Both arcs are joined to the same two battery terminals, so they are in parallel and share the same potential difference $V = 1.5\ \mathrm{V}$. Hence $I_1 = V/R_1 = 0.1\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_2 = V/R_2 = 0.3\ \mathrm{A}$, giving $I_1:I_2 = 1:3$ — choice B. The key idea is that at equal voltage, current is inversely proportional to resistance. Notice that the battery emf and the total $20\ \Omega$ never enter the ratio; only how the length (hence resistance) splits between the two parallel branches matters.

questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident normally on a single slit of width $a$. If $I_0$ denotes the intensity at the central maximum, what is the intensity of the light observed on the screen at an angle $\theta$ such that $a\sin\theta = \lambda/2$?
questions.hint: Use $I = I_0(\sin\beta/\beta)^2$ and compute $\beta = \pi a\sin\theta/\lambda$ for the given direction.
questions.solution: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction gives the intensity $I(\theta) = I_0\,(\sin\beta/\beta)^2$, where $\beta = (\pi a \sin\theta)/\lambda$ is half the phase difference between waves from the two edges of the slit. Here $a\sin\theta = \lambda/2$, so $\beta = \pi/2$. Therefore $I = I_0\,\big(\sin(\pi/2)/(\pi/2)\big)^2 = I_0/(\pi/2)^2 = 4I_0/\pi^2 \approx 0.405\,I_0$ — choice D. Interpretation: the first minimum lies at $a\sin\theta = \lambda$ (i.e. $\beta = \pi$); our direction is only halfway there, yet the intensity has already fallen to about $40\%$ of the central value. It is the $(\sin\beta/\beta)^2$ diffraction envelope, not any straight-line shadow argument, that sets this falloff — which is why $\pi^2$ appears in the answer.

questions.question: A spring of length $L$ is cut into two parts in the ratio $4:5$. What is the ratio of the spring constant of the longer segment to that of the shorter segment?
questions.hint: Spring constant is inversely proportional to the number of coils, i.e. to the length of the segment.
questions.solution: For a uniform spring the stiffness is inversely proportional to its length: cutting a spring of constant $k_0$ into $n$ equal pieces gives each piece constant $n k_0$, because the same force stretches each piece by only $1/n$ of the original extension. Here the pieces have lengths $4L/9$ and $5L/9$, so $k_{\text{short}} \propto 9/(4L)$ and $k_{\text{long}} \propto 9/(5L)$. The requested ratio (longer : shorter) is $k_{\text{long}}/k_{\text{short}} = (1/5)/(1/4) = 4/5$ — choice A. Watch the wording: the longer piece is the softer one, so its spring constant is smaller and the ratio must be less than 1. Answers like $5:4$ or $25:16$ come from inverting the proportionality or forgetting that $k \propto 1/L$, not $k \propto L$.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is released from rest at a height $nR$ above the Earth's surface, where $n > 0$ and $R$ and $M$ are the radius and mass of the Earth. The air resistance is proportional to the velocity and is given by $F = -\beta v$. What is the maximum velocity attained by the particle?
questions.hint: Terminal velocity balances drag against gravity; ask where along the fall the local $g = GM/r^2$ is largest.
questions.solution: With linear drag the equation of motion is $m\,dv/dt = m\,g(r) - \beta v$, where the local gravitational acceleration is $g(r) = GM/r^2$. The speed always approaches the terminal value $v_t(r) = m\,g(r)/\beta$ from below (the particle starts from rest), so at every instant $v < v_t(r)$. During the fall the distance from the Earth's center decreases from $(n+1)R$ toward $R$, and since $g(r)$ grows as $r$ shrinks, the largest terminal velocity on the trajectory occurs at the surface: $v_{\max} = m\,GM/(\beta R^2)$ — choice E. The particle can only approach this value asymptotically, never exceed it, because in the terminal state drag exactly balances gravity. As a check, the answer must contain $\beta$ and $m$ (a weaker drag or heavier particle means a higher terminal speed), which rules out the square-root options A, C and D.

questions.question: A car of mass $m$ moves on a circular track of radius $r$ that is banked at an angle $\theta = 45^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The coefficients of static and kinetic friction are $\mu$ and $\mu'$, respectively. What is the maximum speed at which the car can negotiate the turn without skidding?
questions.hint: At top speed friction points down the slope; combine the radial and vertical force balances and use $\tan 45^{\circ} = 1$.
questions.solution: At the maximum speed the car tends to slide up the banking, so static friction acts down the slope with $f = \mu N$. Resolve forces vertically and radially (horizontal, toward the center): vertical: $N\cos\theta - \mu N\sin\theta = mg$; radial: $N\sin\theta + \mu N\cos\theta = mv^2/r$. Dividing the two equations eliminates $N$: $v^2/(rg) = (\tan\theta + \mu)/(1 - \mu\tan\theta)$. With $\theta = 45^{\circ}$, $\tan\theta = 1$, so $v_{\max} = \sqrt{(\mu+1)\,rg/(1-\mu)}$ — choice D. (The printed option shows $(\mu - 1)$ in the denominator, an evident sign typo; the denominator must be $1 - \mu$, positive for $\mu < 1$.) Kinetic friction $\mu'$ plays no role because the tyres never skid — choosing any expression containing $\mu'$ (C or E) is the standard trap. Limiting check: with $\mu = 0$ this reduces to the frictionless banked-turn result $v = \sqrt{rg}$.

questions.question: A man can jump to a maximum height of $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ on Earth. What is the radius of a fictitious planet of the same density as Earth from which the man can escape with a single jump of the same energy? (Radius of Earth $= 6400\ \mathrm{km}$)
questions.hint: Equate the jump specific energy $g_E h$ with the escape specific energy $GM_p/R_p$, expressing both via the common density.
questions.solution: The jump gives each unit of mass a kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 = g_E h$ with $h = 1.5\ \mathrm{m}$. Escaping from a planet of radius $R_p$ requires $\tfrac{1}{2}v^2 \ge GM_p/R_p$. With the same density $\rho$, $M_p = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi\rho R_p^3$, so the escape specific energy is $GM_p/R_p = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho\,R_p^2$. On Earth, $g_E = GM_E/R_E^2 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho\,R_E$. Setting the jump energy equal to the escape energy: $R_p^2 = R_E h$, hence $R_p = \sqrt{R_E h} = \sqrt{(6400\times10^3\ \mathrm{m})(1.5\ \mathrm{m})} = \sqrt{9.6\times10^6}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 3.1\ \mathrm{km}$ — choice C. Elegant feature: for fixed density the escape-by-jump radius depends only on $\sqrt{R_E h}$, independent of the man's mass or muscle power, since both the jump energy and the escape energy scale with the same quantities.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ and radius $r$ is released from rest from a height $H$ inside a vertical tube filled with a viscous fluid of coefficient of viscosity $\eta$. The viscous drag force acting on the particle is given by $F = -6\pi\eta r v$, where $v$ is the velocity of the particle. Which of the following quantities has the dimensions of time?
questions.hint: First extract $[\eta]$ from the drag law itself, then cancel dimensions in each option.
questions.solution: Read the dimensions of viscosity directly from the drag law $F = 6\pi\eta r v$: $[\eta] = [F]/([r][v]) = (\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})/(\mathrm{m}\cdot\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}) = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ (equivalently $\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$). Now test the candidates. $m/(\eta r)$: $\mathrm{kg}/(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}s^{-1}}\cdot\mathrm{m}) = \mathrm{kg}/(\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}) = \mathrm{s}$ — time, choice B. For contrast, $mg/(\eta r)$ gives $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}/(\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}) = \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, a velocity; $m\eta v$ gives $\mathrm{kg^2\,s^{-2}}$; and $m\eta/(rv)$ mixes in $\mathrm{s/m}$. Physical meaning: $\tau = m/(\eta r)$ is exactly the viscous relaxation time of the falling particle — the time over which the drag damps its velocity deviations by a factor $e$ — so a time dimension is expected.

questions.question: A long cylindrical conductor of radius $r$ carries a steady current $I$, uniformly distributed over its cross-section. The conductor is bent to form a circular loop of radius $R$, where $R \gg r$. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at the center of the loop?
questions.hint: Since $R \gg r$, treat the loop as thin and use the standard center-of-loop field formula.
questions.solution: Picture the thick conductor as many parallel thin filaments, each carrying a share of $I$ and each bent into a circle of radius essentially $R$ (their centers are displaced from the loop center by at most $r$, and $R \gg r$). By the Biot–Savart law, a circular loop of radius $a$ carrying current $i$ produces a field $B = \mu_0 i/(2a)$ at its center, directed along the loop axis. All filament fields point the same way and add linearly: $B = \sum_j \mu_0 i_j/(2R) = \mu_0 I/(2R)$ — choice E. The condition $R \gg r$ is what makes the wire thickness irrelevant; if $r \sim R$, the current elements would lie at noticeably different distances from the center and the simple formula would fail. The uniform cross-sectional distribution is a distractor — it matters for the field inside a straight wire, not for the field at the loop center.

questions.question: A $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ block moving to the right with a speed of $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ collides head-on with a stationary $6\ \mathrm{kg}$ block. The collision is perfectly inelastic and the blocks stick together after the collision. What is the loss in kinetic energy?
questions.hint: Conserve momentum to get the common final velocity, then compare kinetic energies before and after.
questions.solution: Momentum is conserved in the collision: $(2)(4) = (2+6)v_f$, so the combined blocks move at $v_f = 1\ \mathrm{m/s}$. Kinetic energy before: $K_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(2)(4)^2 = 16\ \mathrm{J}$. After: $K_f = \tfrac{1}{2}(8)(1)^2 = 4\ \mathrm{J}$. Loss $= 16 - 4 = 12\ \mathrm{J}$ — choice D. Cross-check with the standard shortcut for perfectly inelastic collisions, $\Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{\text{red}} v_{\text{rel}}^2$, with reduced mass $\mu_{\text{red}} = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2) = 12/8 = 1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ and relative speed $v_{\text{rel}} = 4\ \mathrm{m/s}$: $\Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}(1.5)(16) = 12\ \mathrm{J}$, agreeing. The lost kinetic energy is converted into heat and deformation; momentum, by contrast, is fully conserved, which is why $v_f$ is found from momentum first.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of quantities have the same dimension? (The quantities have their usual meanings.)
questions.hint: Rewrite every quantity in base units kg, m, s, A and compare one pair at a time — one pair shares the units of an energy density.
questions.solution: Compare base-unit expressions pair by pair. (A) Torque $\tau = rF$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$; $\hbar k$ is $(\mathrm{J\,s})(\mathrm{m^{-1}}) = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, a momentum — different. (B) $B^2/\mu_0$ is twice the magnetic energy density, with units of pressure $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$; $\rho v^2 = (\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}) = \mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ — a match. (C) Since $\sqrt{LC}$ is a time, $LC \sim \mathrm{s^2}$, while $R/\omega = \Omega\cdot\mathrm{s}$ = henry, the unit of inductance — not a match. (D) $E/B$ is a velocity (from $qvB = qE$), i.e. $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, not $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$ like $c^2$. (E) Work is in joules, current in amperes. Only option (B) works.

questions.question: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is $C$. If the separation between the plates is increased by 2%, and the plate area is decreased by 3%, while keeping the dielectric unchanged, what will be the new capacitance?
questions.hint: Capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor scales linearly with area and inversely with separation — apply each percentage change as a multiplying factor.
questions.solution: For a parallel-plate capacitor $C = \kappa\epsilon_0 A/d$: capacitance is directly proportional to plate area and inversely proportional to separation. The changes multiply, they do not add. New area $A' = (1-0.03)A = 0.97A$; new separation $d' = (1+0.02)d = 1.02d$; the dielectric (hence $\kappa\epsilon_0$) is unchanged. Therefore $C' = \kappa\epsilon_0 (0.97A)/(1.02d) = (0.97/1.02)C = 0.951C$. Since the area shrinks while the gap widens, the capacitance must drop below $C$ — but only slightly, ruling out the large drops like $0.634C$. Answer (E).

questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the initial fringe width is $\beta$. If the slit separation is tripled, the screen distance is reduced to one-fourth, and the wavelength of light is doubled, what will be the new fringe width?
questions.hint: Write the fringe-width formula and track how each of the three factors ($\lambda$, $D$, $d$) rescales it.
questions.solution: The fringe (interference) width in Young's double-slit experiment is $\beta = \lambda D/d$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength, $D$ the slit–screen distance and $d$ the slit separation. Each factor changes: $\lambda' = 2\lambda$, $D' = D/4$, $d' = 3d$. Hence $\beta' = \lambda'D'/d' = (2\lambda)(D/4)/(3d) = (2/12)\lambda D/d = \beta/6$. Quick check: doubling $\lambda$ alone would double $\beta$, but shrinking $D$ fourfold and tripling $d$ shrinks it twelvefold; the net factor is $2/12 = 1/6$. Answer (E).

questions.question: A uniform thin rod of length $L$ and mass $M$ lies along the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=L$. An axis passes through the point $x = L/4$ and is perpendicular to the rod. What is the moment of inertia of the rod about this axis?
questions.hint: Shift the standard center-of-mass result using the parallel-axis theorem — first find how far the new axis sits from the rod's midpoint.
questions.solution: Use the parallel-axis theorem. The center of mass of the rod is at $x = L/2$, where the moment of inertia about a perpendicular axis is $I_{cm} = ML^2/12$. The given axis at $x = L/4$ is a distance $d = L/2 - L/4 = L/4$ from the center of mass. Therefore $I = I_{cm} + Md^2 = ML^2/12 + M(L/4)^2 = ML^2(1/12 + 1/16) = ML^2(4/48 + 3/48) = 7ML^2/48$. Sanity check: the result must lie between $I_{cm} \approx 0.083\,ML^2$ and $I_{\text{end}} = ML^2/3 \approx 0.333\,ML^2$; indeed $7/48 \approx 0.146$. Answer (E).

questions.question: Two uniformly charged rings, each of radius $R$, lie in planes parallel to the $xy$-plane, with their centers on the $z$-axis at $z = +R$ and $z = -R$. They carry equal and opposite charges $+Q$ and $-Q$, respectively. Take $k = 1/(4\pi\epsilon_0)$. At the finite point on the common axis where the electric potential is zero, what is the magnitude of the electric field?
questions.hint: On the axis, first find where the two rings' potentials cancel, then add each ring's on-axis field at that point.
questions.solution: On the axis of a ring, the potential is $V = kq/\sqrt{R^2 + (z-z_c)^2}$, where $z_c$ is the center's position. At the midpoint $z = 0$ both rings are a distance $\sqrt{R^2+R^2} = \sqrt{2}\,R$ away, so $V = kQ/(\sqrt2 R) - kQ/(\sqrt2 R) = 0$ — this is the finite point where the potential vanishes. The on-axis field of a ring at distance $z$ from its center is $E = kqz/(R^2+z^2)^{3/2}$; here $z = R$, giving $E_1 = kQR/(2R^2)^{3/2} = kQ/(2\sqrt2 R^2)$. The $+Q$ ring pushes a positive test charge away from $z=+R$, and the $-Q$ ring pulls it toward $z=-R$: both fields point in the $-z$ direction and add, so $E = 2 \times kQ/(2\sqrt2 R^2) = kQ/(\sqrt2 R^2)$. Answer (A).

questions.question: The root-mean-square (RMS) speed of oxygen molecules ($O_2$) is $v$ at a certain temperature $T$. If the gas is heated so that its absolute temperature is quadrupled and the diatomic oxygen molecules dissociate into individual oxygen atoms, what will be the RMS speed of the resulting atomic gas?
questions.hint: RMS speed goes as the square root of temperature divided by particle mass — apply both changes inside the square root.
questions.solution: The RMS speed comes from $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3k_B T/m}$. Two changes happen at once: the temperature quadruples ($T \to 4T$) and each $O_2$ molecule of mass $m$ splits into two oxygen atoms of mass $m/2$. Therefore $v_{rms}' = \sqrt{3k_B(4T)/(m/2)} = \sqrt{8 \cdot 3k_BT/m} = \sqrt{8}\,v = 2\sqrt2\,v$. Physically, hotter and lighter particles both move faster, so the new speed must exceed $v$ — ruling out $v/2$ and $v/\sqrt2$. Answer (E).

questions.question: The self-inductance of a coil is 2 mH. The current passing through this coil is given by $I = A\,t\,e^{-t^2}$, where $A$ is a constant. Except at the beginning, at what time does the induced electromotive force in the coil become zero?
questions.hint: The emf vanishes when the current is at an extremum — differentiate the product $te^{-t^2}$ and set the derivative to zero.
questions.solution: By Faraday's law the induced emf is $\mathcal{E} = -L\,dI/dt$. With $L \neq 0$, the emf vanishes exactly when $dI/dt = 0$, so the value of the inductance never enters the answer. Differentiate $I = Ate^{-t^2}$ with the product rule: $dI/dt = Ae^{-t^2} + At(-2t)e^{-t^2} = Ae^{-t^2}(1 - 2t^2)$. Since $Ae^{-t^2} \neq 0$ at any finite time, set $1 - 2t^2 = 0$, giving $t = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71$ s. This is the instant the current peaks; afterwards the emf reverses sign as the current decays. Answer (C).

questions.question: An incompressible fluid flows through a pipe. At one point, the pipe has a circular cross-section of radius $r$, and the fluid speed is $v$. At another point, the cross-section is square, and the fluid speed is $v/4$. What is the side length of the square?
questions.hint: The volume flow rate is the same at both sections — set circular area times speed equal to square area times speed.
questions.solution: For an incompressible fluid the volume flow rate is the same at every section (equation of continuity): $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$.
