questions.question: Water flows through a pipe with a varying cross-section. The velocity of the fluid at point $A$, where the cross-sectional radius is $r$, is $v_A$. What is the velocity of the fluid at point $B$, where the cross-sectional area is half of that at point $A$?
questions.hint: Apply conservation of volume flow rate between A and B, working with cross-sectional areas rather than radii.
questions.solution: Water is essentially incompressible, so the continuity equation applies: the volume flow rate is the same through every cross-section, $A_A v_A = A_B v_B$. Since $A_B = A_A/2$, we get $v_B = (A_A/A_B)·v_A = 2v_A$. Note that the area scales as $r^2$, so halving the area corresponds to the radius shrinking by $√2$ — it is the area, not the radius, that enters the flow-rate balance. The fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows, the same effect that makes a jet shoot faster when you partly cover a hose opening with your thumb.

questions.question: A $4\ \mu F$ capacitor is charged to a potential difference of $100\ V$ and then connected in parallel with an uncharged $2\ \mu F$ capacitor. What is the common voltage across the combination after the connection?
questions.hint: No charge escapes the pair: compute the initial charge, then divide it by the combined parallel capacitance.
questions.solution: Charge is conserved because the plates are isolated from the rest of the circuit. The charged capacitor initially stores $Q = CV = 4\ \mu F × 100\ V = 400\ \mu C$. In parallel, capacitances simply add: $C_{eq} = 4 + 2 = 6\ \mu F$. The charge redistributes until both capacitors share one common voltage: $V = Q/C_{eq} = 400/6 ≈ 66.7\ V = 200/3\ V$. Checks: the voltage must drop below 100 V (the same charge now sits on more capacitance) and equals $100 × 4/6$ by the charge-sharing ratio. The missing electrostatic energy is dissipated during the redistribution.

questions.question: An atom in a solid is modeled as a harmonic oscillator with potential energy $V_0(x) = \frac{1}{2}Kx^2$, which is symmetric under $x \leftrightarrow -x$. What is the displacement of the oscillator averaged over one full period of oscillation, and why?
questions.hint: The potential is symmetric, so the oscillator spends equal time on both sides -- think of the average of a cosine over a full period.
questions.solution: Because $V_0$ is an even function of $x$, for any energy $E$ the motion runs between symmetric turning points $x = \pm\sqrt{2E/K}$. The motion is sinusoidal, $x(t) = x_{\max}\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ with $x_{\max} = \sqrt{2E/K}$, and the time average of a cosine over a full period is zero: $\langle x\rangle = \frac{1}{T_0}\int_0^{T_0}x\,dt = 0$. Physically, the oscillator spends equal time at $+x$ and $-x$, so positive and negative displacements cancel exactly. This vanishing mean is a special property of the symmetric harmonic potential -- part (e) shows that adding the asymmetric $-gx^3$ term breaks the $x \leftrightarrow -x$ symmetry and produces a nonzero, temperature-dependent mean displacement (thermal expansion).

questions.question: The three sides of a box are measured with a meter stick of smallest division $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ as $L_1 = 11.4 \pm 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, $L_2 = 23.7 \pm 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ and $L_3 = 7.3 \pm 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$. Compute the volume $V = L_1 L_2 L_3$ and the uncertainty $\Delta V$ incorporated in it (fractional uncertainties of the factors add).
questions.hint: For a product of measured quantities, the fractional errors of the factors add.
questions.solution: The volume is the product of the three sides: $V = 11.4 \times 23.7 \times 7.3\ \mathrm{mm^3} = 1972.3\ \mathrm{mm^3} \approx 1.97\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. For a product of factors the fractional (relative) uncertainties add: $\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{\Delta L_1}{L_1} + \frac{\Delta L_2}{L_2} + \frac{\Delta L_3}{L_3} = \frac{0.5}{11.4} + \frac{0.5}{23.7} + \frac{0.5}{7.3} = 0.0439 + 0.0211 + 0.0685 = 0.133$. Hence $\Delta V = 0.133 \times 1972.3 \approx 263\ \mathrm{mm^3} \approx 0.26\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, and $V = (1.97 \pm 0.26)\times10^3\ \mathrm{mm^3} \approx (2.0 \pm 0.3)\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. Note that the shortest side contributes the largest fractional error (6.8%), so it dominates the volume uncertainty, and the result should be quoted only to the precision justified by the ~13% error.

questions.question: Alkaid and Merak are two stars that can be seen from Earth with the naked eye. Their distances from Earth are 138 LY and 77 LY respectively, and the angle between their directions in the Earth's sky is $25.6^\circ$. What is the distance between the two stars, in light-years? [LY = light year]
questions.hint: Use the cosine rule with the two distances as sides and $25.6^\circ$ as the included angle.
questions.solution: Earth and the two stars form a triangle with two known sides and the included angle (SAS configuration). By the cosine rule, $d^2 = 138^2 + 77^2 - 2(138)(77)\cos 25.6^\circ$ $= 19044 + 5929 - 21252 \times 0.9018 \approx 24973 - 19165 = 5808$, so $d = \sqrt{5808} \approx 76.2$ LY. Note the stars are much closer to each other than to Earth, which is typical for stars of the same constellation (both belong to the Big Dipper).

questions.question: An object of mass $m$ is placed on an inclined plane that makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the ground. The force required to just start the object moving up the plane is 5 (five) times the force required to just hold it in position (on the verge of sliding down). Determine the coefficient of friction $\mu$ of the plane surface.
questions.hint: Write both limiting-force expressions (friction down when starting up, friction up when holding) and set $F_1 = 5F_2$.
questions.solution: Along the plane, gravity pulls with $mg\sin 45^\circ$ and the normal force is $mg\cos 45^\circ$. To just start motion upward, friction acts down the plane at its limiting value: $F_1 = mg\sin 45^\circ + \mu mg\cos 45^\circ$. To just prevent sliding down, friction acts up the plane at its limiting value: $F_2 = mg\sin 45^\circ - \mu mg\cos 45^\circ$. The condition $F_1 = 5F_2$ gives $\sin 45^\circ + \mu\cos 45^\circ = 5\sin 45^\circ - 5\mu\cos 45^\circ$, so $6\mu\cos 45^\circ = 4\sin 45^\circ$ and $\mu = \frac{4}{6}\tan 45^\circ = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$.

questions.question: In a lake there is a place where the lake is 2 m deep, and a vertical totem pole stands on the bottom, sticking out of the water up to a height of 1 m above the water level. Rays coming from the setting Sun, located at an altitude of $30^\circ$ above the horizon, are incident on the totem. How long (in metres) is the shadow cast by the totem onto the bottom of the lake? Refractive indices of water and air are $n = 1.33$ and $n' = 1$ respectively.
questions.hint: Trace the grazing ray: horizontal offsets are $1/\tan 30^\circ$ in air and $2\tan\theta_w$ in water, with Snell's law at the surface.
questions.solution: The far edge of the shadow is set by the ray grazing the top of the totem. In air this ray descends 1 m while travelling horizontally $x_1 = 1/\tan 30^\circ = 1.73$ m. At the water surface it makes $60^\circ$ with the vertical, so Snell's law gives $\sin\theta_w = \sin 60^\circ/1.33 = 0.651$, i.e. $\theta_w \approx 40.6^\circ$. Underwater the ray travels $x_2 = 2\tan\theta_w \approx 1.72$ m horizontally before reaching the bottom. The shadow, measured from the totem's base, is $x_1 + x_2 = 1.73 + 1.72 \approx 3.45$ m; refraction toward the normal makes the underwater part shorter than the straight-ray value $2/\tan 30^\circ$.

questions.question: A square plate of side length $L$ and negligible thickness lies horizontally on a table. It rotates about the axis MN, where M and N are the midpoints of two adjacent sides of the square. The moment of inertia of the plate about this axis is $I = k\,mL^2$, where $m$ is the mass of the plate and $k$ is a real constant. Find $k$.
questions.hint: For a lamina, the moment of inertia about an in-plane axis at 45 degrees through a point is the average of the moments about the perpendicular in-plane pair through that point.
questions.solution: Put the square on $0 \le x,y \le L$; the axis joins $(L/2,0)$ and $(0,L/2)$, i.e. the line $x+y = L/2$ with direction $(1,-1)/\sqrt{2}$. A point $(x,y)$ lies at distance $|x+y-L/2|/\sqrt{2}$ from it, so $I = \frac{m}{L^2}\iint \frac{(x+y-L/2)^2}{2}\,dx\,dy = \frac{m}{2L^2}\cdot\frac{5L^4}{12} = \frac{5}{24}mL^2$. Equivalently, for two perpendicular in-plane axes through the same point: $I_x = mL^2/3$ (parallel-axis: $mL^2/12 + m(L/2)^2$) and $I_y = mL^2/12$ (through the centre); a $45^\circ$ axis takes the average, $I = \frac{I_x+I_y}{2} = \frac{5mL^2}{24}$. Hence $k = 5/24 \approx 0.208$.

questions.question: We have some identical hemispherical water droplets (flat face down) whose total mass is 10 g. The droplets are subjected to a radiation of heat flux $5\times10^4\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ incident perpendicular to their (curved) surfaces, and starting at $30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it takes them one minute to vaporize completely. Considering only radiative transmission of heat (no conduction or convection), how many water droplets were there? (Give the nearest integer for a fractional result.) Specific heat of water $c = 4.2\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg\cdot K)}$, latent heat of evaporation $L = 2257\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$.
questions.hint: The per-droplet energy balance (mass times specific heat + latent heat = flux times curved area times 60 s) fixes the radius; then divide 10 g by one droplet's mass.
questions.solution: Per kilogram, heating from $30^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to boiling and vaporizing needs $c\Delta T + L = 4.2\times 70 + 2257 = 2551$ kJ. For a droplet of radius $r$: mass $m_d = \rho\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$ and absorbed power $P = q\,(2\pi r^2)$ (flux normal to every curved-surface element). Vaporizing in $t = 60$ s requires $\rho\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3 (2.551\times10^6) = 60\times 5\times10^4 \times 2\pi r^2$, which fixes the radius: $r = \frac{120\,q}{(2/3)\rho(c\Delta T+L)} \approx 3.53$ mm. Then $m_d = \frac{2}{3}\pi(1000)(3.53\times10^{-3})^3 \approx 9.2\times10^{-5}$ kg $= 0.092$ g, so $N = 10/0.092 \approx 108.7 \approx 109$ droplets.

questions.question: You are travelling from Dhaka to Chittagong on a train 350 m long. On the way you see another train going to Dhaka from Chittagong (moving in the exactly opposite direction to yours). Judging from your own train you measure the velocity of that train as 120 km/h, but its actual (ground) velocity is 70 km/h. How long will your train take to completely cross a 350 m long platform?
questions.hint: Opposite-direction relative speed is the sum of speeds; distance to clear a platform is platform length plus train length.
questions.solution: Because the trains move in opposite directions, your measured relative speed is the sum of the two ground speeds: $120 = v_{you} + 70$, so your train's actual ground speed is $v_{you} = 50$ km/h $= 50 \times \frac{5}{18} = 13.89$ m/s. To clear the platform, the front of the train must traverse the platform (350 m) plus the train's own length (350 m) so that the tail leaves it: $d = 700$ m. Hence $t = 700/13.89 = 50.4$ s.

questions.question: A ball is released from a height $h$. After hitting the ground it rises to half of its previous height. After hitting the ground $n$ times, the potential energy of the ball (at the top of a bounce) becomes $1/8$-th of its initial potential energy. What is the value of $n$?
questions.hint: Potential energy at the top of a bounce is proportional to the bounce height, which halves on every hit.
questions.solution: At the top of each bounce the speed is momentarily zero, so the potential energy there equals the mechanical energy the ball carries between bounces. Each flight conserves energy, and the rebound height halves every hit: $h,\ h/2,\ h/4,\ \dots$ Since $E \propto h$, after $n$ bounces $E_n = E_0/2^n$. Setting $2^n = 8$ gives $n = 3$: after the 1st bounce the height is $h/2$, after the 2nd $h/4$, and after the 3rd $h/8$, one eighth of the initial potential energy.

questions.question: A capacitor is made of two square plates, each of side length $L$ and negligible thickness, and has capacitance $C$. The disconnected capacitor (so its charge stays fixed) is put in a microwave oven, which increases the side length of each square plate by 1% while the plate separation does not change. By what percent does the voltage between the two plates of the capacitor change?
questions.hint: Area scales as $L^2$, so $C$ grows by $(1.01)^2$; with $Q$ fixed, $V = Q/C$ falls by the inverse factor.
questions.solution: For a parallel-plate capacitor $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d = \varepsilon_0 L^2/d$, so $C \propto L^2$. The side length grows by a factor 1.01, hence $C' = (1.01)^2 C = 1.0201\,C$. With the charge $Q$ fixed on the isolated capacitor, $V = Q/C$, so $V' = Q/C' = V/1.0201 = 0.9803\,V$. The voltage therefore changes by $0.9803 - 1 = -0.0197$, i.e. it decreases by about $1.97\% \approx 2\%$. (If the capacitor stayed connected to a battery the voltage would be fixed and the charge would increase instead.)

questions.question: A person stands clapping in front of a wall 50 m away from him. The velocity of sound in air is 333 m/s. When he claps, an echo is produced. The person wants the echo of each clap to exactly overlap the sound of the next clap. To do so, how many claps does he need to make in 5 seconds?
questions.hint: Echo delay is $2d/v$; count how many claps spaced by that delay fit inside 5 seconds.
questions.solution: An echo returns after the round trip: $\Delta t = 2d/v = 2\times 50/333 = 0.3003$ s. For every echo to coincide with the next clap, the claps must be spaced exactly $\Delta t$ apart, i.e. at a rate of $1/0.3003 = 3.33$ claps per second. In 5 s this allows $5/0.3003 = 16.65$ clap-to-clap intervals, so he makes 17 claps: at $t = 0,\ 0.3003,\ \dots,\ 16\times 0.3003 = 4.80$ s; an 18th clap would fall at 5.11 s, beyond the 5 s limit.

questions.question: The cross-section of a prism of refractive index 1.5 is an equilateral triangle, standing with one side horizontal and the apex up. A ray of light comes in horizontally from air into the left slanted face of the prism, refracts, and just has the opportunity to leave the prism through the right slanted face. Find $\theta$, the angle the emerging ray makes with respect to that surface of the triangle, in degrees, rounded to the nearest whole number.
questions.hint: Get both face normals from the 60-degree geometry; the ray escapes only because the second incidence angle sits just below the critical angle.
questions.solution: Each face of an apex-up equilateral prism makes $60^\circ$ with the horizontal. On the entry face the normal points $30^\circ$ below the horizontal, so the horizontal ray has $i_1 = 30^\circ$; Snell's law: $\sin r_1 = 0.5/1.5 \Rightarrow r_1 = 19.47^\circ$, and the internal ray travels $10.53^\circ$ below the horizontal. The exit face's normal is $30^\circ$ above the horizontal, so the internal incidence angle is $i_2 = 30^\circ + 10.53^\circ = 40.53^\circ$, just under the critical angle $\arcsin(1/1.5) = 41.8^\circ$ - that is why the ray only just escapes. Outside, $\sin e = 1.5\sin 40.53^\circ = 0.975 \Rightarrow e = 77.1^\circ$ from the normal, so $\theta = 90^\circ - 77.1^\circ = 12.9^\circ \approx 13^\circ$.

questions.question: A sphere of radius $r$ is floating in water with exactly half of it submerged. Determine the density of the sphere's material. (Density of water $\rho_w = 1000\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.)
questions.hint: Weight = buoyant force, and only half the volume displaces water.
questions.solution: In floating equilibrium the weight equals the buoyant force (Archimedes' principle): $\rho_s V g = \rho_w V_{sub} g$ with $V_{sub} = V/2$. Hence $\rho_s = \rho_w/2 = 500\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$. The radius cancels out: in general the submerged fraction equals the density ratio $\rho_s/\rho_w$, so a body floats with half its volume under water exactly when its density is half that of the liquid.

questions.question: A rock is dropped off a cliff of height $h$. As it falls, a camera takes several photographs at random moments, and in each picture the distance the rock has fallen is measured. Let the average (expected value) of all of these distances be $k\,h$. If the number of photographs taken is huge, find $k$ - i.e. the time-average of the distance travelled, divided by $h$.
questions.hint: Average $\frac{1}{2}gt^2$ over $t \in [0,T]$ and use $h = \frac{1}{2}gT^2$.
questions.solution: Random exposure times are uniformly distributed over the total fall time $T$, where $h = \frac{1}{2}gT^2$. The distance fallen by time $t$ is $s(t) = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, so the expected distance is $\langle s\rangle = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \frac{1}{2}gt^2\,dt = \frac{gT^2}{6}$. Since $gT^2 = 2h$, we get $\langle s\rangle = \frac{2h}{6} = \frac{h}{3}$. Hence $k = 1/3 \approx 0.33$: because the distance grows as $t^2$, the mean of uniformly sampled distances sits at one third of the final value, not one half.

Outside, $\sin e = 1.5\sin 40.53^\circ = 0.975 \Rightarrow e = 77.1^\circ$ from the normal, so $\theta = 90^\circ - 77.1^\circ = 12.9^\circ \approx 13^\circ$.

questions.question: A square plate of side length $L$ and negligible thickness lies horizontally on a table. It rotates about the axis MN, where M and N are the midpoints of two adjacent sides of the square. The moment of inertia of the plate about this axis is $I = k\,mL^2$, where $m$ is the mass of the plate and $k$ is a real constant. Find $k$.
questions.hint: For a lamina, the moment of inertia about an in-plane axis at 45 degrees through a point is the average of the moments about the perpendicular in-plane pair through that point.
questions.solution: Put the square on $0 \le x,y \le L$; the axis joins $(L/2,0)$ and $(0,L/2)$, i.e. the line $x+y = L/2$ with direction $(1,-1)/\sqrt{2}$. A point $(x,y)$ lies at distance $|x+y-L/2|/\sqrt{2}$ from it, so $I = \frac{m}{L^2}\iint \frac{(x+y-L/2)^2}{2}\,dx\,dy = \frac{m}{2L^2}\cdot\frac{5L^4}{12} = \frac{5}{24}mL^2$. Equivalently, for two perpendicular in-plane axes through the same point: $I_x = mL^2/3$ (parallel-axis: $mL^2/12 + m(L/2)^2$) and $I_y = mL^2/12$ (through the centre); a $45^\circ$ axis takes the average, $I = \frac{I_x+I_y}{2} = \frac{5mL^2}{24}$. Hence $k = 5/24 \approx 0.208$.

questions.question: A point light source is placed on the axis of a solid glass cylinder, just outside one flat end face (base); the distance between the source and the base is negligible. Rays from the source enter the cylinder through the base. Determine the minimum refractive index $n$ of the cylinder material for which none of the rays entering the base can emerge from the curved lateral surface.
questions.hint: Test the extreme rays entering at grazing incidence on the base; demand total internal reflection at the side wall.
questions.solution: The worst case is a ray striking the flat base at grazing incidence, $i \to 90^\circ$. Snell's law at the base gives $n\sin\theta_r = \sin i \le 1$, so inside the cylinder the ray makes angle $\theta_r$ with the axis with $\sin\theta_r = 1/n$ in the limit. Such a ray hits the cylindrical wall at incidence $\phi = 90^\circ - \theta_r$ from the wall normal. For no ray to escape, even this ray must undergo total internal reflection: $\sin\phi = \cos\theta_r \ge \frac{1}{n}$. With $\sin\theta_r = \frac{1}{n}$ this becomes $\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{n^2}} \ge \frac{1}{n}$, so $n^2 \ge 2$ and $n_{\min} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$.

questions.question: Hulk once became angry and pushed the Earth so hard that its radius became half of its present value, while the Earth's mass stayed the same and no external torque acted on it. Treating the Earth as a uniform sphere, how many hours would one day (one full rotation about the axis) now last?
questions.hint: Angular momentum $I\omega$ is conserved and $I \propto R^2$ for fixed mass, so $\omega$ quadruples.
questions.solution: With no external torque the spin angular momentum is conserved: $I\omega = I'\omega'$. For a uniform sphere $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$, so shrinking the radius to half at constant mass gives $I' = \frac{I}{4}$. Conservation then demands $\omega' = 4\omega$: the Earth spins four times faster. The length of a day is the rotation period $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}$, which is inversely proportional to the angular velocity, so $T' = \frac{T}{4} = \frac{24\ \text{h}}{4} = 6$ hours. Note that angular momentum, not energy, is the conserved quantity here because the (idealized) collapse involves internal forces only.

questions.question: An ice ballerina rotates at constant angular velocity at one particular point (she does not translate). Her arms are fully extended as she rotates, and her moment of inertia is then $I$. She pulls her arms in, and her moment of inertia becomes $I/7$. What is the ratio of the new kinetic energy (arms in) to the initial kinetic energy (arms out)?
questions.hint: Angular momentum is conserved; using $K = L^2/2I$ makes the ratio just $I/I'$.
questions.solution: No external torque acts about her spin axis, so her angular momentum is conserved: $I\omega = \frac{I}{7}\omega'$, which gives $\omega' = 7\omega$ — she spins seven times faster. Since $L = I\omega$ itself is unchanged, it is easiest to write the kinetic energy as $K = \frac{L^2}{2I}$. Then $\frac{K_{\text{in}}}{K_{\text{out}}} = \frac{L^2/2I'}{L^2/2I} = \frac{I}{I'} = \frac{I}{I/7} = 7$. Her rotational kinetic energy increases seven-fold; the extra energy is the work she did pulling her arms inward against the centrifugal tendency of her hands.

questions.question: In a parallel universe, when the temperature of an ideal gas falls by $7\,^\circ\text{C}$, the volume of the gas decreases by $\frac{1}{7}$ of its value at $0\,^\circ\text{C}$, the pressure being held fixed (linear volume-temperature behaviour, as in Charles's law). Let $V_0$ be the volume of the gas at $0\,^\circ\text{C}$. Find the absolute zero of temperature of that universe on the Celsius scale.
questions.hint: Extrapolate the linear law $V = V_0(1 + T/T_0)$ to $V = 0$.
questions.solution: By Charles's-law behaviour the volume depends linearly on the Celsius temperature, decreasing by $\frac{V_0}{7}$ for every $7\,^\circ\text{C}$ of cooling, i.e. by $\frac{V_0}{49}$ per degree. Hence $V(T) = V_0\left(1 + \frac{T}{49}\right)$ with $T$ in °C. Absolute zero is the temperature at which the extrapolated volume of the ideal gas vanishes: $V = 0 \Rightarrow T = -49\,^\circ\text{C}$. This exactly mirrors our own universe, where the volume drops by $\frac{1}{273}$ of $V_0$ per $1\,^\circ\text{C}$ and absolute zero is $-273\,^\circ\text{C}$; the constant in $V = V_0(1 + T/T_0)$ is the negative of the absolute zero on the Celsius scale.

questions.question: A ball is released from rest and falls from a height of $8\,\text{m}$. At the same instant, a stone is thrown from ground level at a horizontal distance of $32\,\text{m}$ from the ball's vertical line, launched at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. The initial speed of the stone is chosen so that it hits the ball. Find the value of $\theta$.
questions.hint: Both objects share the same $-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$ term, so it cancels when you match heights.
questions.solution: Let the collision occur at time $t$ after release. Horizontally the stone must cover $32\,\text{m}$: $v_0\cos\theta\,t = 32$. Vertically, the ball's height is $y_b = 8 - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ while the stone's is $y_s = v_0\sin\theta\,t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$. For a hit, $y_s = y_b$; the $-\frac{1}{2}gt^2$ terms cancel because both bodies fall with the same acceleration, leaving $v_0\sin\theta\,t = 8$. Dividing this by the horizontal equation eliminates $v_0$ and $t$: $\tan\theta = \frac{8}{32} = 0.25$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1}(0.25) \approx 14.0^\circ$. Remarkably, the answer is independent of $g$ and of the launch speed, which only decides whether and when the hit occurs.

questions.question: A point light source is outside a glass cylinder, on its axis and near the flat end face (base); the distance between the source and the base is negligible. Determine the minimum refractive index of the cylinder material for which none of the rays entering the base will emerge from the lateral (curved) surface.
questions.hint: Check total internal reflection for the grazing-incidence rays, which leave the base at the shallowest angle to the axis.
questions.solution: The limiting rays are those entering the base at grazing incidence, $i \to 90^\circ$. Snell's law at the base: $n\sin\theta_r = \sin i \le 1$, so inside the cylinder the refracted ray makes at least the angle $\theta_r$ with the axis, with $\sin\theta_r = 1/n$ in the limit. Such a ray meets the curved wall at incidence $\phi = 90^\circ - \theta_r$ from the normal to the wall. For no ray to emerge, even this ray must be totally internally reflected: $\sin\phi = \cos\theta_r \ge \frac{1}{n}$. Substituting $\sin\theta_r = \frac{1}{n}$ gives $\sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{n^2}} \ge \frac{1}{n}$, hence $n^2 \ge 2$ and $n_{\min} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$. The trapped light then escapes only at the far end face — the principle of optical fibres.

questions.question: A boy was running with constant velocity. He reaches a field, which is $120\,\text{m}$ away from his home, in $20\,\text{s}$. If his mass is $40\,\text{kg}$, what is his kinetic energy?
questions.hint: First get $v = d/t$, then apply $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$.
questions.solution: Running at constant velocity means zero acceleration, so his speed is simply distance over time: $v = \frac{120\ \text{m}}{20\ \text{s}} = 6\ \text{m/s}$. Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its motion, $K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. Substituting, $K = \frac{1}{2}(40\ \text{kg})(6\ \text{m/s})^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times 40 \times 36 = 720\ \text{J}$. Since $v$ is constant, this value is the same at every moment of the run: no net work is done on the runner overall (his internal chemical energy only replaces losses such as air drag and foot friction).

questions.question: An object is thrown horizontally with speed $u$ from the top of a cliff 100 m high. Take $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$ and ignore air resistance. What is the minimum $u$ for which the object arrives at the ground with a total speed of at least 50 m/s?
questions.hint: Vertical and horizontal motions are independent; only the vertical component gains speed during the fall.
questions.solution: Treat the horizontal and vertical motions independently. Falling 100 m from rest gives a vertical impact speed $v_y = √(2gh) = √(2×9.8×100) = √1960 ≈ 44.3$ m/s; the vertical motion is the same whatever $u$ is. With no air resistance the horizontal component stays $u$. The ground speed is therefore $v = √(u^2 + v_y^2)$. Requiring $v ≥ 50$ m/s gives $u^2 ≥ 50^2 - 1960 = 2500 - 1960 = 540$, so $u_{min} = √540 ≈ 23.2$ m/s. A slower throw lands with less than 50 m/s; a faster throw exceeds it. Note that 23.2 m/s is much less than 50 m/s because gravity already supplies most of the speed.

questions.question: A cylinder with moment of inertia $I = (3/5)MR^2$ about its axis rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height $h$ and inclination angle $θ$ (energy dissipated by friction is negligible). A block of wood also slides down the same ramp from rest without friction and reaches speed $√(2gh)$ at the bottom. Find the ratio of the cylinder's speed $v_c$ at the bottom to the block's speed there.
questions.hint: For rolling without slipping $ω = v/R$, and static friction does no work, so mechanical energy is conserved.
questions.solution: Use energy conservation on the cylinder. Its potential energy $Mgh$ becomes translational plus rotational kinetic energy: $Mgh = ½Mv_c^2 + ½Iω^2$. Rolling without slipping means $ω = v_c/R$, so $½Iω^2 = ½·(3/5)MR^2·(v_c^2/R^2) = (3/10)Mv_c^2$. Thus $Mgh = ½Mv_c^2 + (3/10)Mv_c^2 = (4/5)Mv_c^2$, giving $v_c^2 = (5/4)gh$, i.e. $v_c = √(5gh/4)$. The frictionless block converts all its potential energy into translation: $v_b = √(2gh)$. The ratio is $v_c/v_b = √(5/8) ≈ 0.79$. The cylinder is slower because about 37.5% of its energy is stored in rotation, not translation.

questions.question: A neutron of kinetic energy $K = 1876$ MeV is incident on a neutron at rest. The two neutrons scatter elastically, leaving at equal angles $θ$ on either side of the incident direction. Given that the rest energy of a neutron is $m_n c^2 = 938$ MeV, find $θ$.
questions.hint: Use relativistic energy and momentum conservation; the total energy 4mc² splits equally between the two identical neutrons.
questions.solution: The kinetic energy equals twice the rest energy, so relativity is essential. Initially: total energy $E_i = K + m_n c^2 = 3m_n c^2$, and $p_i c = √(E_i^2 - m_n^2c^4) = √(9-1) m_n c^2 = 2√2 m_n c^2$. Total energy is $4m_n c^2$, shared equally by the identical final neutrons: each has $E = 2m_n c^2$ and $pc = √(E^2 - m_n^2c^4) = √3 m_n c^2$. For symmetric scattering the transverse momenta cancel and the longitudinal components add: $2√3 m_n c cosθ = 2√2 m_n c$, so $cosθ = √(2/3)$ and $θ ≈ 35.3°$. (Nonrelativistically the opening angle would be 90°, i.e. 45° each; the MeV data signal the relativistic result.)

questions.question: Using the cross-section formula $σ = 4πq^4/(m^2c^4)$ (Gaussian units), evaluate $σ$ for a proton. Take $q = 4.80×10^{-10}$ esu, $m_p = 1.67×10^{-24}$ g and $c = 3.00×10^{10}$ cm/s.
questions.hint: Compute q⁴ and m²c⁴ separately in cgs units, then divide and multiply by 4π.
questions.solution: Work through the Gaussian-cgs numbers. $q^4 = (4.80×10^{-10})^4 = 5.32×10^{-38}$ esu$^4$. Also $m_p^2 = (1.67×10^{-24})^2 = 2.80×10^{-48}$ g$^2$ and $c^4 = (3.00×10^{10})^4 = 8.10×10^{41}$, so $m_p^2c^4 = 2.27×10^{-6}$. Then $σ = 4π(5.32×10^{-38})/(2.27×10^{-6}) ≈ 2.96×10^{-31}$ cm$^2$, i.e. about $3×10^{-35}$ m$^2$. The $m^2$ in the denominator makes the proton's scattering cross-section roughly $(m_e/m_p)^2 ≈ 3×10^{-7}$ times the electron's: heavy charges are very poor scatterers, which is crucial when balancing radiation against gravity for a star.

questions.question: The outward radiation force on an infalling proton must not exceed the star's gravitational pull $F_g = GMm_p/R^2$, otherwise the proton is blown away. Using $F_{rad} = σL/(4πR^2c)$ with $σ ≈ 3×10^{-35}$ m$^2$ (from $σ = 4πq^4/(m_p^2c^4)$), find the upper limit on the luminosity of the star and evaluate it for $M = 2×10^{30}$ kg. Take $G = 6.67×10^{-11}$ N·m$^2$/kg$^2$, $m_p = 1.67×10^{-27}$ kg, $c = 3×10^8$ m/s.
questions.hint: Equate σL/(4πR²c) with GMm_p/R²; R cancels and the limit depends only on the stellar mass.
questions.solution: Set the radiation force equal to gravity: $σL/(4πR^2c) = GMm_p/R^2$. The radius cancels — the limit is universal for a given mass: $L_{max} = 4πGMm_pc/σ$, which using $σ = 4πq^4/(m_p^2c^4)$ can also be written $GMm_p^3c^5/q^4$. Numerically: $4π(6.67×10^{-11})(2×10^{30})(1.67×10^{-27})(3×10^8) = 8.4×10^2$, and dividing by $σ ≈ 3×10^{-35}$ m$^2$ gives $L_{max} ≈ 2.8×10^{37}$ W, about $7×10^{10}$ times the Sun's luminosity. (Using electrons as the scatterers instead of protons gives the classical Eddington limit, $≈1.5×10^{31}$ W ≈ $3×10^4$ solar luminosities.)

questions.question: A, B and C are three points in space with AB = 6 m, BC = 8 m and AC = 13 m. Charges of +2 C, +5 C and +7 C are held at A, B and C respectively; each charged object has mass 10 kg. The charge at A is released from rest while the charges at B and C are kept fixed. What will be its speed at infinite distance? (k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C²)
questions.hint: Energy conservation: all of A's electrostatic potential energy from B and C becomes its kinetic energy at infinity.
questions.solution: Only A's interactions change, since B and C never move and their mutual energy is irrelevant. The initial electrostatic potential energy of A is $U_i = k q_A q_B/AB + k q_A q_C/AC = 8.99×10^9 × [ (2×5)/6 + (2×7)/13 ] = 8.99×10^9 × (1.667 + 1.077) = 8.99×10^9 × 2.744 ≈ 2.47×10^{10}$ J. At infinity the potential energy is zero, so all of it becomes kinetic energy of A: $½mv^2 = U_i$ with $m = 10$ kg. Thus $v = √(2U_i/m) = √(4.93×10^9) ≈ 7.0×10^4$ m/s (about 70 km/s). Note the distance BC = 8 m never enters the calculation.

questions.question: A truck of mass $M_1$ transporting sand of mass $M_2$ moves horizontally at constant speed $v$. The sand leaks out through a hole in the floor at the rate $λ$ (kg/s), dropping vertically onto the ground. What horizontal force is needed to keep the truck moving uniformly with speed $v$?
questions.hint: The leaking sand keeps the truck's horizontal velocity v, so no horizontal momentum transfer — and no force — is required.
questions.solution: The key is the velocity of the sand as it leaves. The sand drops through a hole, so at the moment of leaving it already has the truck's full horizontal velocity $v$; afterwards it merely gains vertical velocity while falling. Therefore no horizontal momentum is exchanged between the truck and the departing sand — the truck does not have to accelerate or decelerate the leaking mass. Newton's second law for the remaining truck-plus-sand then requires zero net horizontal force: $F = 0$, independent of $M_1$, $M_2$, $λ$ and $v$. Contrast the classic companion case: loading sand at rate $λ$ that arrives with no horizontal speed would require $F = λv$ to keep the speed constant.

questions.question: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution law is written as $dN = 4πN (m/(2πk_BT))^{3/2} v^x e^{-mv^2/(2k_BT)} dv$, where $dN$ is the number of molecules with speeds between $v$ and $v+dv$, $m$ is the molecular mass, $T$ the absolute temperature, $k_B$ Boltzmann's constant and $N$ the total number of molecules. Using dimensional analysis, find the value of $x$.
questions.hint: dN is dimensionless, so the remaining right-hand side must have the dimensions of 1/velocity; match powers of m/s.
questions.solution: Count molecules: $dN$ is dimensionless. Examine the prefactor: $m/(k_BT)$ has units kg/(kg·m²/s²) = s²/m², so $(m/2πk_BT)^{3/2}$ carries s³/m³. The exponential is dimensionless, and $dv$ contributes m/s. For the whole right side to be dimensionless, $v^x$ must supply m³/s³ ÷ (m/s) = m²/s², which are exactly the dimensions of $v^2$. Hence $x = 2$. This is not an accident: the $v^2$ factor is the surface area $4πv^2$ of the sphere of radius $v$ in velocity space, multiplied into the Gaussian weight $e^{-mv^2/2k_BT}$ — dimensional analysis alone recovers the geometric factor.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 500 nm is shined perpendicularly on a slab of refractive index 2.0. Oil of refractive index 1.5 is poured on top of the slab (air remains above the oil), forming a thin film whose thickness grows until the intensity of the reflected light is minimized. What is the minimum thickness of the oil film?
questions.hint: Both reflections are low→high index so the π shifts cancel; minimum reflection needs 2nt = λ/2 for the thinnest film.
questions.solution: Identify the two interfering reflections: at the air-to-oil surface (1.0 to 1.5) and at the oil-to-slab surface (1.5 to 2.0). Both reflections occur going from lower to higher refractive index, so BOTH beams pick up a $π$ phase shift, which cancel in the relative phase. The only remaining phase difference is the round trip through the oil: $Δφ = (2π/λ_0)·2nt$ with $n = 1.5$. Destructive interference (minimum reflection) requires $Δφ = (2m+1)π$, i.e. $2nt = (m + ½)λ_0$. The thinnest such film ($m = 0$) has $t = λ_0/4n = 500/(4×1.5) = 83.3$ nm.

questions.question: Two solid conducting spheres of radii 10 cm and 20 cm carry charges 5 μC and 30 μC respectively and are kept 2 m apart (their mutual influence is negligible). They are then connected by a thin conducting wire. Find the amount of heat generated in this process. (k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C²)
questions.hint: Charge redistributes until the potentials are equal; the heat is the decrease in stored electrostatic energy.
questions.solution: Charge flows through the wire until both spheres reach the same potential: $kq_1/r_1 = kq_2/r_2$, so $q_1/q_2 = r_1/r_2 = 1/2$. With total charge $Q = 35$ μC, $q_1 = 35/3 μC ≈ 11.67$ μC and $q_2 = 70/3 μC ≈ 23.33$ μC. The electrostatic energy of isolated spheres is $U = ½k(q_1^2/r_1 + q_2^2/r_2)$. Before: $U_i = ½(9×10^9)[(5×10^{-6})^2/0.1 + (30×10^{-6})^2/0.2] = 21.375$ J. After: $U_f = ½(9×10^9)[(35/3×10^{-6})^2/0.1 + (70/3×10^{-6})^2/0.2] = 18.375$ J. The lost energy dissipates as heat in the wire: $H = U_i - U_f = 3.0$ J.

questions.question: A bomb bursts at ground level and the fragments all acquire the same constant speed of 20 m/s, flying out in all upward directions. Taking $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$ and neglecting air resistance, what area of ground will the fragments cover?
questions.hint: The circle's radius is the maximum projectile range v²/g, achieved at a 45° launch angle.
questions.solution: Each fragment is a projectile launched at $v = 20$ m/s from ground level. The horizontal range of a projectile is $R = v^2 sin(2θ)/g$, maximized when $θ = 45°$ (so $sin2θ = 1$), giving the maximum reach $R_{max} = v^2/g = 400/9.8 = 40.8$ m. Since fragments fly out in every azimuthal direction, the landing points fill a disk of radius $R_{max}$: fragments thrown below the horizontal hit the ground immediately and land inside the same disk. The covered area is $A = πR_{max}^2 = π(40.8)^2 ≈ 5.23×10^3$ m$^2$, a little over half a hectare.

questions.question: Lily is in a spaceship moving at speed $u = 0.5c$ with respect to a viewer at rest on Earth. She watches Severus going forward at speed $v_S = 0.8c$ and James going backward at speed $v_J = 0.85c$ (both speeds measured in Lily's frame). How fast is James going according to Severus?
questions.hint: Apply u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²) with u = −0.85c and v = +0.8c.
questions.solution: Use the relativistic velocity transformation. Take forward as positive. In Lily's frame, Severus moves at $+0.8c$ and James at $-0.85c$. Severus's frame moves at $v = +0.8c$ relative to Lily's frame, and James's velocity transforms as $u' = (u - v)/(1 - uv/c^2)$ with $u = -0.85c$: $u' = (-0.85c - 0.8c)/(1 - (-0.85)(0.8)) = -1.65c/1.68 = -0.982c$. So Severus sees James moving backward at about $0.982c$. Note the classical subtraction would have given $1.65c$, faster than light; the relativistic denominator keeps every relative speed below $c$, however close the individual speeds are to it.

questions.question: A cell of EMF $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r = 0.2\ \Omega$ is connected to an external circuit between points A and B; the total resistance of the external circuit from A to B is $R$, so the same current $I$ flows through the cell and through the external resistance. If the power dissipated inside the cell (in its internal resistance) is equal to the power dissipated as the current flows from A to B through $R$, calculate the value of $R$.
questions.hint: The same $I$ flows through $r$ and $R$, so simply compare $I^2 r$ with $I^2 R$.
questions.solution: In this single-loop circuit the same current $I$ passes through the internal resistance $r$ and through the external resistance $R$. The power dissipated inside the cell is $P_{cell} = I^2 r$; the power dissipated in the external circuit between A and B is $P_{ext} = I^2 R$. The given condition is $I^2 r = I^2 R$, and the common factor $I^2$ cancels, so the result is independent of the EMF and the current: $R = r = 0.2\ \Omega$. This illustrates a general rule: a real source with internal resistance $r$ dissipates power in its load at the same rate as it dissipates internally exactly when the load resistance equals $r$.

questions.question: A sphere and a cylinder of equal mass $m$ and equal radius $R$ start from rest at the same instant and roll without slipping down two identical inclined planes from the same height $h$. The moments of inertia are $I_{sphere} = \frac{2}{5}mR^2$ and $I_{cylinder} = \frac{1}{2}mR^2$. What is the ratio $v_{sphere}/v_{cylinder}$ of the speeds of their centers of mass when they reach the bottom of the inclines?
questions.hint: Energy conservation with $v = \omega R$: the body with larger rotational inertia converts more of $mgh$ into spin and moves slower.
questions.solution: Rolling without slipping links translation and rotation, $v = \omega R$, and static friction does no work, so mechanical energy is conserved: $mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\left(1 + \frac{I}{mR^2}\right)$. Writing $I = \beta mR^2$ gives $v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1+\beta}}$. For the sphere $\beta = 2/5$: $v_s^2 = \frac{2gh}{7/5} = \frac{10gh}{7}$. For the cylinder $\beta = 1/2$: $v_c^2 = \frac{2gh}{3/2} = \frac{4gh}{3}$. Hence $\frac{v_s}{v_c} = \sqrt{\frac{10/7}{4/3}} = \sqrt{\frac{30}{28}} = \sqrt{\frac{15}{14}} \approx 1.035$. The sphere arrives faster because a smaller share of $mgh$ is stored as rotational kinetic energy; the ratio is independent of $m$, $R$ and the slope.

questions.question: A stationary (standing) electromagnetic wave is formed between two partially reflecting parallel plates separated by $L = 2$ cm. The frequency of the wave is $f = 3\times10^{12}$ Hz and electromagnetic waves travel at $c = 3\times10^8$ m/s. Calculate the number of points between the plates where the amplitude of the stationary wave is maximum.
questions.hint: Find how many half-wavelengths fit into the 2 cm gap; each half-wavelength contains one antinode.
questions.solution: The wavelength is $\lambda = \frac{c}{f} = \frac{3\times10^8\ \text{m/s}}{3\times10^{12}\ \text{Hz}} = 10^{-4}$ m $= 0.1$ mm. In any standing wave, amplitude maxima (antinodes) occur once every half-wavelength, i.e. every $\lambda/2 = 0.05$ mm. The gap between the plates holds $N = \frac{L}{\lambda/2} = \frac{20\ \text{mm}}{0.05\ \text{mm}} = 400$ half-wavelengths. With the electric field forced to have nodes at the two reflecting plates, each half-wavelength segment contains exactly one maximum, and the endpoints themselves are nodes. So there are $400$ antinodal points between the plates.

questions.question: Protons (charge $+e$, mass $m_p$) drop from rest through an accelerating potential $V_0 = 2$ MV and emerge as a beam. To deflect the beam, a pair of curved plates bent along a circle is used; the plates are very close together compared to their radius of curvature, separated by an insulating gap $d = 1$ cm, and a voltage $V' = 20$ kV is applied across them, producing a uniform electric field $E = V'/d$ pointing radially across the gap. What should the radius of curvature of the curved plates be so that the beam follows the circular gap?
questions.hint: Equate $\frac{mv^2}{\rho}$ to $qE$ and eliminate $v$ using $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = qV_0$.
questions.solution: The accelerator gives each proton kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}m_p v^2 = eV_0$. Inside the gap the electric force $eE$ must supply the centripetal force for the circular path: $\frac{m_p v^2}{\rho} = eE$, where $E = V'/d$. Substituting $m_p v^2 = 2eV_0$ gives $\frac{2eV_0}{\rho} = \frac{eV'}{d}$, so $\rho = \frac{2V_0 d}{V'} = \frac{2 \times (2\times10^{6}\ \text{V}) \times (10^{-2}\ \text{m})}{2\times10^{4}\ \text{V}} = 2$ m. The plates must therefore be curved with a radius of $2$ m; note that the field must point toward the center of the circle to bend the positive beam.

questions.question: In the same deflection setup (particles accelerated through $V_0 = 2$ MV; curved plates separated by $d = 1$ cm with $V' = 20$ kV applied across them), the protons are replaced by deuterium ions, which carry the same charge $+e$ but roughly twice the mass, $m \approx 2m_p$. What is the radius of curvature of the deuterium beam?
questions.hint: Write $\rho = 2V_0 d/V'$ and check whether the particle's mass appears anywhere.
questions.solution: From $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = eV_0$, every particle gains $mv^2 = 2eV_0$ regardless of its mass; the mass only sets the speed, $v = \sqrt{2eV_0/m}$. The deflector requires $\frac{mv^2}{\rho} = eE$, and substituting $mv^2$ gives $\rho = \frac{2V_0}{E} = \frac{2V_0 d}{V'}$ — an expression containing no mass. Since the deuterium ion carries the same charge $+e$, the field per unit charge is unchanged, and the heavier but slower ions need exactly the same orbit radius to match $v^2/\rho$ to $eE/m$. Hence $\rho = \frac{2 \times (2\times10^{6}) \times (10^{-2})}{2\times10^{4}} = 2$ m, the same as for protons.

questions.question: A planet has twice the mass of Earth and half its radius ($R_E = 6370$ km, surface gravity $g_E = 9.8$ m/s$^2$). Any object placed on the planet's surface is held down by its gravity everywhere except at the equator, where the rotation makes the effective gravity exactly zero, so objects there just float. How long is one day (the rotation period) on this planet?
questions.hint: Set $\omega^2 R_p = g_p$ with $g_p = 8g_E$ and $R_p = R_E/2$, then $T = 2\pi/\omega$.
questions.solution: Surface gravity: $g_p = \frac{GM_p}{R_p^2} = \frac{G(2M_E)}{(R_E/2)^2} = 8\frac{GM_E}{R_E^2} = 8g_E = 78.4$ m/s$^2$. At the equator, an object co-rotating with the planet just loses contact when the required centripetal acceleration equals the gravitational acceleration: $\omega^2 R_p = g_p$. With $R_p = 6370/2 = 3185$ km $= 3.185\times10^{6}$ m: $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{78.4}{3.185\times10^{6}}} = 4.96\times10^{-3}$ rad/s. The length of one day is $T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R_p}{g_p}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{3.185\times10^{6}}{78.4}} \approx 1266$ s $\approx 21$ minutes — vastly shorter than Earth's day because the planet is small yet very dense.

questions.question: A coherent beam of monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda = 500\,\mathrm{nm}$ is directed towards two thin slits separated by $d = 1.0\,\mathrm{mm}$. The screen covers an angular region of $60^\circ$ centred on the symmetry axis of the slits, i.e. it receives light travelling in all directions from $-30^\circ$ to $+30^\circ$ (as shown in the figure). Approximately how many bright interference bands are visible on the screen?
questions.hint: Set $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ and count the integer orders $m$ that fit within $\pm 30^\circ$.
questions.solution: Bright fringes appear where light from the two slits arrives in phase, i.e. where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. The largest direction the screen covers is $\theta_{\max} = 30^\circ$, so the highest visible order is $m_{\max} = \frac{d\sin 30^\circ}{\lambda} = \frac{(1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})(0.5)}{500\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}} = 1000$. Every integer order $m$ with $|m| \le 1000$ produces exactly one bright band: from $m = -1000$ on one edge, through the central maximum $m = 0$, to $m = +1000$ on the other edge. Orders beyond $\pm 1000$ would require $|\sin\theta| > 0.5$, outside the screen. Hence the number of bright bands is $2\times 1000 + 1 = 2001$.

questions.question: A solid cube has sides of length 1 cm and a mass of 1 g. What is the density of the material of the cube?
questions.hint: Use $\rho = m/V$ with $V$ the cube's volume, then convert $\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ to $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.
questions.solution: Density is mass per unit volume, $\rho = m/V$. The volume of the cube is $V = (1\,\mathrm{cm})^3 = 1\,\mathrm{cm}^3 = 1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^3$, and the mass is $m = 1\,\mathrm{g} = 1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}$. Directly, $\rho = 1\,\mathrm{g}/1\,\mathrm{cm}^3 = 1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. In SI units, $\rho = \frac{1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}}{1.0\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^3} = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$. This is exactly the density of water — a useful sanity check, since $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$ is the standard density of water and the unit conversion $1\,\mathrm{g/cm^3} = 1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ is one worth memorising.

questions.question: Two plane mirrors are placed perpendicular to each other (as shown in the figure), and a point object is placed at point P in front of both mirrors. How many images of P will be formed? State where each image is located (the original task asks to mark them on the figure).
questions.hint: Count the two single-reflection images plus the double-reflection image formed by successive reflection in both mirrors.
questions.solution: Each mirror forms an image by a single reflection: mirror 1 gives $P_1$, the mirror image of P across mirror 1, and mirror 2 gives $P_2$ across mirror 2. Light can also reflect once in each mirror in succession, producing a third image $P_3$ — the image of an image. If the mirrors lie along the $x$ and $y$ axes and P is at $(x, y)$, then $P_1 = (-x, y)$, $P_2 = (x, -y)$, and the double-reflection image $P_3 = (-x, -y)$, which is the reflection of P through the corner point where the mirrors meet. No further images arise because after two reflections the ray direction reverses back into the object's quadrant. Hence exactly 3 images are formed, and each is as far behind its mirror as P is in front.

questions.question: A torsional pendulum is an oscillator whose restoring torque is torsion: if an object suspended by a wire is twisted by an angle $\phi$, the restoring torque is $\tau=-\kappa\phi$, where $\kappa$ is the torsional constant of the wire. A bird feeder consists of a disk of mass $250\ \mathrm{g}$ and diameter $50\ \mathrm{cm}$, suspended by a wire at its centre (use the disk mass of 250 g as the problem instructs). Two birds of equal mass sit on opposite sides of the disk's rim, and the feeder undergoes torsional oscillation at $2.6\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The torsional constant of the wire is $5.00\ \mathrm{N\cdot m/rad}$. Determine the mass of each bird.
questions.hint: Set $\kappa/I=\omega^2$ with $\omega=2\pi f$, then subtract the disk's $\tfrac12MR^2$ from the total $I$ and divide the remainder by $2R^2$.
questions.solution: Newton's second law for rotation gives $I\ddot\phi=-\kappa\phi$, the SHM equation with $\omega=\sqrt{\kappa/I}$ and $f=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\kappa/I}$. Hence the total moment of inertia is $I=\frac{\kappa}{(2\pi f)^2}=\frac{5.00}{(2\pi\times2.6)^2}=\frac{5.00}{266.9}=0.01874\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. The disk (mass $0.250\ \mathrm{kg}$ as instructed, radius $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$) contributes $I_d=\frac12MR^2=\frac12(0.250)(0.25)^2=0.00781\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, the same $\frac12MR^2$ form as any uniform disk. Each bird, treated as a point mass sitting at the rim, contributes $mR^2$; together $I_{birds}=2mR^2=0.125m$. So $m=\frac{0.01874-0.00781}{0.125}=0.0874\ \mathrm{kg}\approx87\ \mathrm{g}$ per bird.

questions.question: A coil of 15 turns, each of radius $1\ \mathrm{cm}$, is rotating at a constant angular velocity $300\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.5\ \mathrm{T}$. Assume that at time $t=0$ the normal $\hat n$ to the coil plane is along the $y$ direction, and that the self-inductance of the coil can be neglected. If the coil resistance is $9\ \Omega$, what is the magnitude (amplitude) of the induced current in milliamperes?
questions.hint: Peak EMF is $NBA\omega$ with $A=\pi r^2$; divide by $R$ and convert to milliamperes.
questions.solution: The flux through the rotating coil is $\Phi=NBA\cos(\omega t)$; the given $t=0$ orientation of the normal only decides whether the emf is a sine or a cosine, not its size. Faraday's law gives $\varepsilon=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$ with amplitude $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega=15\times0.5\times\pi(0.01)^2\times300=0.707\ \mathrm{V}$. Since the self-inductance is neglected, the coil behaves as a pure resistance and the current amplitude is $I_0=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{R}=\frac{0.707}{9}=0.0785\ \mathrm{A}\approx78.5\ \mathrm{mA}$. The current alternates at $f=\omega/2\pi\approx47.7\ \mathrm{Hz}$, but its magnitude (peak value) is $78.5\ \mathrm{mA}$.

questions.question: A torsional pendulum is an oscillator whose restoring torque is torsion: if an object suspended by a wire is twisted by an angle $\phi$, the restoring torque is $\tau=-\kappa\phi$, where $\kappa$ is the torsional constant of the wire. A bird feeder consists of a $340\ \mathrm{g}$ disk, $50\ \mathrm{cm}$ in diameter, suspended by a wire at its centre. Two birds of equal mass sit on opposite sides of the disk, and the feeder undergoes torsional oscillation at $2.6\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The torsional constant of the wire is $5.00\ \mathrm{N\cdot m/rad}$. Determine the mass of each bird (treat each bird as a point mass at the rim).
questions.hint: Total $I=\kappa/(2\pi f)^2$; subtract the disk's $\tfrac12MR^2$ and divide the remainder by $2R^2$.
questions.solution: The torsional pendulum obeys $I\ddot\phi=-\kappa\phi$, so $f=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\kappa/I}$ and the total moment of inertia is $I=\frac{\kappa}{(2\pi f)^2}=\frac{5.00}{(2\pi\times2.6)^2}=\frac{5.00}{266.9}=0.01874\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. The disk of mass $0.340\ \mathrm{kg}$ and radius $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ contributes $I_d=\frac12MR^2=\frac12(0.340)(0.0625)=0.010625\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2}$. The two birds sit at the rim on opposite sides, each treated as a point mass, so their moments of inertia simply add: $I_{birds}=2mR^2=2m(0.0625)=0.125m$. Hence $m=\frac{0.01874-0.010625}{0.125}=0.0649\ \mathrm{kg}\approx65\ \mathrm{g}$ per bird — a plausible mass for a small songbird, which confirms the data are consistent.

questions.question: The rotational kinetic energy of a circular disk spinning about its central axis is written $E = k\,m r^2 \omega^2$, where $k$ is a factor characteristic of the disk shape, $m$ its mass, $r$ its radius and $\omega$ its angular velocity. For a uniform solid disk of radius 0.5 m, thickness 0.01 m and density 500 kg/m$^3$ rotated by a motor, the electrical energy fed in is measured for various angular velocities and plotted. What is the factor $k$ for an ideal uniform disk?
questions.hint: Express E through the disk's moment of inertia and match coefficients with the given form.
questions.solution: Concept: rotational kinetic energy $E = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ with the moment of inertia of a uniform solid disk about its symmetry axis, $I = \frac{1}{2}mr^2$ (integrate rings: $dm = \frac{m}{\pi r^2}\,2\pi s\,ds$, so $\int s^2\,dm = \frac{1}{2}mr^2$). Hence $E = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}mr^2\omega^2 = \frac{1}{4}mr^2\omega^2$, i.e. $k = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25$. Note $k$ is purely geometric: the mass ($m = \rho\,\pi r^2 t = 500\times\pi\times0.25\times0.01 \approx 3.9$ kg) cancels out. Among the paper's options, the value consistent with the ideal $0.25$ (tiny excess attributable to real-graph rounding) is $0.251$ — choice C. ($k = 0.5$ would describe a hoop with all its mass at the rim, $I = mr^2$.)

questions.question: Subarno has a square metal plate of side 10 m with a circular hole of radius 100 cm cut at its centre. He raises the temperature by 50 degree Celsius and finds that the radius of the hole has changed. Given the linear expansion coefficient of the metal $\alpha = 6\times10^{-5}\ /\mathrm{K}$, what is the change in the hole's radius?
questions.solution: Every linear dimension of a plate — including the radius of a hole in it — expands by the same factor: $\Delta r = \alpha\,r\,\Delta T = 6\times10^{-5}\times1\,\mathrm{m}\times50 = 3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m} = 3$ mm increase (the hole opens up as if drawn on the metal; the 10 m side is a distractor). Excluded from the bank because thermal expansion of solids is not in the Category C syllabus list.

questions.question: In a room, two loudspeakers play music simultaneously; the two sound outputs are unrelated (incoherent) waves. The intensity of the total sound at a point is two times the intensity that speaker 1 alone would produce there. If speaker 1 emits waves of amplitude $A$, what is the amplitude of speaker 2's waves? (Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.)
questions.hint: For unrelated sources ask whether amplitudes or intensities add, then use the square-law link between them.
questions.solution: Concept: waves from unrelated (incoherent) sources have a rapidly and randomly varying phase difference, so the interference term averages to zero and INTENSITIES simply add: $I_{\mathrm{tot}} = I_1 + I_2$. The given $I_{\mathrm{tot}} = 2I_1$ forces $I_2 = I_1$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared ($I \propto A^2$ for waves of the same frequency in the same medium), equal intensities mean equal amplitudes: $A_2 = A$ — choice C. Watch the trap: $(\sqrt{2}-1)A$ is what you would get for two coherent, in-phase waves forced to satisfy $(A + A_2)^2 = 2A^2$ — a different physical situation that two speakers 'playing music' rules out.

questions.question: In a fanciful 'bubble universe', distance is quantized: two objects can be separated only by whole numbers of metres (1 m, 2 m, 100 m, ... — never 1.55 m or 3.1415 m). On a planet of this universe, lifting a 1 kg mass from $r$ m to $(r+1)$ m requires work $\frac{KM}{2r}$ J, where $r$ is the distance from the planet's centre and $M$ the planet's mass. Treating the planet as a point mass, what is the gravitational potential at infinity for this planet?
questions.hint: Potential values are fixed by convention — ask where the zero of gravitational potential is defined to be.
questions.solution: Concept: gravitational potential is DEFINED by choosing its zero at infinity — $V(\infty) \equiv 0$ — with $V(r)$ the work per unit mass needed to bring a body from infinity to $r$. This convention is part of the definition of potential and holds whatever the force law, even in a universe with the quirky per-step cost $\frac{KM}{2r}$. Consistency checks: for an ordinary point planet $V(r) = -KM/r \to 0$ as $r \to \infty$; and in the bubble universe the per-step work $\frac{KM}{2r}$ itself shrinks to zero as $r$ grows, so the potential flattens toward the same reference value far away. Hence the potential at infinity is $0$ — choice A.

questions.question: A sun ray strikes a spherical raindrop, refracts at the front surface (angle of incidence $i$, angle of refraction $r$), reflects once from the back surface of the drop, and refracts out — the geometry of the primary rainbow. In terms of $i$ and $r$, what is the total deviation angle $d$ between the original incident direction and the final emerging ray?
questions.hint: Add the direction changes at entry, at the back-surface reflection, and at the exit.
questions.solution: Concept: the deviation of a ray at one interaction is the angle through which its direction turns; the total deviation is the sum over the three interactions. (1) Entry refraction (air $\to$ water): the ray bends toward the normal, turning by $i - r$. (2) Internal reflection at the back of the drop: by the chord symmetry of a circle, the incidence angle there equals $r$ again, and reflection at incidence $r$ turns the direction through $180^{\circ} - 2r$. (3) Exit refraction (water $\to$ air): the ray bends away from the normal, turning by $i - r$ once more. Summing: $d = (i - r) + (180^{\circ} - 2r) + (i - r) = 180^{\circ} + 2i - 4r$ — choice B. (Minimizing $d$ over $i$, using $\sin i = n\sin r$, locates the bright primary-rainbow direction.)

questions.question: In a room whose air is at 16 degree Celsius, three rulers — one of steel, one of wood, one of rubber — have been lying for hours. Which ruler is the coldest?
options: They will all be at the same temperature
questions.hint: Separate temperature (a state) from the feeling of cold (a rate of heat flow into your hand).
questions.solution: Concept: the zeroth law of thermodynamics — objects left in contact with their surroundings reach thermal equilibrium. After hours in the room, each ruler has exchanged heat with the air until no net heat flow remains, so every ruler sits at exactly the air temperature, 16 degrees Celsius; none is colder than another. Steel only FEELS coldest: its thermal conductivity is far larger than that of wood or rubber, so it drains heat from your 37 degree hand quickly and produces a stronger cold sensation. The sensation of cold reports the rate of heat flow out of your skin, not the object's temperature — choice D.

questions.question: A block oscillates harmonically along the $x$-axis with amplitude $A$, its position given by $x = A\sin\omega t$. What is the probability of finding the block's centre of mass between $x = -A/2$ and $x = +A/2$?
questions.hint: Probability equals the fraction of a period spent in the interval — find the time to travel from the centre to A/2.
questions.solution: Concept: for periodic motion the probability of being in a spatial interval equals the fraction of each period spent there. The block reaches $x = A/2$ when $\sin\omega t = 1/2$, i.e. $\omega t = \pi/6$, so travelling from the centre to $A/2$ takes $\pi/(6\omega)$. In each quarter-period (duration $\pi/2\omega$) the block is inside $|x| \le A/2$ for exactly $\pi/(6\omega)$. Over a full period $T = 2\pi/\omega$ the total time inside is $4\times\frac{\pi}{6\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{3\omega}$, giving $P = \frac{2\pi/3\omega}{2\pi/\omega} = \frac{1}{3}$ — choice C. Sense check: the block moves fastest at the centre (speed maximum at $x = 0$) and dwells near the turning points, so it spends less than half its time in the central half of its range; the two outer strips share the remaining $2/3$.

questions.question: A thin spherical shell of radius $R$ carries a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$. A small circular hole is cut out of the shell; the hole is small enough to be treated as flat. Find the electric field at a point just outside the shell, directly above the centre of the hole, so close to the hole that the hole behaves like an infinite charged plane.
questions.hint: Build the answer by superposition: complete-shell field minus the field of the piece that was cut out.
questions.solution: Concept: superposition — the punctured shell equals the complete shell MINUS the small disk of charge that was removed. Complete uniformly charged shell: Gauss's law gives a field just outside of $E_{\mathrm{shell}} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$, pointing radially outward (from $E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R^2}$ with $Q = \sigma\,4\pi R^2$). The removed disk, viewed from a point just above its centre, is indistinguishable from an infinite charged plane with field $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$, also pointing outward on the top side. Subtracting: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} - \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ outward — choice B. The same subtraction just inside the hole gives $\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$ pointing into the interior: the field reverses across the hole because the shell's own field jumps by $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ at the surface.

questions.question: A bowling ball accidentally falls out of the cargo bay of an airliner that is flying horizontally at constant speed. Neglecting air resistance, as observed by a person standing on the ground, which trajectory does the ball follow after leaving the airplane?
options: It drops straight down and lands directly below the release point.
It falls behind the airplane, curving backwards relative to the plane's direction of motion.
It keeps the airplane's horizontal speed while accelerating downward, following a parabola whose tangent is horizontal at the moment of release.
It shoots forward faster than the airplane along a straight slanted line.
It first travels horizontally, then drops vertically straight down.
questions.hint: Ask what the ball's velocity is at the instant of release, and whether gravity can change the horizontal component.
questions.solution: Concept: projectile motion with a non-zero initial horizontal velocity. At release the ball shares the airplane's velocity: horizontal $v_0$, vertical $0$. Gravity accelerates it only vertically, so the horizontal velocity stays $v_0$ while the vertical velocity grows as $gt$: $x = v_0 t$ and $y = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$, which combine into the parabola $y = \frac{g x^2}{2v_0^2}$. Its tangent at release is horizontal (initial vertical velocity is zero) and it curves smoothly downward — choice C. Check: the ball keeps the plane's horizontal speed, so it remains vertically below the airplane at every instant while tracing this parabola as seen from the ground.

questions.question: Inside a conducting spherical ball of outer radius $R$ there is an off-centre, irregularly shaped cavity, and a point charge $q = +4e$ sits inside the cavity. What is the surface charge density on the OUTER surface of the ball?
options: Variable, highest on the side closest to the cavity.
Variable, lowest on the side closest to the cavity.
Zero, because a conductor's surface is always an equipotential surface.
questions.hint: Use Gauss's law in the metal to find the cavity-wall charge, conserve charge for the outside, then ask what symmetry the exterior field can have.
questions.solution: Concept: Gauss's law applied inside the conducting material, plus charge conservation, then a symmetry argument for the exterior. Draw a Gaussian surface lying wholly in the metal (where $E = 0$) enclosing the cavity: the net enclosed charge must vanish, so $-4e$ is induced on the cavity wall (spread non-uniformly, hugging the cavity's irregular shape). The ball is neutral overall, so the outer surface must carry $+4e$. On the OUTER surface the charge spreads uniformly: the conductor shields the exterior from everything inside, leaving a spherically symmetric exterior problem whose only solution has the field radial, so $\sigma = \frac{4e}{4\pi R^2} = \frac{e}{\pi R^2}$ — choice C.

questions.question: Two atoms interact through the Lennard-Jones potential $U(r) = \varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)^{12} - 2\left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)^{6}\right]$, where $\varepsilon$ and $r_0$ are positive constants (the minimum $U = -\varepsilon$ lies at $r = r_0$). If the motion of a point mass $m_0$ were governed by this potential, what would be the angular frequency of small oscillations about the equilibrium separation?
questions.hint: Expand the potential to second order about its minimum; the curvature there is the effective spring constant.
questions.solution: Concept: near any potential minimum the potential acts like a spring — expand to second order, $U \approx U(r_0) + \frac{1}{2}U''(r_0)\,x^2$ with $x = r - r_0$, giving force $F = -U''(r_0)\,x$ and SHM with $\omega = \sqrt{U''(r_0)/m_0}$. Equilibrium: $\frac{dU}{dr} = \varepsilon\left[-\frac{12r_0^{12}}{r^{13}} + \frac{12r_0^{6}}{r^{7}}\right] = 0$ gives $r = r_0$. Curvature: $\frac{d^2U}{dr^2} = \varepsilon\left[\frac{156\,r_0^{12}}{r^{14}} - \frac{84\,r_0^{6}}{r^{8}}\right]$, and at $r = r_0$ this is $(156 - 84)\frac{\varepsilon}{r_0^2} = \frac{72\varepsilon}{r_0^2}$. Hence $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{72\,\varepsilon}{m_0 r_0^2}}$ — choice B. (The potential formula, lost in the scanned text, is the standard Lennard-Jones form restated above; it is the only form consistent with the options.)

questions.question: An uncharged rectangular dielectric slab is being inserted between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor while the capacitor remains connected to a battery (constant voltage). Which of the following statement(s) is/are true during this process?
options: The capacitor exerts no force on the slab.
The energy stored in the capacitor increases.
The energy stored in the capacitor decreases.
questions.hint: Track how C changes at constant V, and which direction the energy gradient pushes the slab.
questions.solution: Concept: capacitance with a dielectric, $C = \kappa C_0$ with $\kappa > 1$, evaluated at fixed voltage. As the slab slides in, the filled fraction grows and $C$ rises, so the stored energy $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$ increases — statement C is true. The energy gain is largest when more dielectric is inside: the fringing field at the plate edges polarizes the slab and pulls it inward, so the capacitor attracts the slab — statement A is true and B is false. Energy bookkeeping: the battery pushes extra charge $\Delta Q = V\Delta C$ through, delivering $V^2\Delta C$; half of that becomes the extra stored energy and the other half does the work of pulling the slab in. Answer: A and C.

questions.question: One mole of an ideal gas is taken along the process $A \to B \to C$ shown on a $pV$ diagram; points $A$ and $C$ lie on the same isotherm. What is the change in the internal energy of the gas along $A \to B \to C$?
questions.hint: Internal energy of an ideal gas is a state function of temperature alone — compare only the endpoints.
questions.solution: Concept: for a fixed amount of ideal gas the internal energy depends only on the temperature, $U = n C_V T$, and is a state function — its change depends only on the endpoints, never on the path. Since $A$ and $C$ lie on the SAME isotherm, $T_A = T_C$, so $\Delta U = n C_V (T_C - T_A) = 0$, whatever detour the path makes through $B$ — choice D. The listed expressions are of the work/heat type (areas under process curves), which need not vanish on a path that returns to the initial temperature; only $\Delta U$ is pinned to the temperature difference alone.

questions.question: The position of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is $x = 4\cos(\omega t) + \cos(2\omega t)$, with $x$ in metres. What is the maximum speed of the particle?
questions.hint: Differentiate x, collapse sin2t with the double-angle identity, then maximize over the phase.
questions.solution: Concept: velocity is the time derivative of position; maximize its magnitude. $v = \frac{dx}{dt} = -4\omega\sin\omega t - 2\omega\sin 2\omega t = -4\omega\sin\theta\,(1 + \cos\theta)$ with $\theta = \omega t$, using $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$. Maximize $f(\theta) = 4\omega\sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta)$: setting $\frac{df}{d\theta} = 4\omega(\cos\theta + \cos 2\theta) = 4\omega(2\cos^2\theta + \cos\theta - 1) = 0$ gives $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}$ (the other root $\cos\theta = -1$ gives $v = 0$). At $\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}$: $\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $|v|_{\max} = 4\omega\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) = 3\sqrt{3}\,\omega \approx 5.2\,\omega$ — choice B. Boundary check: at $\theta = \pi/2$, $|v| = 4\omega$, smaller than $3\sqrt{3}\omega$, confirming the interior maximum.

questions.question: A uniform wire of length $L$ and resistance $R$ is bent into an equilateral triangle, and its two end-points, which now meet at one vertex, are connected to an ideal voltage source of emf $E$. What current $I$ does the source deliver?
questions.hint: The joined ends split the loop into a one-side branch and a two-side branch in parallel across the source.
questions.solution: Concept: resistors in parallel. The two terminals (the joined ends) divide the closed triangle into two branches connected between the same pair of nodes: one side, of length $L/3$ and resistance $R/3$, and the remaining two sides together, of resistance $2R/3$. Their parallel equivalent is $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{(R/3)(2R/3)}{R/3 + 2R/3} = \frac{2R^2/9}{R} = \frac{2R}{9}$, so $I = \frac{E}{R_{\mathrm{eq}}} = \frac{9E}{2R}$ — choice B. Sanity check: $R_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2R/9$ is smaller than either branch alone, so the current must exceed $3E/R$; indeed $9/2 = 4.5 > 3$.

questions.question: A point charge of mass $m = 2\,\mathrm{kg}$ and charge $q = 4\,\mathrm{C}$ hangs from a string of length $L = 6\,\mathrm{m}$ in the Earth's gravitational field ($g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$). A uniform horizontal electric field of strength $E = \sqrt{11}\,\mathrm{N/C}$ is also present. The charge is displaced slightly from its (new) equilibrium position and released. Find the frequency of the small oscillations.
questions.hint: Combine gravity and the constant electric force into one effective 'gravity' vector; the small-oscillation pendulum formula then applies unchanged.
questions.solution: Gravity $mg$ (down) and the constant electric force $qE$ (horizontal) add to a single constant force. A pendulum under a constant net force behaves exactly like a simple pendulum in an effective gravity $g_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + (qE/m)^2}$, with equilibrium along that effective field. Here $qE/m = (4\sqrt{11})/2 = 2\sqrt{11}$, so $g_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{10^2 + (2\sqrt{11})^2} = \sqrt{100 + 44} = \sqrt{144} = 12\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The pendulum frequency is $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g_{\mathrm{eff}}/L} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{12/6} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.225\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (period $\approx 4.44$ s; angular frequency $\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{rad/s}$). Limit check: with $E = 0$ this reduces to the ordinary $\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{g/L} \approx 0.205$ Hz, close to our value since $g_{\mathrm{eff}} = 12 \approx g$.

questions.question: A hollow cylinder contains a monatomic ideal gas and is closed at the top by a movable piston. The only forces on the piston are the atmospheric pressure, the gas pressure and the piston's weight, so the gas pressure stays constant at $P_0$. If heat $Q$ is supplied slowly to the gas (heat capacities of cylinder and piston negligible), what is the change in volume of the gas?
questions.hint: The free piston fixes the pressure, so use $Q = nC_P\Delta T$ with the monatomic $C_P$ and convert $\Delta T$ to $\Delta V$ via the ideal-gas law.
questions.solution: Because the piston is free and moves slowly, the gas pressure remains $P_0$: the process is isobaric. First law: $Q = \Delta U + W$. For a monatomic ideal gas $\Delta U = \frac{3}{2}nR\,\Delta T$, and the expansion work is $W = P_0\,\Delta V = nR\,\Delta T$ (ideal-gas law at fixed $P_0$). Hence $Q = \frac{5}{2}nR\,\Delta T = \frac{5}{2}P_0\,\Delta V$, i.e. $Q = nC_P\Delta T$ with the monatomic $C_P = \frac{5}{2}R$. Solving, $\Delta V = \frac{2Q}{5P_0}$ — option (a). Sanity check: only $2/5$ of the heat goes into internal energy while $3/5$ leaves as work, so $\Delta V$ must be smaller than $Q/P_0$, which it is.

questions.question: A uniform disk of mass $M$ and radius $R$ is spinning with angular velocity $\omega$ about its symmetry axis when it is placed flat on a horizontal surface whose coefficient of (kinetic) friction is $\mu = 0.5$. How long will it take the disk to stop rotating?
questions.hint: Integrate the frictional torque over the disk face (average lever arm $2R/3$), then use $t = \omega/\alpha$ with $I = MR^2/2$.
questions.solution: Every element of the contact face slides, so each mass element $dm$ feels friction $\mu\,dm\,g$ opposing its local motion. The net retarding torque is $\tau = \int \mu g\,r\,dm$. With areal mass density $M/\pi R^2$ and $\int r\,dA = \int_0^R r\,(2\pi r\,dr) = \frac{2\pi R^3}{3}$, we get $\tau = \mu g\,\frac{M}{\pi R^2}\cdot\frac{2\pi R^3}{3} = \frac{2}{3}\mu M g R$ — friction effectively acts at the average radius $2R/3$. With $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$, the angular deceleration is constant: $\alpha = \tau/I = \frac{4\mu g}{3R}$. The disk stops after $t = \omega/\alpha = \frac{3\omega R}{4\mu g} = \frac{3\omega R}{4(0.5)g} = \frac{3\omega R}{2g}$ — option (b).

questions.question: For a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion, a graph of position ($x$, vertical axis) versus velocity ($v$, horizontal axis) is plotted. What is the shape of this graph?
questions.hint: Write $x$ and $v$ as sine and cosine of the same phase and eliminate $t$.
questions.solution: Take $x = A\sin(\omega t)$; then $v = A\omega\cos(\omega t)$. Eliminating the time using $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ gives $\left(\frac{x}{A}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{v}{A\omega}\right)^2 = 1$ — the canonical equation of an ellipse with semi-axes $A$ (along $x$) and $A\omega$ (along $v$). It degenerates to a circle only in the special case $A\omega = A$ (i.e. $\omega = 1$ with equal axis scalings), and it can never be a straight line because $x$ and $v$ are a quarter period out of phase — when $x$ is maximal, $v$ is zero. Answer: (c) elliptic.

questions.question: A planar figure shaped like the letter 'B' is bent from uniform wire: two equal semicircular arcs of radius $r$, each closed by its own straight diameter of length $2r$. The two diameters lie end-to-end along one common line — the straight 'spine' of the B, of total length $4r$ — and both arcs bulge to the same side. The figure is suspended freely from a pivot at the top end of the spine (its top-left corner). What angle does the straight spine make with the vertical in equilibrium?
questions.hint: Locate the centre of mass of the wire 'B' relative to the spine (a semicircular arc's CM sits $2r/\pi$ from its diameter), then note the pivot-to-CM line must end up vertical.
questions.solution: A freely suspended body hangs with its centre of mass (CM) vertically below the pivot. Put the spine on the $y$-axis from $y=0$ to $y=4r$, pivot at $(0,4r)$, arcs bulging in $+x$. Masses (wire of linear density $\lambda$): each arc has mass $\lambda\pi r$ with CM at distance $2r/\pi$ from its diameter, at heights $y = r$ and $y = 3r$; each diameter has mass $\lambda(2r)$ with CM on the spine ($x=0$). By symmetry the overall CM is at mid-height, $y_{\rm cm} = 2r$, and $x_{\rm cm} = \frac{2(\lambda\pi r)(2r/\pi)}{2\lambda\pi r + 4\lambda r} = \frac{4r^2}{2r(\pi+2)} = \frac{2r}{\pi+2} \approx 0.389r$. In equilibrium the line pivot-to-CM is vertical, so the spine tilts by $\theta$ with $\tan\theta = \frac{x_{\rm cm}}{4r - 2r} = \frac{1}{\pi+2} = 0.1945$, giving $\theta \approx 11.0^\circ$ — option (c).

questions.question: Two identical blocks, each of mass $m$, hang vertically in the Earth's gravitational field: the ceiling holds spring 1 (constant $k$), whose lower end carries the upper block; spring 2 (also constant $k$) connects the upper block to the lower block hanging beneath it. How much is each spring stretched when the system hangs in equilibrium?
questions.hint: Draw a free-body cut just under each spring and count the total weight hanging from that point.
questions.solution: Cut just below each spring and ask what weight hangs from it. Spring 2 supports only the lower block, so its tension is $T_2 = mg$ and Hooke's law gives the stretch $x_2 = T_2/k = mg/k$. Spring 1 supports both blocks — its tension equals the total weight below it — so $T_1 = 2mg$ and $x_1 = 2mg/k$. That is option (d). Equivalently, the upper block's free-body diagram reads $T_1 = mg + T_2 = mg + mg = 2mg$. Note the upper spring does not care how the load below is arranged, only its total weight; that is why the answer is not $mg/k$ for both springs.

questions.question: A solid hemisphere of uniform density has radius $R$. What is the distance of its centre of mass from the centre of its flat circular face (the sphere's centre), measured along the symmetry axis toward the curved surface?
questions.hint: Slice into thin disks parallel to the flat face and integrate $z\,dm$; the density cancels because only a ratio of integrals is needed.
questions.solution: Put the flat face in the plane $z = 0$ with the dome along $+z$ and slice the hemisphere into thin disks of thickness $dz$ at height $z$; each disk has mass $dm = \rho\pi(R^2 - z^2)\,dz$. Then $z_{\rm cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int_0^R z\,dm = \frac{\int_0^R z(R^2 - z^2)\,dz}{\int_0^R (R^2 - z^2)\,dz}$. The numerator is $\left[\frac{R^2z^2}{2} - \frac{z^4}{4}\right]_0^R = \frac{R^4}{4}$; the denominator is $R^3 - \frac{R^3}{3} = \frac{2R^3}{3}$. So $z_{\rm cm} = \frac{R^4/4}{2R^3/3} = \frac{3R}{8}$ — option (c). The CM is closer to the flat face than to the dome because the wider, heavier slices sit near $z = 0$.

questions.question: A spherical ball of proper volume $V$ moves with speed $v = 0.8c$ relative to an observer on the ground. What is the volume of the ball measured by that observer?
questions.hint: Only the dimension parallel to the motion contracts, by the factor $1/\gamma$.
questions.solution: Special relativity: lengths contract only along the direction of motion, by the factor $1/\gamma$ with $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.64} = 5/3$. The two transverse dimensions are unchanged, so the observed volume is $V' = V/\gamma = \frac{3}{5}V$ — option (b), the paper's marked answer. Recorded for completeness; excluded from the in-syllabus bank.
